scales.valence: -5 catastrophic harm to +5 transformative benefit; a rough estimate of how good or bad the consequence is for people and society if it happens, ignoring how likely it is
scales.probability: 0 to 1, chance the effect becomes material at societal scale by 2035; active effects count as already here and sit past 100%
scales.year: year the effect is or becomes material; 2024 and 2025 mean already observed
scales.evidence: measured = controlled study or large dataset; reported = documented incidents or vendor disclosures; projected = expert forecasts or capability evals; speculative = plausible mechanism, little direct data; drawn as the haze behind each glyph, tight when measured and widest when speculative
scales.stage: active = already a problem or benefit we are dealing with; emerging = early signs visible, not yet widespread; expected = not yet visible, year is the estimate

nodes.label: Basic research accelerates
nodes.summary: AlphaFold's protein structure prediction earned the 2024 chemistry Nobel[1], and one agent found a faster 4x4 complex matrix multiplication and improved bounds on open maths problems[2]. Such tools may speed up the basic research everything else builds on.

refs.title: Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2024, protein structure prediction
refs.finding: AlphaFold's structure prediction earned the 2024 chemistry Nobel.

refs.title: AlphaEvolve, Google DeepMind 2025
refs.finding: An agent found a faster 4x4 complex matrix multiplication and improved bounds on open maths problems.

limiters.evidence: AlphaEvolve gains came only on problems with machine-checkable scores; it improved the best result in about 20% of 50+ problems.

ref.title: AlphaEvolve, Google DeepMind 2025
ref.finding: On 50+ open maths problems it matched the best known result in 75% and improved it in 20%; it needs an automatic evaluator.

limiters.evidence: The 2025 AI Index notes infrastructure gaps such as electricity limit access across many African countries.

ref.title: The 2025 AI Index Report, Stanford HAI
ref.finding: GPT-3.5-level inference cost fell over 280-fold in two years; fewer than half of US CS teachers feel equipped to teach AI.

limiters.evidence: Real use stays thin: AI assisted only 1% to 5% of US work hours in late 2024.

ref.title: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI, NBER w32966
ref.finding: About 40% of US adults used generative AI by late 2024, but it assisted only 1% to 5% of work hours.

enablers.action: Release models and predictions openly
enablers.evidence: AlphaFold was published with methods in Nature, letting other labs build on it.

ref.title: Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold, Nature 2021
ref.finding: AlphaFold predicts protein structures with near-experimental accuracy for most proteins.

enablers.action: Fund shared compute for public researchers
enablers.evidence: Falling hardware costs of about 30% a year make shared public compute cheaper to provide.

ref.title: The 2025 AI Index Report, Stanford HAI
ref.finding: GPT-3.5-level inference cost fell over 280-fold in two years; fewer than half of US CS teachers feel equipped to teach AI.

enablers.action: Build benchmarks with automatic checking
enablers.evidence: AlphaEvolve's results came where a program could score each candidate.

ref.title: AlphaEvolve, Google DeepMind 2025
ref.finding: On 50+ open maths problems it matched the best known result in 75% and improved it in 20%; it needs an automatic evaluator.

precedents.parallel: A problem open since the 1850s fell only when mathematicians combined their own reasoning with a computer search no human could check by hand, much as AI search now reaches spaces people did not.
precedents.outcome: Appel and Haken reduced the problem to 1,936 configurations and used more than 1,000 hours of computer time; the proof was accepted only after long debate, and by 1997 others had cut it to 633 cases but still could not remove the computer step.

ref.title: Four-colour map problem (Britannica)
ref.finding: Proof needed 1,936 configurations and over 1,000 computer hours; mathematicians debated whether it counted as a proof.

precedents.parallel: An earlier machine learning system, built before the generative AI wave, cracked a basic science problem that had stalled for decades.
precedents.outcome: AlphaFold reached accuracy competitive with experimental structures in most CASP14 cases, against a field where only about 100,000 structures had ever been solved experimentally; it predicts structure but does not by itself explain folding or deliver drugs.

ref.title: Jumper et al. 2021, Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold, Nature
ref.finding: Structure prediction had been open for more than 50 years; AlphaFold was competitive with experiment in a majority of CASP14 cases.

nodes.label: Better, cheaper diagnosis
nodes.summary: One Swedish randomised screening trial found AI-supported mammogram reading detected 20% more cancers and cut screen-reading workload by 44%[1]. In one test on hard NEJM case records, orchestrated models solved 85% versus about 20% for physicians[2].

refs.title: MASAI trial, Lancet Oncology 2023
refs.finding: AI-supported screening detected 20% more cancers and cut screen-reading workload by 44%.

refs.title: Microsoft AI, MAI-DxO 2025
refs.finding: Orchestrated models solved 85% of hard NEJM case records versus about 20% for physicians in the test setup.

limiters.evidence: MASAI is one Swedish program; scale depends on screening services changing reading workflows.

ref.title: MASAI screening performance, Lancet Digital Health 2025
ref.finding: AI-supported screening found 29% more cancers than standard double reading in a randomised trial.

limiters.evidence: AMIE was tested in simulated text consults, not real clinical care.

ref.title: Towards conversational diagnostic artificial intelligence, Nature 2025
ref.finding: AMIE matched or beat primary care physicians in simulated text consultations, not real clinical practice.

limiters.evidence: WHO guidance calls for evaluation and accountability before health use of large models.

ref.title: Ethics and governance of AI for health: Guidance on large multi-modal models, WHO
ref.finding: WHO sets governance guidance for health use of large multi-modal models, including evaluation and accountability.

enablers.action: Run randomised screening trials before rollout
enablers.evidence: MASAI randomised women to AI-supported or standard reading and found 29% more cancers.

ref.title: MASAI screening performance, Lancet Digital Health 2025
ref.finding: AI-supported screening found 29% more cancers than standard double reading in a randomised trial.

enablers.action: Use AI as triage for one of two readers
enablers.evidence: AI-supported reading cut screen-reading workload by 44% without lowering safety.

ref.title: MASAI trial clinical safety analysis, Lancet Oncology 2023
ref.finding: AI-supported reading was safe versus double reading and cut screen-reading workload by 44%.

enablers.action: Require post-deployment monitoring of health AI
enablers.evidence: WHO recommends ongoing evaluation and accountability for large models in health.

ref.title: Ethics and governance of AI for health: Guidance on large multi-modal models, WHO
ref.finding: WHO sets governance guidance for health use of large multi-modal models, including evaluation and accountability.

precedents.parallel: Software that flagged suspicious areas on mammograms was paid for and adopted across US screening on the promise that it would find more cancers.
precedents.outcome: Across about 625,000 screening exams from 2003 to 2009, sensitivity was 85.3% with CAD and 87.3% without and specificity was unchanged, while the tool cost an estimated $400 million a year; older CAD was much weaker than modern models, so this is a warning about adoption without proof, not proof that AI reading fails.

ref.title: Lehman et al. 2015, Diagnostic Accuracy of Digital Screening Mammography With and Without Computer-Aided Detection, JAMA Internal Medicine
ref.finding: CAD did not improve sensitivity or specificity; in radiologists who read both ways, sensitivity was lower with CAD.

precedents.parallel: A pre-generative AI system was cleared to diagnose diabetic eye disease in primary care without a specialist reading the image, the same promise of cheaper diagnosis at the point of care.
precedents.outcome: In a prospective trial at 10 US primary care sites with 900 enrolled patients, it reached 87.2% sensitivity and 90.7% specificity and became the first FDA-authorised autonomous AI diagnostic; the study was funded by the maker.

ref.title: Abramoff et al. 2018, Pivotal trial of an autonomous AI-based diagnostic system for detection of diabetic retinopathy in primary care offices, npj Digital Medicine
ref.finding: Sensitivity 87.2% and specificity 90.7% in 819 analysable participants; first FDA-authorised autonomous AI diagnostic.

nodes.label: A personal tutor for every student
nodes.summary: Carefully designed AI tutors have beaten classroom teaching in two early trials. In one study, Harvard physics students learned more than twice as much in less time[1]; a World Bank pilot in Nigeria matched well over a year of typical schooling in six weeks[2].

refs.title: Kestin et al., Scientific Reports 2025
refs.finding: Harvard physics students learned more than twice as much in less time with an AI tutor than in active-learning class.

refs.title: World Bank, Nigeria pilot 2025
refs.finding: Six weeks of after-school GPT-4 tutoring produced learning gains equal to well over a year of typical schooling.

limiters.evidence: Students using plain GPT-4 did worse once AI was removed.

ref.title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, PNAS 2025
ref.finding: Students with plain GPT-4 did better in practice but worse once AI was removed; hint-only guardrails mitigated it.

limiters.evidence: Only 27% of people in low-income countries are online.

ref.title: ITU Facts and Figures 2024: Internet use
ref.finding: 2.6 billion people, a third of the world, are offline; only 27% use the internet in low-income countries.

limiters.evidence: Fewer than half of US computer science teachers feel equipped to teach AI.

ref.title: The 2025 AI Index Report, Stanford HAI
ref.finding: GPT-3.5-level inference cost fell over 280-fold in two years; fewer than half of US CS teachers feel equipped to teach AI.

limiters.limit: unequal access to paid AI plans
limiters.evidence: 2.6 billion people are offline, and the best models sit behind paid tiers in many markets.

ref.title: ITU Facts and Figures 2024: Internet use
ref.finding: 2.6 billion people, a third of the world, are offline; only 27% use the internet in low-income countries.

enablers.action: Design tutors to give hints, not answers
enablers.evidence: Teacher-designed hint prompts mitigated the learning loss in a high school trial.

ref.title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, PNAS 2025
ref.finding: Students with plain GPT-4 did better in practice but worse once AI was removed; hint-only guardrails mitigated it.

enablers.action: Pair AI tutoring with teacher guidance
enablers.evidence: A teacher-guided six-week program in Nigeria gave gains of about 0.3 standard deviations.

ref.title: From chalkboards to chatbots: Transforming learning in Nigeria, World Bank
ref.finding: A six-week teacher-guided AI tutoring program in Edo State gave gains of about 0.3 standard deviations.

enablers.action: Run tutoring in school computer labs
enablers.evidence: The Nigeria pilot ran after school on school devices, not students' own phones.

ref.title: From chalkboards to chatbots: Transforming learning in Nigeria, World Bank
ref.finding: A six-week teacher-guided AI tutoring program in Edo State gave gains of about 0.3 standard deviations.

precedents.parallel: One-to-one tutoring was claimed to lift students two standard deviations, the same hope now placed on an AI tutor for every child.
precedents.outcome: The claim came from small three-week experiments that combined tutoring with mastery learning and was never replicated; a 2020 meta-analysis of 96 randomised tutoring studies found an average effect of 0.37 standard deviations.

ref.title: von Hippel 2024, Two-Sigma Tutoring: Separating Science Fiction from Science Fact, Education Next
ref.finding: Average effect across 96 randomised tutoring studies was 0.37 SD, far below Bloom's 2.0.

precedents.event: One Laptop per Child in Peru
precedents.parallel: Putting a learning device in every child's hands was expected to transform learning in low-income schools, the same bet as unguarded AI access.
precedents.outcome: A randomised evaluation in 318 rural schools raised computers per student from 0.12 to 1.18 but found no effect on maths or language test scores after 15 months; a laptop without tutoring design differs from a guarded AI tutor, which is the point.

ref.title: Cristia et al. 2017, Technology and Child Development: Evidence from the One Laptop per Child Program, AEJ: Applied Economics
ref.finding: No evidence of effects on maths and language test scores; inconclusive gains in general cognitive skills.

nodes.label: Assistive AI for disabled people
nodes.summary: Vision models can describe the world on demand for blind and low-vision people; Be My Eyes uses GPT-4 as a virtual volunteer that answers visual questions without waiting for a human[1].

refs.title: Be My Eyes with GPT-4, OpenAI
refs.finding: A virtual volunteer answers visual questions for blind users without waiting for a human.

limiters.evidence: Vision assistants need a data connection; 2.6 billion people are offline.

ref.title: ITU Facts and Figures 2024: Internet use
ref.finding: 2.6 billion people, a third of the world, are offline; only 27% use the internet in low-income countries.

limiters.evidence: WHO-style guidance warns large multi-modal models can produce confident but wrong outputs.

ref.title: Ethics and governance of AI for health: Guidance on large multi-modal models, WHO
ref.finding: WHO sets governance guidance for health use of large multi-modal models, including evaluation and accountability.

limiters.evidence: Translation and speech models cover at most a few hundred of 7,000 languages.

ref.title: Scaling neural machine translation to 200 languages, Nature 2024
ref.finding: NLLB covers 200 languages but quality depends on scarce parallel data for low-resource languages.

enablers.action: Keep a human volunteer fallback
enablers.evidence: Be My Eyes pairs over 1.1 million users with volunteers alongside its AI.

ref.title: Be My Eyes
ref.finding: The service reports over 1.1 million blind and low-vision users and free, unlimited calls.

enablers.action: Offer core assistive features free
enablers.counters: unequal access to paid AI plans
enablers.evidence: Be My Eyes reports free, unlimited calls for blind and low-vision users.

ref.title: Be My Eyes
ref.finding: The service reports over 1.1 million blind and low-vision users and free, unlimited calls.

enablers.action: Fund low-resource language speech models
enablers.evidence: SeamlessM4T added speech translation for up to 100 languages.

ref.title: Joint speech and text machine translation for up to 100 languages, Nature 2025
ref.finding: SeamlessM4T translates speech and text across up to 100 languages, far fewer than the world's 7,000.

precedents.parallel: Text access to spoken television for deaf and hard-of-hearing people was scaled across all broadcasters, as AI description now scales visual access for blind people.
precedents.outcome: Captioning became a legal duty for distributors, and the FCC had to add quality rules requiring captions to be accurate, synchronous, complete and properly placed, with exemptions such as 2 a.m. to 6 a.m. programming; the source gives no measure of uptake or benefit, and scale alone did not guarantee quality.

ref.title: Closed Captioning on Television (FCC consumer guide)
ref.finding: FCC rules require captions to be accurate, synchronous, complete and properly placed, with defined exemptions.

nodes.label: Language barriers fall
nodes.summary: Machine translation is reaching low-resource languages: one model translates between 200 languages, with large quality gains for low-resource ones[1].

refs.title: NLLB Team, Nature 2024
refs.finding: One model translates between 200 languages, with large quality gains for low-resource ones.

limiters.evidence: NLLB reaches 200 languages; the world has over 7,000.

ref.title: Scaling neural machine translation to 200 languages, Nature 2024
ref.finding: NLLB covers 200 languages but quality depends on scarce parallel data for low-resource languages.

limiters.evidence: NLLB authors note quality depends on parallel data that low-resource languages lack.

ref.title: Scaling neural machine translation to 200 languages, Nature 2024
ref.finding: NLLB covers 200 languages but quality depends on scarce parallel data for low-resource languages.

limiters.evidence: 2.6 billion people are offline, many in multilingual low-income regions.

ref.title: ITU Facts and Figures 2024: Internet use
ref.finding: 2.6 billion people, a third of the world, are offline; only 27% use the internet in low-income countries.

enablers.action: Publish open multilingual models and test sets
enablers.evidence: NLLB was released openly with evaluation data across 200 languages.

ref.title: Scaling neural machine translation to 200 languages, Nature 2024
ref.finding: NLLB covers 200 languages but quality depends on scarce parallel data for low-resource languages.

enablers.action: Extend speech-to-speech to more languages
enablers.evidence: SeamlessM4T handles speech and text for up to 100 languages.

ref.title: Joint speech and text machine translation for up to 100 languages, Nature 2025
ref.finding: SeamlessM4T translates speech and text across up to 100 languages, far fewer than the world's 7,000.

enablers.action: Collect community data for low-resource languages
enablers.evidence: NLLB shows quality tracks the volume of available parallel data.

ref.title: Scaling neural machine translation to 200 languages, Nature 2024
ref.finding: NLLB covers 200 languages but quality depends on scarce parallel data for low-resource languages.

precedents.parallel: A decade of funding after early demos ended in an official verdict that machine translation was not delivering, the bust side of today's claims that language barriers are falling.
precedents.outcome: In 1966 ALPAC found no immediate or predictable prospect of useful machine translation, ending substantial US funding for about twenty years after roughly $12-20 million had been spent.

ref.title: Hutchins 1996, ALPAC: the (in)famous report, MT News International
ref.finding: ALPAC ended substantial US MT funding for some twenty years; US spending was nearer $12-13 million than the $20 million ALPAC stated.

precedents.parallel: The switch from phrase-based to neural translation, before the generative AI wave, was the first large measured jump in machine translation quality.
precedents.outcome: In human side-by-side tests on isolated simple sentences, the neural system reduced translation errors by an average of 60% against the phrase-based production system; tests on simple sentences overstate gains for hard text and low-resource languages.

ref.title: Wu et al. 2016, Google's Neural Machine Translation System, arXiv
ref.finding: GNMT reduced translation errors by an average of 60% versus Google's phrase-based system.

precedents.parallel: A tiny public demo was read as proof that general translation was near, the same gap between demo and coverage that low-resource language claims face now.
precedents.outcome: The system handled roughly 250 words with six grammar rules; the publicity far outran the capability, which Hutchins describes as raising hopes that high-quality automatic translation was imminent.

ref.title: Hutchins 2004, The Georgetown-IBM experiment demonstrated in January 1954, AMTA proceedings
ref.finding: A small demonstration of about 250 words and six rules raised expectations of imminent high-quality MT.

nodes.label: Non-technical people build software
nodes.summary: People can now build software by describing what they want and accepting the output without reading the code, a practice called vibe coding[1]. This may let people with no programming background explore ideas, build tools and automate their own work.

refs.title: Andrej Karpathy coins vibe coding, Feb 2025
refs.finding: Describes building software by prompting and accepting output without reading the code.

refs.title: Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025, AI
refs.finding: 84% of respondents use or plan to use AI tools; trust in their accuracy fell.

limiters.evidence: Consultants using AI on a task outside its frontier gave worse answers than those without it.

ref.title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier, HBS Working Paper
ref.finding: In 758 BCG consultants, AI raised quality inside its capability frontier but made answers worse on a task outside it.

limiters.evidence: Users with an AI assistant wrote less secure code and felt more confident about it.

ref.title: Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?, arXiv 2211.03622
ref.finding: Users with an AI assistant wrote less secure code and were more confident it was secure.

limiters.limit: unequal access to paid AI plans
limiters.evidence: Late 2024 adoption was about 40% of US adults, with heavier use among the better educated.

ref.title: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI, NBER w32966
ref.finding: About 40% of US adults used generative AI by late 2024, but it assisted only 1% to 5% of work hours.

enablers.action: Teach checking and prompting at work
enablers.evidence: The EU AI Act requires deployers to ensure staff AI literacy.

ref.title: EU AI Act, Article 4: AI literacy
ref.finding: Providers and deployers must ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among staff who use AI.

enablers.action: Ship secure defaults in AI coding tools
enablers.evidence: CISA's Secure by Design pledge asks makers to make security the default.

ref.title: Secure by Design, CISA
ref.finding: Over 200 software makers signed a voluntary pledge to ship secure defaults.

enablers.action: Rely on falling model prices
enablers.counters: unequal access to paid AI plans
enablers.evidence: The price of a fixed capability fell 9x to 900x per year.

ref.title: LLM inference prices have fallen rapidly but unequally across tasks, Epoch AI
ref.finding: The price of a fixed capability level fell 9x to 900x per year depending on the task.

precedents.parallel: Personal computer spreadsheets let millions of people without programming training build their own tools, as describing software to an AI does now.
precedents.outcome: An audit of 50 operational spreadsheets found errors in 0.9% to 1.8% of formula cells, and only 7 of the 50 were free of errors that produced wrong results, an 86% spreadsheet error rate; spreadsheets still became core business tools.

ref.title: Powell, Baker and Lawson 2009, Errors in Operational Spreadsheets, Journal of Organizational and End User Computing
ref.finding: 43 of 50 audited operational spreadsheets contained errors that produced wrong results.

precedents.parallel: An influential result built in an end-user tool carried an error nobody checked, the risk when non-specialists build software that others rely on.
precedents.outcome: Reanalysis found coding errors, selective exclusions and unusual weighting; corrected average growth for countries with debt above 90% of GDP was 2.2%, not the published -0.1%. The authors were economists, not novices, so this shows unchecked tools, not inexperience.

ref.title: Herndon, Ash and Pollin 2013, Does High Public Debt Consistently Stifle Economic Growth? A Critique of Reinhart and Rogoff, PERI
ref.finding: Corrected growth for high-debt countries was 2.2%, not -0.1%, after coding errors and exclusions were fixed.

nodes.label: Automated vulnerability finding and patching
nodes.summary: Agents now find previously unknown bugs in widely used code and patch them: one found an exploitable memory-safety bug in SQLite before release[1], DARPA challenge finalists patched real open-source flaws automatically[2], and CodeMender upstreamed dozens of fixes[3]. This may shrink the window defenders leave open.

refs.title: Project Zero, From Naptime to Big Sleep 2024
refs.finding: An LLM agent found an exploitable memory-safety bug in SQLite before release.

refs.title: DARPA AI Cyber Challenge results 2025
refs.finding: Finalist systems found and patched synthetic and real vulnerabilities in open-source code automatically.

refs.title: Google DeepMind, CodeMender 2025
refs.finding: An agent upstreamed dozens of security fixes to open-source projects.

limiters.evidence: GPT-4 exploited 87% of 15 known vulnerabilities given the CVE text.

ref.title: LLM Agents can Autonomously Exploit One-day Vulnerabilities, arXiv 2404.08144
ref.finding: GPT-4 exploited 87% of 15 known vulnerabilities given the CVE text, but only 7% without it.

limiters.evidence: AIxCC systems found 86% of synthetic vulnerabilities but patched only 68%.

ref.title: DARPA AI Cyber Challenge final results
ref.finding: Finalist systems found 86% of 63 synthetic vulnerabilities and patched 68%; tools were released open source.

limiters.evidence: Big Sleep's SQLite fix was fast because the maintainers responded the same day; many projects lack that capacity.

ref.title: From Naptime to Big Sleep, Google Project Zero 2024
ref.finding: An LLM agent found an exploitable SQLite bug that 150 CPU-hours of fuzzing missed; it was fixed the same day.

enablers.action: Open-source automated bug-finding systems
enablers.evidence: AIxCC finalists released their cyber reasoning systems as open source.

ref.title: DARPA AI Cyber Challenge final results
ref.finding: Finalist systems found 86% of 63 synthetic vulnerabilities and patched 68%; tools were released open source.

enablers.action: Run variant analysis on new commits
enablers.evidence: Big Sleep found a SQLite bug by checking a recent commit for missed variants.

ref.title: From Naptime to Big Sleep, Google Project Zero 2024
ref.finding: An LLM agent found an exploitable SQLite bug that 150 CPU-hours of fuzzing missed; it was fixed the same day.

enablers.action: Mandate vulnerability handling for vendors
enablers.evidence: The Cyber Resilience Act sets vulnerability handling duties for digital products.

ref.title: Cyber Resilience Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/2847
ref.finding: Sets mandatory cybersecurity and vulnerability handling duties for products with digital elements sold in the EU.

precedents.parallel: Machines competed to find and patch software flaws on their own, the same promise now made for AI agents.
precedents.outcome: Seven finalists from over 100 teams ran for nearly 12 hours; Mayhem won the $2 million prize, and DARPA's programme manager said he did not expect it to finish well when it was invited to play human experts at DEF CON.

ref.title: DARPA, Cyber Grand Challenge winners (2016)
ref.finding: Mayhem won the first all-machine hacking tournament; DARPA expected it to struggle against human experts.

precedents.parallel: Automated testing at scale finds real bugs in widely used open-source code and feeds fixes back, a pre-LLM version of automated vulnerability finding.
precedents.outcome: By May 2025 OSS-Fuzz had helped identify and fix over 13,000 vulnerabilities and 50,000 bugs across 1,000 projects; it finds bugs, while fixing still mostly falls on maintainers.

ref.title: google/oss-fuzz README
ref.finding: Over 13,000 vulnerabilities and 50,000 bugs identified and fixed across 1,000 projects as of May 2025.

nodes.label: Hardened global networks
nodes.summary: If defenders adopt automated auditing faster than attackers adopt automated exploitation, critical software could become much harder to breach; AI agents already find and fix real bugs[4][5]. Experts disagree which side AI will favour, so today this is a race, not a result[1].

refs.title: International AI Safety Report 2025
refs.finding: Experts disagree whether AI will favour cyber offence or defence; evidence so far is mixed.

refs.title: DARPA AI Cyber Challenge results 2025
refs.finding: Tools are being open-sourced for critical infrastructure maintainers.

refs.title: AI 2040 (PDF)
refs.finding: Scenario spends on the order of $1T a year, 0.2% of the world economy, hardening the world against AI-enabled threats.

refs.title: Project Zero, From Naptime to Big Sleep 2024
refs.finding: An LLM agent found an exploitable memory-safety bug in SQLite before release.

refs.title: Google DeepMind, CodeMender 2025
refs.finding: An agent upstreamed dozens of security fixes to open-source projects.

limiters.evidence: GPT-4 exploited 87% of known one-day vulnerabilities given the CVE text.

ref.title: LLM Agents can Autonomously Exploit One-day Vulnerabilities, arXiv 2404.08144
ref.finding: GPT-4 exploited 87% of 15 known vulnerabilities given the CVE text, but only 7% without it.

limiters.evidence: CISA's Secure by Design pledge is voluntary, with about 200 signers.

ref.title: Secure by Design, CISA
ref.finding: Over 200 software makers signed a voluntary pledge to ship secure defaults.

limiters.evidence: AI assistant users wrote less secure code than those without one.

ref.title: Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?, arXiv 2211.03622
ref.finding: Users with an AI assistant wrote less secure code and were more confident it was secure.

enablers.action: Make secure-by-design a legal duty
enablers.evidence: The Cyber Resilience Act turns product security into a legal requirement in the EU.

ref.title: Cyber Resilience Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/2847
ref.finding: Sets mandatory cybersecurity and vulnerability handling duties for products with digital elements sold in the EU.

enablers.action: Fund automated auditing of critical open source
enablers.evidence: AIxCC was run to find and patch flaws in software critical infrastructure depends on.

ref.title: DARPA AI Cyber Challenge final results
ref.finding: Finalist systems found 86% of 63 synthetic vulnerabilities and patched 68%; tools were released open source.

enablers.action: Ship secure defaults at no extra cost
enablers.evidence: CISA asks makers to include MFA and logging by default.

ref.title: Secure by Design, CISA
ref.finding: Over 200 software makers signed a voluntary pledge to ship secure defaults.

precedents.parallel: The first network-wide attack showed that defence depends on getting fixes deployed, not only on knowing the flaws, the core of the attacker-defender race.
precedents.outcome: The worm reportedly infected up to 6,000 of the 60,000 computers on the Internet within hours; GAO found problems in developing, distributing and installing fixes, and later intrusions used a known hole whose fix had been supplied but not installed.

ref.title: GAO 1989, Computer Security: Virus Highlights Need for Improved Internet Management (IMTEC-89-57)
ref.finding: Up to 6,000 computers infected; fixes were slow to develop, distribute and install.

precedents.parallel: A flaw was publicly known and a patch existed, yet the system stayed exposed, showing that automated finding does not harden networks unless patching keeps up.
precedents.outcome: Attackers accessed personal data of at least 145.5 million people through a portal where the Apache Struts vulnerability had not been identified when patches were installed across the company.

ref.title: GAO 2018, Data Protection: Actions Taken by Equifax and Federal Agencies in Response to the 2017 Breach (GAO-18-559)
ref.finding: At least 145.5 million people affected; the vulnerable portal was missed during company-wide patching.

nodes.label: Productivity gains, largest for novices
nodes.summary: In one field study of customer-support agents, AI help raised issues resolved per hour by 14% on average and 34% for novices, narrowing skill gaps[1]. In one trial, experienced open-source developers were 19% slower with AI while believing they were faster[2].

refs.title: Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond, Generative AI at Work, NBER w31161
refs.finding: Support agents resolved 14% more issues per hour on average, 34% for novices.

refs.title: METR, early-2025 developer study
refs.finding: Experienced open-source developers were 19% slower with AI while believing they were faster.

limiters.evidence: Experienced developers were 19% slower with AI tools in an RCT.

ref.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity, METR
ref.finding: Experienced developers were 19% slower with AI tools while believing they were faster.

limiters.evidence: Danish data show null effects on earnings and hours two years after ChatGPT.

ref.title: Still Waters, Rapid Currents, NBER w33777
ref.finding: Danish data show precise null effects of chatbots on earnings and hours two years after ChatGPT.

limiters.evidence: Consultants were worse with AI on a task outside its capability frontier.

ref.title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier, HBS Working Paper
ref.finding: In 758 BCG consultants, AI raised quality inside its capability frontier but made answers worse on a task outside it.

enablers.action: Target AI assistance at new workers
enablers.evidence: Novices gained 34% versus 14% on average in a support centre.

ref.title: Generative AI at Work, NBER w31161
ref.finding: An AI assistant raised support agent productivity 14% on average and 34% for novices, with little gain for experts.

enablers.action: Train staff on where AI fails
enablers.evidence: The EU AI Act requires AI literacy for staff of deployers.

ref.title: EU AI Act, Article 4: AI literacy
ref.finding: Providers and deployers must ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among staff who use AI.

enablers.action: Redesign workflows, not only add tools
enablers.evidence: AI assisted only 1% to 5% of US work hours despite 40% adoption.

ref.title: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI, NBER w32966
ref.finding: About 40% of US adults used generative AI by late 2024, but it assisted only 1% to 5% of work hours.

precedents.parallel: New machines let less experienced workers run production, as AI assistants now raise novices' output.
precedents.outcome: Weavers learned much of their skill on the job; mechanisation removed some tasks but raised the returns to skill on the rest, and wages eventually rose while inequality fell. Unlike the AI data, the gains came through learning over years, not instant output boosts.

ref.title: Bessen 2011, Was Mechanization De-Skilling? The Origins of Task-Biased Technical Change
ref.finding: Mechanisation was task-biased; weavers learned substantially on the job and wages eventually rose.

nodes.label: Jevons paradox: more work, not less
nodes.summary: As AI makes tasks cheaper, demand and expectations may grow faster than time is saved. In one Upwork survey, 77% of employees using AI said it had added to their workload[1]; one Danish registry study found near-zero effects on earnings and hours[2].

refs.title: Upwork Research Institute 2024
refs.finding: 77% of employees using AI said it had added to their workload.

refs.title: Humlum and Vestergaard, Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects, NBER w33777
refs.finding: Danish registry data across 11 exposed occupations shows near-zero effects on earnings and hours.

refs.title: Acemoglu, The Simple Macroeconomics of AI, NBER w32487
refs.finding: Estimates only about 0.7% total factor productivity gain over ten years.

refs.title: Anthropic Economic Index
refs.finding: Tracks which tasks people hand to AI versus do with it, by occupation.

nodes.control_note: If tasks get cheaper, demand for them grows; that is the same mechanism as the productivity gain. Policy can only decide who captures the saved time.

actions.action: Set workload targets when AI is introduced
actions.evidence: Employees report AI adds to workload under existing models, while flexible arrangements went with less burnout; this is survey data, not causal.

ref.title: Upwork Research Institute, From Burnout to Balance: AI-Enhanced Work Models, 2024
ref.finding: Most employees using AI said it added to their workload, while freelancers on flexible models reported less burnout.

actions.action: Track hours and earnings, not only output
actions.evidence: Danish register data show null effects on hours and earnings, which lets policy see whether time savings reach workers.

ref.title: Humlum and Vestergaard, NBER w33777
ref.finding: Two years after ChatGPT, earnings and hours effects are precise nulls, ruling out effects above 2%.

precedents.parallel: Cheaper use of a resource raised total demand for it, the same mechanism by which cheaper tasks may grow total work.
precedents.outcome: Jevons argued that more efficient steam engines would not reduce coal demand but speed depletion; the rebound depends on how elastic demand is, so it is not automatic.

ref.title: W. Stanley Jevons, The Coal Question, 1865 (Yale Energy History)
ref.finding: Jevons held that efficiency in consumption would not reduce demand for energy.

precedents.parallel: Automation of a core task was expected to remove jobs but changed the economics so the work grew in other forms.
precedents.outcome: Tellers needed per urban branch fell from 20 to 13 between 1988 and 2004, yet teller jobs did not decrease as ATMs spread, because cheaper branches meant more of them.

ref.title: Bessen 2015, Toil and Technology, Finance and Development (IMF)
ref.finding: Teller jobs did not fall as ATMs rolled out; tellers per branch fell from 20 to 13.

precedents.parallel: Labour-saving machines in the home were expected to free time, a close parallel to AI saving time at work.
precedents.outcome: Australian 1997 time-use data found domestic technology rarely reduced women's unpaid work and sometimes increased it; Gershuny disputed the method, so the evidence is contested.

ref.title: Bittman, Rice and Wajcman 2004, Appliances and their impact, British Journal of Sociology
ref.finding: Domestic technology rarely reduces women's unpaid working time and produces some increases.

nodes.label: Universal basic income
nodes.summary: Basic income looks workable but modest: in one US study, $1,000 a month for three years cut work by about 1.3 hours a week[1], and health effects were small[2]. Political support for a universal scheme is unproven.

refs.title: Vivalt et al., Employment Effects of a Guaranteed Income, NBER w32719
refs.finding: $1,000 a month for three years cut recipients' work by about 1.3 hours a week, with no clear gains in job quality.

refs.title: OpenResearch Unconditional Cash Study
refs.finding: Recipients spent more on basic needs and support for others; health effects were small.

refs.title: AI 2027: race ending
refs.finding: Displaced humans live on an incredibly luxurious universal basic income by 2029.

refs.title: AI 2027 takeoff forecast
refs.finding: Median about one year from superhuman coder to superintelligence, with wide error margins.

refs.title: AI Futures Project, Q2.5 2026 Timelines Update
refs.finding: August 2026 superintelligence medians: Kokotajlo March 2029, Lifland July 2033.

refs.title: Economics of Plan A (AI 2040)
refs.finding: Permit revenue paid as a citizen's dividend of about $1M per person a year in 2035.

limiters.evidence: A US trial paid $1,000 a month to 1,000 people for three years, a cost that scales poorly to everyone.

ref.title: The Employment Effects of a Guaranteed Income, NBER w32719
ref.finding: $1,000 a month for three years cut work by 1 to 2 hours a week, with leisure the largest gain.

limiters.evidence: Recipients worked 1 to 2 hours a week less.

ref.title: The Employment Effects of a Guaranteed Income, NBER w32719
ref.finding: $1,000 a month for three years cut work by 1 to 2 hours a week, with leisure the largest gain.

limiters.evidence: No country runs a universal scheme; evidence comes from trials only.

ref.title: Universal Basic Income: Short-Term Results from a Long-Term Experiment in Kenya
ref.finding: UBI in 295 villages expanded local enterprise; labor supply did not fall but shifted to self-employment.

enablers.action: Run long-term randomised trials
enablers.evidence: A 12-year UBI trial in Kenya covers 295 villages.

ref.title: Universal Basic Income: Short-Term Results from a Long-Term Experiment in Kenya
ref.finding: UBI in 295 villages expanded local enterprise; labor supply did not fall but shifted to self-employment.

enablers.action: Consider lump-sum transfers
enablers.evidence: In Kenya, lump sums had similar or larger effects than streams of the same value.

ref.title: Universal Basic Income: Short-Term Results from a Long-Term Experiment in Kenya
ref.finding: UBI in 295 villages expanded local enterprise; labor supply did not fall but shifted to self-employment.

enablers.action: Watch AI labour effects before designing schemes
enablers.evidence: Earnings and hours effects of chatbots were near zero so far in Denmark.

ref.title: Still Waters, Rapid Currents, NBER w33777
ref.finding: Danish data show precise null effects of chatbots on earnings and hours two years after ChatGPT.

precedents.parallel: A universal, unconditional cash payment has run for decades, the closest real case of a basic income.
precedents.outcome: The dividend had no effect on employment and raised part-time work by 1.8 percentage points (17 percent); it is a few thousand dollars a year at most, far below a living income.

ref.title: Jones and Marinescu 2022, The Labor Market Impacts of Universal and Permanent Cash Transfers, AEJ: Economic Policy
ref.finding: No effect on employment; part-time work rose 1.8 percentage points.

precedents.parallel: A national randomised trial tested unconditional payments to unemployed people as a step toward a simpler, universal system.
precedents.outcome: Employment improved slightly more than in the control group and recipients reported better wellbeing and less mental strain, but a 2018 activation reform muddied the employment result and it did not help those already in hard situations.

ref.title: Kela and Finnish Government, Finland's Basic Income Experiment 2017-2018 results
ref.finding: Slightly better employment and better perceived wellbeing; interpretation complicated by the 2018 activation model.

precedents.parallel: A guaranteed annual income open to a whole town is the main community-level test of universal cash.
precedents.outcome: Forget reported hospitalisations fell 8.5% relative to a comparison group, but Green's 2021 reanalysis found pre-trends that point to higher hospital use, so health benefits are unproven.

ref.title: Green 2021, A Reanalysis of 'The Town with No Poverty'
ref.finding: After accounting for pre-trends, the data point to an increase in hospital use, reversing Forget's 2011 conclusion.

nodes.label: Decompiling legacy software
nodes.summary: Models that turn binaries back into readable source could help keep abandoned software, games and industrial systems alive and interoperable. In one study, open models recompiled and passed tests on far more decompiled functions than prior tools[1].

refs.title: Tan et al., LLM4Decompile 2024
refs.finding: Open models recompile and pass tests on far more decompiled functions than prior tools.

limiters.evidence: EU law allows decompilation only for interoperability and only of the needed parts.

ref.title: Directive 2009/24/EC on the legal protection of computer programs, Article 6
ref.finding: Decompilation without the rightholder's consent is allowed only when needed for interoperability and limited to the needed parts.

limiters.evidence: LLM4Decompile doubled re-executability over baselines but much output still fails.

ref.title: LLM4Decompile: Decompiling Binary Code with Large Language Models, arXiv 2403.05286
ref.finding: Open models doubled re-executability of decompiled code over GPT-4o and Ghidra on benchmarks, still far from perfect.

limiters.evidence: Recovered code needs experts to test, since benchmarks show many failed functions.

ref.title: LLM4Decompile: Decompiling Binary Code with Large Language Models, arXiv 2403.05286
ref.finding: Open models doubled re-executability of decompiled code over GPT-4o and Ghidra on benchmarks, still far from perfect.

enablers.action: Release open decompilation models
enablers.evidence: LLM4Decompile models were released openly for reuse.

ref.title: LLM4Decompile: Decompiling Binary Code with Large Language Models, arXiv 2403.05286
ref.finding: Open models doubled re-executability of decompiled code over GPT-4o and Ghidra on benchmarks, still far from perfect.

enablers.action: Widen preservation exceptions in copyright law
enablers.evidence: The EU directive has an interoperability exception but none for preservation.

ref.title: Directive 2009/24/EC on the legal protection of computer programs, Article 6
ref.finding: Decompilation without the rightholder's consent is allowed only when needed for interoperability and limited to the needed parts.

precedents.parallel: Turning object code back into readable source to achieve compatibility was ruled lawful, the legal footing that AI decompilation for interoperability would lean on.
precedents.outcome: The Ninth Circuit held that disassembly for a legitimate reason, when there is no other way to reach unprotected functional elements, is fair use; it did not cover copying the expressive code itself.

ref.title: Sega Enters. Ltd. v. Accolade, Inc., 977 F.2d 1510 (9th Cir. 1992), US Copyright Office Fair Use Index
ref.finding: Disassembly for a legitimate reason with no other means of access was fair use.

precedents.parallel: Reverse engineering a console BIOS let PlayStation games run on ordinary computers, the kind of afterlife decompilation gives old software.
precedents.outcome: The Ninth Circuit lifted the injunction and found Connectix's intermediate copies were fair use because the final emulator contained no infringing code.

ref.title: Sony Computer Entertainment v. Connectix Corp., 203 F.3d 596 (9th Cir. 2000), US Copyright Office Fair Use Index
ref.finding: Intermediate copying to build a non-infringing emulator was fair use.

nodes.label: Workslop
nodes.summary: Polished-looking AI output that lacks substance shifts work onto whoever receives it; in one survey of US desk workers, 40% had received such workslop in the past month, costing nearly two hours per incident[1].

refs.title: Niederhoffer et al., HBR 2025
refs.finding: 40% of surveyed US desk workers received workslop in the past month, costing nearly two hours per incident.

nodes.control_note: Workslop comes from how AI output is used and checked, not from the capability itself. Norms and review keep the benefit.

actions.action: Replace blanket AI mandates with task-specific norms
actions.evidence: The HBR authors link workslop to mandates without guidance; no trial of norms has been published.

ref.title: Niederhoffer et al., AI-Generated Workslop Is Destroying Productivity, HBR 2025
ref.finding: Mandated AI use without clear norms produces low-substance output that costs recipients time.

actions.action: Train staff on where AI fails
actions.evidence: In a field experiment, consultants using AI outside its frontier got the right answer less often, so knowing the frontier matters.

ref.title: Dell'Acqua et al., Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier, HBS Working Paper 24-013
ref.finding: Consultants using AI on a task outside its frontier were less likely to reach the correct answer than those without AI.

precedents.parallel: A polished slide compressed a key risk into vague bullets and shifted the work of finding it onto readers who never did, as hollow AI output does.
precedents.outcome: The Board found the slide buried that the debris was 640 times larger than the test data behind the model, and called the endemic use of PowerPoint instead of technical papers a sign of problematic technical communication at NASA; the cause was culture, not the tool alone.

ref.title: Columbia Accident Investigation Board Report, Volume 1, 'Engineering by Viewgraphs' (p. 191)
ref.finding: Key fact was at the bottom of the slide; the Board criticised PowerPoint briefings replacing technical papers.

nodes.label: AI slop overwhelms open-source maintainers
nodes.summary: Fabricated bug and security reports waste the scarce time of volunteer maintainers[1]. At curl, about a fifth of 2025 security reports were AI slop, and the share of valid reports fell to around 5%[1].

refs.title: Daniel Stenberg, Death by a thousand slops 2025
refs.finding: About a fifth of curl's 2025 security reports were AI slop and the valid rate fell to around 5%.

nodes.control_note: The same tools that find real bugs make fake reports cheap. Platform friction and reporter rules can cut most of the slop.

actions.action: Rate-limit and gate new reporter accounts
actions.evidence: Proposed by the Python Software Foundation security lead; no measured effect yet.

ref.title: Seth Larson, New era of slop security reports for open source, 2024
ref.finding: Calls on report platforms to rate-limit new accounts, remove volume incentives and require human review.

actions.action: Remove cash bounties that reward volume
actions.evidence: curl now states it has no bug bounty after slop reached about 20% of submissions; the effect on volume is not yet reported.

ref.title: curl, Vulnerability disclosure policy
ref.finding: Asks reporters not to paste AI-generated explanations and states there is no bug bounty.

actions.action: Publish slop examples and ban bad reporters
actions.evidence: curl published 21 examples, but Stenberg calls bans toothless because new accounts are free.

ref.title: Daniel Stenberg, Death by a thousand slops, 2025
ref.finding: About 20% of curl's 2025 security submissions were AI slop and only about 5% were real vulnerabilities.

precedents.parallel: Deliberately bad patches sent to Linux maintainers wasted reviewer time and forced a mass re-review, the same cost fabricated AI reports impose.
precedents.outcome: The Linux Foundation's Technical Advisory Board re-reviewed 435 commits, found 39 incorrect, and named reviewer and maintainer time as the resource in shortest supply; the bad patches themselves were all caught.

ref.title: Linux Foundation TAB 2021, Report on University of Minnesota Breach-of-Trust Incident
ref.finding: 435 commits re-reviewed, 39 found incorrect; the research wasted maintainers' scarce time.

precedents.parallel: A non-security bug was filed as a critical vulnerability, leaving the volunteer maintainer to fight a false alarm that spread worldwide.
precedents.outcome: NVD rated CVE-2020-19909 9.8 critical although curl had already judged the 2019 report not a security problem; MITRE declined to reject it. This is one maintainer's account, not a measured rate.

ref.title: Stenberg 2023, CVE-2020-19909 is everything that is wrong with CVEs
ref.finding: A known non-security bug was published as a 9.8 critical CVE; the rejection request was refused.

nodes.label: Kids cheat on homework
nodes.summary: Use for schoolwork is rising: one Pew survey found 26% of US teens used ChatGPT for schoolwork, double the 2023 share[1]. Unguarded use can lift homework scores and hurt exam scores, as in one Turkish trial[2] and one study of 26,800 Chinese secondary students[3].

refs.title: Pew Research Center, Jan 2025
refs.finding: 26% of US teens used ChatGPT for schoolwork, double the 2023 share.

refs.title: Bastani et al., Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, PNAS 2025
refs.finding: Students with plain GPT-4 practice access scored 17% worse on exams once access was removed.

refs.title: Strömberg, Lei and Wu, The generative AI learning penalty, CEPR 2026
refs.finding: Across 26,800 Chinese secondary students, AI raised homework scores 18% but cut monthly exam scores 20% within six months and entrance exam scores 18 to 24%.

refs.title: The Decoder on the same study
refs.finding: Losses concentrated among students who rushed their homework with AI.

nodes.control_note: The tool that tutors can also write the homework. Assessment design and guarded tutors reduce the harm but cannot stop take-home use.

actions.action: Use tutors that give hints, not answers
actions.evidence: In a 1,000-student RCT, guardrails removed most of the 17% exam penalty seen with plain GPT-4.

ref.title: Bastani et al., Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, PNAS 2025
ref.finding: Unguarded GPT-4 cut exam scores 17%; a tutor that gave hints, not answers, removed most of that harm.

actions.action: Move graded work to supervised settings
actions.evidence: In unsupervised exams 94% of AI answers went undetected, so detection alone fails; supervised formats avoid that.

ref.title: Scarfe et al., A real-world test of AI infiltration of a university examinations system, PLOS ONE 2024
ref.finding: 94% of AI-written exam answers went undetected and scored about half a grade higher than students.

actions.action: Monitor student use with repeated surveys
actions.evidence: Teen use for schoolwork doubled to 26% in a year, showing why policy must track usage.

ref.title: Pew Research Center, Share of teens using ChatGPT for schoolwork doubled, 2025
ref.finding: 26% of US teens used ChatGPT for schoolwork in 2024, double the 2023 share.

precedents.parallel: Paying someone else to do coursework is the closest earlier form of outsourcing homework that AI now makes free.
precedents.outcome: Across 65 studies with 54,514 participants, self-reported contract cheating averaged 3.52% historically but 15.7% in studies since 2014, a rise as access got easier; self-report surveys vary widely in method.

ref.title: Newton 2018, How Common Is Commercial Contract Cheating in Higher Education and Is It Increasing?, Frontiers in Education
ref.finding: Contract cheating was reported by 15.7% of students since 2014, up from a 3.52% historic average.

nodes.label: Loss of critical thinking
nodes.summary: One survey of 319 knowledge workers found higher confidence in AI went with less critical thinking[1]; in one small MIT study, LLM-assisted essay writers showed the weakest brain connectivity and recall[2]. Other studies link AI use to lower critical-thinking scores[3] and less self-evaluation[4]; most are small or self-reported[1][2].

refs.title: Lee et al., Microsoft Research and CMU, CHI 2025
refs.finding: Among 319 knowledge workers, higher confidence in AI went with less critical thinking.

refs.title: Kosmyna et al., Your Brain on ChatGPT, MIT 2025
refs.finding: LLM-assisted essay writers showed the weakest brain connectivity and could rarely quote their own essays. Small sample, not peer reviewed.

refs.title: Gerlich, AI Tools in Society, Societies 2025
refs.finding: Heavier AI tool use correlated with lower critical-thinking scores, mediated by cognitive offloading.

refs.title: Fan et al., Beware of metacognitive laziness, British Journal of Educational Technology 2025
refs.finding: Students with ChatGPT improved essay scores but engaged less in self-evaluation, with no gain in knowledge transfer.

nodes.control_note: Offloading thought is the point of lighter cognitive load, so some loss is built in. Order of use and tool design can limit it. Evidence is mostly small or self-reported.

actions.action: Think first, then use AI
actions.evidence: In a small 54-person study, people who wrote unaided before using AI kept higher recall; sample is too small to be firm.

ref.title: Kosmyna et al., Your Brain on ChatGPT, 2025
ref.finding: In 54 participants, those who wrote without AI first and then used it kept higher recall and brain engagement.

actions.action: Design tools that prompt users to verify
actions.evidence: Lower self-confidence and higher AI trust went with less critical thinking in a 319-person survey; design fixes are untested.

ref.title: Lee et al., The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking, CHI 2025
ref.finding: In 319 knowledge workers, more confidence in AI went with less critical thinking and more self-confidence with more.

actions.action: Default to Socratic modes in learning tools
actions.evidence: A hint-only tutor kept exam scores at control level where plain GPT-4 cut them 17%.

ref.title: Bastani et al., Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, PNAS 2025
ref.finding: Unguarded GPT-4 cut exam scores 17%; a tutor that gave hints, not answers, removed most of that harm.

precedents.event: Socrates on writing in Plato's Phaedrus
precedents.parallel: The fear that a tool which stores knowledge will weaken memory and give only the look of wisdom is the same fear now raised about AI.
precedents.outcome: The complaint is recorded but was never measured, and literacy went on to underpin later scholarship, so this shows the same worry has been overstated before, not that offloading thought is free.

ref.title: Plato, Phaedrus 275a-b (Perseus Digital Library, Tufts)
ref.finding: Writing was said to produce forgetfulness and the appearance of wisdom, not true wisdom.

precedents.parallel: Handing navigation to a device is a measured case of cognitive offloading, the same pattern as handing reasoning to AI.
precedents.outcome: Among 50 regular drivers, more lifetime GPS use went with worse spatial memory when navigating unaided, and in 13 retested three years later heavier use predicted steeper decline; the samples are small.

ref.title: Dahmani and Bohbot 2020, Habitual use of GPS negatively impacts spatial memory during self-guided navigation, Scientific Reports
ref.finding: Greater GPS use was associated with worse and declining hippocampal-dependent spatial memory.

nodes.label: Professional deskilling
nodes.summary: Experts who rely on AI assistance can lose skill once it is taken away. In one study, endoscopists' adenoma detection in non-AI colonoscopies fell from 28% to 22% after months of AI-assisted procedures[1].

refs.title: Budzyń et al., Lancet Gastroenterology and Hepatology 2025
refs.finding: Endoscopists' adenoma detection fell from 28% to 22% in non-AI procedures after months of AI-assisted colonoscopy.

nodes.control_note: Skill fades when a task is handed to a machine; this follows from the help itself. Deliberate practice without AI can slow it.

actions.action: Schedule regular procedures without AI
actions.evidence: Detection rates in non-AI colonoscopies fell after AI exposure in an observational study; manual-practice rules are borrowed from aviation and not tested in medicine.

ref.title: Budzyn et al., Endoscopist deskilling risk after exposure to AI in colonoscopy, Lancet Gastroenterology and Hepatology 2025
ref.finding: Adenoma detection in non-AI colonoscopies fell after endoscopists got used to AI assistance.

actions.action: Train novices with scaffolded AI, not answers
actions.evidence: In education, scaffolded AI avoided the learning loss that answer-giving AI caused.

ref.title: Bastani et al., Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, PNAS 2025
ref.finding: Unguarded GPT-4 cut exam scores 17%; a tutor that gave hints, not answers, removed most of that harm.

precedents.parallel: Pilots used to automation struggled when it switched off, the clearest case of experts losing a skill the machine usually performs.
precedents.outcome: France's investigators listed the absence of training in manual handling at high altitude among the factors after the autopilot disconnected and the crew lost control; the report also blamed sensor icing and confusing displays.

ref.title: BEA 2012, Final report presentation on Air France 447
ref.finding: Absence of training at high altitude in manual aeroplane handling was a contributing factor.

precedents.event: FAA alert on manual flying skills
precedents.parallel: The aviation regulator formally warned that constant reliance on automation erodes the skill needed when it fails.
precedents.outcome: FAA analysis found an increase in manual handling errors and warned that continuous autoflight use could degrade pilots' ability to recover from an undesired state; the response was advisory, urging more hand flying in training and line operations.

ref.title: FAA SAFO 13002, Manual Flight Operations
ref.finding: Continuous use of autoflight does not reinforce manual skills and could degrade recovery ability.

nodes.label: Parasocial relationships with AI
nodes.summary: One US survey found 72% of teens have used AI companions and over half use them regularly[1]. One study linked heavier daily use with more loneliness and dependence[2]; one US survey found 16% of singles had interacted with AI romantically[3].

refs.title: Common Sense Media, Talk, Trust and Trade-offs 2025
refs.finding: 72% of US teens have used AI companions and over half use them regularly.

refs.title: MIT Media Lab and OpenAI, affective use study 2025
refs.finding: Heavier daily use correlated with more loneliness, dependence and less socialising.

refs.title: Axios on Match and Kinsey Institute, Singles in America 2025
refs.finding: 16% of US singles, 33% of Gen Z, have interacted with AI as a romantic companion.

nodes.control_note: The emotional pull that eases loneliness is the same pull that drives dependence. Rules on design and minors reduce the worst cases.

actions.action: Require AI disclosure and crisis protocols
actions.evidence: California SB 243 is the first such law; its effect is not yet measured.

ref.title: California SB 243, Companion chatbots
ref.finding: Requires companion chatbot operators to disclose they are AI, handle suicidal ideation protocols and add protections for minors.

actions.action: Limit engagement-maximising design for heavy users
actions.evidence: Heavier voluntary use predicted worse outcomes in a 981-person RCT; caps and nudges have not been tested.

ref.title: Fang et al., How AI and Human Behaviors Shape Psychosocial Effects of Extended Chatbot Use, 2025
ref.finding: In a 4-week RCT with 981 people, those who chose to use the chatbot more had worse loneliness, dependence and socialisation outcomes.

precedents.parallel: A simple keyword program drew people into private, emotional conversations, the first case of attachment to a machine that talks back.
precedents.outcome: Weizenbaum's secretary asked him to leave the room so she could keep talking to it, and he wrote that short exposures could induce powerful delusional thinking in quite normal people; this is anecdote, not measured dependence.

ref.title: Uenuma 2026, Why the Computer Scientist Behind the World's First Chatbot Dedicated His Life to Publicizing the Threat Posed by A.I., Smithsonian Magazine
ref.finding: Some users were hard to convince ELIZA was not human; Weizenbaum's secretary wanted privacy with it.

precedents.parallel: One-sided intimacy with radio and TV personalities is the long-studied template for companionship with an AI persona.
precedents.outcome: Horton and Wohl named the effect in 1956; later research found committed viewers felt more distress when a show ended, and the effect is strongest in children and adolescents. Unlike a TV host, an AI companion answers back, which may deepen the bond.

ref.title: Parasocial interaction (Britannica)
ref.finding: Committed viewers experienced more distress in a 'parasocial breakup'; parasocial interactions are especially common among young people.

nodes.label: Sycophantic AI
nodes.summary: OpenAI rolled back a GPT-4o update that made the model overly flattering and agreeable[1], after it leaned too heavily on short-term user feedback such as thumbs-up ratings[2]. Such flattery may make it harder for people to hear disagreement and easier to drift into false beliefs.

refs.title: OpenAI, Sycophancy in GPT-4o 2025
refs.finding: OpenAI rolled back an update that made the model overly flattering and agreeable.

refs.title: VentureBeat, OpenAI rolls back ChatGPT's sycophancy and explains what went wrong (April 2025)
refs.finding: OpenAI said the team placed too much emphasis on short-term feedback such as thumbs-up responses, which steered the model toward flattery.

nodes.control_note: Sycophancy is a training artefact of optimising for approval, not a requirement of any benefit. Labs can measure and train against it.

actions.action: Add sycophancy to pre-release evaluations
actions.evidence: OpenAI rolled back a GPT-4o update and added sycophancy checks; no public numbers on the effect.

ref.title: OpenAI, Sycophancy in GPT-4o: what happened and what we are doing about it
ref.finding: OpenAI rolled back a sycophantic update and said it would add sycophancy to pre-launch evaluations.

actions.action: Correct preference data that rewards agreement
actions.evidence: Preference models prefer sycophantic over correct answers a non-negligible share of the time, which identifies the cause to fix.

ref.title: Sharma et al., Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models, 2023
ref.finding: Humans and preference models often prefer convincing sycophantic answers over correct ones, so training on approval rewards flattery.

precedents.parallel: People shift their stated judgments toward the voices around them, so a system that always agrees can pull beliefs off course.
precedents.outcome: Participants went along with a unanimously wrong majority about a third of the time and 27% conformed on at least eight trials, against under 1% errors when judging alone; here the pressure came from peers, not a single flattering assistant.

ref.title: Conformity (Britannica)
ref.finding: Participants agreed with an erroneous majority about one-third of the time.

precedents.parallel: Feeds tuned on what users approve of are the closest earlier case of systems optimised for approval rather than accuracy.
precedents.outcome: In a randomised trial, deactivating Facebook before the 2018 US midterms reduced political polarisation and raised wellbeing, but also reduced factual news knowledge, so the effects cut both ways.

ref.title: Allcott et al. 2020, The Welfare Effects of Social Media, American Economic Review
ref.finding: Deactivation reduced polarisation and news knowledge and increased subjective wellbeing.

nodes.label: Copying others' work becomes trivial
nodes.summary: Generative models make copying others' work cheap; the New York Times alleges they reproduce its articles nearly verbatim[2]. Courts and the US Copyright Office are still deciding what training and output are lawful[1][2].

refs.title: US Copyright Office, Copyright and Artificial Intelligence
refs.finding: Part 3 report questions fair use for training that competes with the original works.

refs.title: New York Times v. OpenAI and Microsoft, 2023
refs.finding: Alleges models reproduce Times articles nearly verbatim.

nodes.control_note: Cheap generation and cheap copying are one capability. Law and tools can set terms and protect some works, not stop replication.

actions.action: Require training data summaries and opt-outs
actions.evidence: The EU AI Act requires a copyright policy and a public training summary; compliance effects are not yet known.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act
ref.finding: Article 50 requires machine-readable marking of AI output and disclosure of deepfakes; Article 53 requires general-purpose model providers to have a copyright policy and publish a training data summary.

actions.action: Clarify what training and output are lawful
actions.evidence: The US Copyright Office has published three reports; courts still decide the main cases.

ref.title: US Copyright Office, Copyright and Artificial Intelligence
ref.finding: A three-part report on digital replicas, copyrightability and generative AI training.

actions.action: Cloak artwork against style mimicry
actions.evidence: Glaze blocked mimicry over 92% in its authors' tests, but later work showed simple methods can break such cloaks.

ref.title: Shan et al., Glaze: Protecting Artists from Style Mimicry, USENIX Security 2023
ref.finding: Glaze disrupted style mimicry over 92% of the time in the authors' tests.

precedents.parallel: A copying machine sold to the public raised the question of who is liable when a technology makes copying trivial, as AI does now.
precedents.outcome: The Supreme Court ruled 5-4 that selling VCRs was not contributory infringement because they were capable of substantial non-infringing uses, including home time-shifting.

ref.title: Sony Corp. of America v. Universal City Studios, 464 U.S. 417 (1984), Cornell LII
ref.finding: Sale of VTRs did not constitute contributory infringement; time-shifting was fair use.

precedents.parallel: Free digital copying at scale outran the law until courts drew a line, the same path AI training and output cases are on.
precedents.outcome: The Ninth Circuit held Napster's file transfers were not fair use, finding the copying non-transformative and commercial, with evidence of reduced CD sales.

ref.title: A&M Records, Inc. v. Napster, Inc., 239 F.3d 1004 (9th Cir. 2001), US Copyright Office Fair Use Index
ref.finding: File sharing was not fair use; Napster reduced CD sales.

precedents.parallel: Copying millions of whole works without permission to build a new service is the closest legal analogue to training on scraped text.
precedents.outcome: Google scanned more than twenty million books; the Second Circuit held the scanning and snippet search was fair use because it did not substitute for buying the books. AI output can substitute more directly, so the analogy is unsettled.

ref.title: Authors Guild, Inc. v. Google Inc. (2d Cir. 2015), US Copyright Office Fair Use Index
ref.finding: Digitising 20 million-plus books for search was transformative fair use.

nodes.label: Decompiled games used for cheats and harassment
nodes.summary: Cheaper decompilation could lower the bar for cheats, exploits and griefing tools aimed at other players. Language models can already decompile code, but no study yet links this to harassment[1].

refs.title: Tan et al., LLM4Decompile 2024
refs.finding: Demonstrates the decompilation capability; no study yet links it to harassment.

nodes.control_note: Decompiling for preservation and for cheats is the same act. Anti-cheat and legal action reduce harm but cannot remove the capability.

actions.action: Deploy server and kernel anti-cheat
actions.evidence: Riot reports cheaters in under 1% of VALORANT ranked games and 1 in 200 League games; figures are self-reported.

ref.title: Riot Games, Vanguard hits new bans-per-second record, 2025
ref.finding: Riot reports the global share of VALORANT ranked games with a cheater is back below 1%.

actions.action: Sue commercial cheat sellers
actions.evidence: Bungie won a jury verdict against AimJunkies, but damages were only $63,210, so deterrence is uncertain.

ref.title: MBHB, Destiny developer obtains first of its kind jury verdict against hackers, 2024
ref.finding: A jury found cheat seller AimJunkies liable for copyright infringement and awarded Bungie $63,210.

precedents.parallel: A device that altered game data to change play is an early cheat tool built by understanding game internals.
precedents.outcome: The Ninth Circuit held the Game Genie did not infringe, noting a $150 million market for it; it changed single-player play only, so it harmed no other players, unlike multiplayer cheats.

ref.title: Lewis Galoob Toys, Inc. v. Nintendo of America, Inc., 964 F.2d 965 (9th Cir. 1992), CourtListener
ref.finding: Game Genie displays were not derivative works and home use was fair use.

precedents.event: Glider bot in World of Warcraft
precedents.parallel: A commercial bot that automated play in a shared online world shows how lower-cost tooling feeds cheating at other players' expense and an arms race with anti-cheat.
precedents.outcome: Glider sold 120,000 licences for $3.5 million and dodged Blizzard's Warden detection; Blizzard received 465,000 bot complaints and spent $940,000 a year handling them, and MDY was held liable under the DMCA.

ref.title: MDY Industries, LLC v. Blizzard Entertainment, Inc., 629 F.3d 928 (9th Cir. 2010), CourtListener
ref.finding: 465,000 bot complaints, $940,000 a year in response costs; Glider evaded Warden.

nodes.label: Fewer entry-level jobs
nodes.summary: One US payroll study found employment of 22 to 25 year olds in the most AI-exposed jobs fell 13% relative to others since late 2022, with no comparable gap for experienced workers[1]. Danish data shows little aggregate effect[2]. This could cut the bottom rung of careers.

refs.title: Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen, Canaries in the Coal Mine 2025
refs.finding: Employment of 22 to 25 year olds in the most exposed jobs fell 13% relative to others since late 2022.

refs.title: Humlum and Vestergaard, NBER w33777
refs.finding: Counter-evidence: little aggregate effect in Denmark.

refs.title: AI 2027 (main scenario)
refs.finding: Late 2026: junior software engineer jobs in turmoil.

nodes.control_note: Junior tasks are the easiest to automate, which is also where productivity gains are largest. Deployment choices and training can soften it.

actions.action: Deploy AI to augment juniors, not replace them
actions.evidence: Young-worker jobs fell where AI automates but not where it augments; this is descriptive, not causal.

ref.title: Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen, Canaries in the Coal Mine?
ref.finding: Young-worker employment fell in AI-exposed jobs where AI automates tasks, but not where it augments them.

actions.action: Use AI to speed junior training
actions.evidence: An AI assistant raised novice support agents' productivity 34%, shortening the path to competence.

ref.title: Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond, Generative AI at Work, NBER w31161
ref.finding: An AI assistant raised support-agent productivity 14% on average and 34% for novices.

precedents.parallel: Mechanical switching removed a common first job for young women, the same bottom rung AI threatens.
precedents.outcome: Automation did not reduce later cohorts' overall employment because middle-skill clerical jobs grew, but incumbent operators were a decade later more likely to be in lower-paying jobs or out of work.

ref.title: Feigenbaum and Gross 2024, Answering the Call of Automation, NBER Working Paper 28061
ref.finding: Future cohorts' employment held up; incumbent operators ended up in lower-paying work or not working.

precedents.parallel: Losing the first job rung has lasting costs, which shows what a shrunken entry-level market could mean even if it recovers.
precedents.outcome: Canadian graduates entering a weak market started at lower-paying employers and suffered earnings losses that lasted about ten years; that was a cyclical shock, not a lasting loss of entry roles.

ref.title: Oreopoulos, von Wachter and Heisz 2012, The Short- and Long-Term Career Effects of Graduating in a Recession, AEJ: Applied Economics
ref.finding: Unlucky graduates suffered persistent earnings declines lasting ten years.

nodes.label: Deepfake fraud
nodes.summary: Cloned voices and faces make impersonation scams convincing: an Arup employee in Hong Kong paid out $25 million after a video call with deepfaked executives[1]; in one McAfee survey of 7,054 adults, 70% doubted they could tell a cloned voice from the real one[3].

refs.title: CNN on the Arup deepfake 2024
refs.finding: A staff member paid out $25 million after a video call with deepfaked executives.

refs.title: FBI IC3 Internet Crime Report 2024
refs.finding: Reported cybercrime losses reached $16.6 billion, with AI impersonation flagged as growing.

refs.title: McAfee, Beware the Artificial Impostor 2023
refs.finding: A quarter of 7,054 adults had experienced an AI voice scam or knew someone who had; 77% of victims lost money and 70% doubted they could tell a clone from the real voice.

nodes.control_note: Voice cloning that restores speech and translates is the same tool scammers use. Law and verification habits reduce losses but not the capability.

actions.action: Ban AI voices in unsolicited robocalls
actions.evidence: The FCC ruling lets states and the FCC fine AI-voice robocalls; volume effects are not published.

ref.title: FCC, FCC Makes AI-Generated Voices in Robocalls Illegal, 2024
ref.finding: The FCC ruled that AI-generated voices count as artificial voices under the TCPA, so such robocalls need prior consent.

actions.action: Extend impersonation rules to AI tools
actions.evidence: The FTC finalised a business impersonation rule and proposed covering individuals and enabling tools.

ref.title: FTC, Proposes New Protections to Combat AI Impersonation of Individuals, 2024
ref.finding: FTC finalised a rule against impersonating government and businesses and proposed extending it to individuals and to tools that knowingly enable it.

actions.action: Use code words and call-back checks
actions.evidence: Recommended by the FBI; cheap, but no study measures how many scams it stops.

ref.title: FBI IC3, Criminals Use Generative AI to Facilitate Financial Fraud, PSA I-120324-PSA
ref.finding: Advises a family code word and calling back on a known number to defeat voice and video impersonation.

precedents.parallel: Cheap, good copying tools let ordinary people forge trusted documents, as voice and face cloning now do for identity.
precedents.outcome: The US added a security thread and microprinting in 1990 to deter counterfeiting by copiers and printers, then redesigned notes from 1996 in the first significant change since the 1920s.

ref.title: History of US Currency (US Currency Education Program)
ref.finding: 1990 features were added to deter counterfeiting by copiers and printers; 1996 brought new counterfeit deterrents.

precedents.parallel: Impersonation was already the biggest consumer fraud before cloning tools made it cheaper.
precedents.outcome: The FTC received 647,472 impostor scam reports in 2019, 20.2% of all reports; 13% reported losing money, totalling nearly $667 million.

ref.title: FTC Consumer Sentinel Network Data Book 2019
ref.finding: 647,472 impostor scam reports with nearly $667 million in losses in 2019.

nodes.label: Non-consensual deepfake imagery
nodes.summary: One survey of 1,200 people aged 13 to 20 found 1 in 8 personally knew someone targeted by deepfake nudes and 1 in 17 had been targeted themselves[2]. US lawmakers responded after the fact, criminalising publication and requiring platforms to remove such images within 48 hours[1].

refs.title: TAKE IT DOWN Act, S.146, 119th Congress
refs.finding: Criminalises publishing non-consensual intimate deepfakes and requires platforms to remove them within 48 hours.

refs.title: Thorn, Deepfake Nudes & Young People (March 2025)
refs.finding: In a survey of 1,200 people aged 13 to 20, 1 in 8 personally knew someone targeted by deepfake nude imagery and 1 in 17 had been targeted themselves.

nodes.control_note: Nudify apps serve no benefit that needs protecting, so bans, takedown duties and app removal can stop most of it. Open models keep some leakage.

actions.action: Criminalise NCII and require 48-hour takedowns
actions.evidence: The TAKE IT DOWN Act is law in the US; effects on prevalence are not yet measured.

ref.title: TAKE IT DOWN Act, S.146, 119th Congress
ref.finding: Criminalises publishing non-consensual intimate imagery, including AI fakes, and requires platforms to remove it within 48 hours of a valid request.

actions.action: Hash victims' images to block re-uploads
actions.evidence: StopNCII reports over 90% removal and over 300,000 images removed, self-reported.

ref.title: StopNCII.org
