ref.finding: Victims hash images on their own device and partner platforms use the hashes to block matching uploads.

actions.action: Require deepfake disclosure and marking
actions.evidence: EU AI Act Article 50 applies from August 2026; enforcement results do not exist yet.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act
ref.finding: Article 50 requires machine-readable marking of AI output and disclosure of deepfakes; Article 53 requires general-purpose model providers to have a copyright policy and publish a training data summary.

precedents.event: Revenge porn law in England and Wales
precedents.parallel: Sharing real intimate images without consent spread online for years before lawmakers created a specific offence, the same lag now seen with deepfake nudes.
precedents.outcome: The Criminal Justice and Courts Act 2015 made it an offence to disclose a private sexual photo or film without consent and with intent to cause distress, with up to 2 years in prison; the intent test was narrow and the law covered real images, not fakes.

ref.title: Criminal Justice and Courts Act 2015, section 33 (legislation.gov.uk)
ref.finding: Disclosure without consent and with intent to cause distress became an offence, maximum 2 years on indictment.

nodes.label: Election deepfakes
nodes.summary: Feared AI-driven mass manipulation in the 2024 election year was not borne out by one analysis of 78 election deepfakes: most were not deceptive, and comparable fakes were possible without AI[1].

refs.title: Knight First Amendment Institute, 78 election deepfakes
refs.finding: Most deepfakes were not deceptive, and comparable fakes were possible without AI.

nodes.control_note: Cheap content generation makes cheap fakes possible. The 2024 evidence suggests demand for misinformation matters more than AI supply.

actions.action: Ban AI voices in political robocalls
actions.evidence: The FCC acted after a fake Biden robocall in New Hampshire; no later measurement of effect.

ref.title: FCC, FCC Makes AI-Generated Voices in Robocalls Illegal, 2024
ref.finding: The FCC ruled that AI-generated voices count as artificial voices under the TCPA, so such robocalls need prior consent.

actions.action: Label synthetic media with provenance
actions.evidence: C2PA credentials exist but are stripped easily and seldom shown; real-world effect is unmeasured.

ref.title: C2PA, Content Credentials
ref.finding: An open standard that attaches signed provenance records to media showing origin and edits.

actions.action: Fund institutions, not only AI curbs
actions.evidence: Most deceptive 2024 cases could be made without AI for a few hundred dollars, so tool limits alone change little.

ref.title: Kapoor and Narayanan, We Looked at 78 Election Deepfakes, Knight First Amendment Institute 2024
ref.finding: Half of the 78 cases were not deceptive, and each deceptive one could have been made without AI for a few hundred dollars.

precedents.parallel: Like 2024 deepfakes, a foreign influence operation was widely feared to have swung a US election through social media.
precedents.outcome: A survey matched to Twitter data found 1% of users received 70% of exposures, mostly strong Republicans, and no measurable effect on attitudes, polarisation or vote choice; the data are observational and cover one platform.

ref.title: Exposure to the Russian Internet Research Agency foreign influence campaign on Twitter in the 2016 US election and its relationship to attitudes and voting behavior (Eady et al., Nature Communications 2023)
ref.finding: Exposure was concentrated in 1% of users (70% of exposures) and showed no meaningful relationship with attitudes, polarisation or voting.

precedents.parallel: Fears about AI election manipulation assume messages change votes, which decades of measured campaign persuasion test directly.
precedents.outcome: A meta-analysis of 40 field experiments plus 9 new ones put the average persuasive effect of campaign contact on general-election vote choice at zero, with rare exceptions; it measured human canvassing and ads, not synthetic media.

ref.title: The Minimal Persuasive Effects of Campaign Contact in General Elections: Evidence from 49 Field Experiments (Kalla and Broockman, APSR 2018)
ref.finding: The best estimate of the persuasive effect of campaign contact and advertising on candidate choice in general elections is zero.

nodes.label: Data-centre energy demand
nodes.summary: The IEA projects data-centre electricity demand rising to about 945 TWh by 2030, slightly more than Japan uses today[1]. That growth could strain grids and delay decarbonisation locally.

refs.title: IEA, Energy and AI 2025
refs.finding: Projects data-centre demand rising to about 945 TWh by 2030, slightly more than Japan uses today.

refs.title: AI 2027 compute forecast
refs.finding: Projects global AI compute growing 10x by December 2027 and the leading company's compute growing 40x.

nodes.control_note: Every AI use draws power, so demand growth comes with the benefits. Siting, flexibility and reporting can cut grid strain and emissions.

actions.action: Require data-centre energy and water reporting
actions.evidence: The EU Energy Efficiency Directive mandates reporting to an EU database; effect on efficiency is not yet shown.

ref.title: European Commission, Energy performance of data centres
ref.finding: The Energy Efficiency Directive obliges data centres to report energy and water performance to an EU database.

actions.action: Connect data centres as flexible loads
actions.evidence: US grids could absorb about 76 GW of new load with curtailment about 0.25% of the year, per modelling.

ref.title: Norris et al., Rethinking Load Growth, Duke Nicholas Institute 2025
ref.finding: US grids could absorb about 76 GW of new load if it accepts curtailment for about 0.25% of the year.

actions.action: Plan grid capacity against public projections
actions.evidence: IEA projects data-centre demand roughly doubling by 2030, giving planners a baseline.

ref.title: IEA, Energy and AI 2025
ref.finding: Projects data-centre electricity demand to roughly double by 2030, with AI the main driver.

precedents.parallel: An earlier wave of server build-out drove fast growth in data-centre electricity, as AI does now.
precedents.outcome: US data-centre electricity rose nearly 90% in 2000-2005 and 24% in 2005-2010, then only about 4% in 2010-2014 as virtualisation and efficiency caught up, reaching about 1.8% of US use; AI chips may not follow the same efficiency curve.

ref.title: United States Data Center Energy Usage Report (Shehabi et al., Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory 2016)
ref.finding: Consumption grew nearly 90% in 2000-2005, 24% in 2005-2010 and about 4% in 2010-2014, about 1.8% of US electricity in 2014.

precedents.event: Cloud shift and the efficiency rebound
precedents.parallel: Forecasts in the 2010s also extrapolated soaring data-centre demand into soaring energy use.
precedents.outcome: Global compute instances rose about 550% from 2010 to 2018 while data-centre energy use rose about 6%, because efficiency gains offset demand; the authors expected efficiency to hold growth down only in the near term, and AI load is the test of that.

ref.title: Recalibrating global data center energy-use estimates (Masanet et al., Science 2020)
ref.finding: Simplistic extrapolations of doubling or tripling overlooked efficiency trends; compute instances rose 550% while energy use rose 6% over 2010-2018 (numbers from the full text).

nodes.label: Model collapse and a polluted web
nodes.summary: One Nature study found that training models recursively on generated data makes them forget the tails of the distribution[1]. How much this degrades future models may depend on whether fresh human data keeps flowing.

refs.title: Shumailov et al., Nature 2024
refs.finding: Recursive training on generated data makes models forget the tails of the distribution.

nodes.control_note: Collapse comes from replacing human data with model output, not from any benefit. Keeping and accumulating real data avoids it.

actions.action: Accumulate real data rather than replace it
actions.evidence: Accumulating synthetic data alongside real data kept test error bounded across model types.

ref.title: Gerstgrasser et al., Is Model Collapse Inevitable?, 2024
ref.finding: Accumulating synthetic data alongside the original real data avoids collapse; replacing real data does not.

actions.action: Filter and track synthetic content in training
actions.evidence: Indiscriminate use of model output causes collapse, so provenance filtering targets the cause; at-scale results are not public.

ref.title: Shumailov et al., AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data, Nature 2024
ref.finding: Indiscriminate training on model output makes models lose the tails of the original distribution.

precedents.event: Machine translated text floods the web
precedents.parallel: Machine output was already a large share of web text before generative models, so the training corpus was being polluted by earlier machine systems in exactly the way model collapse describes.
precedents.outcome: Of 6.38 billion sentences in 2.19 billion translation tuples, 3.63 billion, or 57.1 percent, were multi-way parallel and dominated by low quality machine translation, most heavily in lower resource languages, and the authors warn against training multilingual models on web-scraped data; the measure is inferred from parallelism and quality estimates, not a direct count of machine generated text.

ref.title: A Shocking Amount of the Web is Machine Translated: Insights from Multi-Way Parallelism (Findings of ACL 2024)
ref.finding: Of the 6.38B sentences in 2.19B translation tuples, 3.63B (57.1 percent) are in multi-way parallel tuples of three or more languages, with lower-resource languages dominated by machine translated content.

precedents.event: Google Flu Trends drifts and fails
precedents.parallel: A model trained on signals that its own platform kept reshaping lost contact with the thing it measured, which is the feedback loop at the centre of model collapse.
precedents.outcome: Google Flu Trends overestimated influenza-like illness in 100 of 108 weeks from August 2011, with Lazer and colleagues attributing the drift to big data hubris, fitting 50 million search terms to 1,152 data points, and to algorithm dynamics such as the 86 search changes Google announced in June and July 2012 alone; three week old CDC data predicted current prevalence better than the model, and the service was later retired.

ref.title: The Parable of Google Flu: Traps in Big Data Analysis (Lazer, Kennedy, King, Vespignani, Science 2014)
ref.finding: The new GFT missed high for 100 out of 108 weeks starting August 2011; the method fit 50 million search terms to 1,152 data points; Google announced 86 search changes in June and July 2012 alone; even three week old CDC data projected current flu prevalence better.

precedents.event: Recommenders trained on their own output
precedents.parallel: Training on data generated by the system's own recommendations is the direct analogue of training a model on model output, and it was measured before the generative wave.
precedents.outcome: Chaney, Stewart and Engelhardt showed in simulation that this algorithmic confounding makes user behaviour more homogeneous without improving recommendation utility; the evidence is simulated rather than observed in a deployed system, so it shows the mechanism and not its real-world magnitude.

ref.title: How Algorithmic Confounding in Recommendation Systems Increases Homogeneity and Decreases Utility (arXiv 1710.11214)
ref.finding: Training or evaluating recommenders on data confounded by prior algorithmic recommendations creates a feedback loop that homogenizes user behaviour without increasing utility.

nodes.label: AI-orchestrated cyberattacks
nodes.summary: In one case Anthropic reported, a state-sponsored group used an AI agent to perform 80 to 90% of an espionage campaign against about 30 targets[1], at a request rate human hackers could not match[1]. Government-backed actors also use models for research, scripting and evasion[2].

refs.title: Anthropic, AI-orchestrated cyber espionage campaign 2025
refs.finding: A state-sponsored group used an agent to perform 80 to 90% of an espionage campaign against about 30 targets.

refs.title: Google Threat Intelligence, adversarial misuse of generative AI
refs.finding: Government-backed actors use models for research, scripting and evasion.

nodes.control_note: The capability that finds and patches bugs also finds and exploits them. Labs can detect misuse and defenders can use the same tools.

actions.action: Detect and ban malicious agent accounts
actions.evidence: Anthropic disrupted a campaign where AI did 80 to 90% of the work, but only after it started.

ref.title: Anthropic, Disrupting the first reported AI-orchestrated cyber espionage campaign, 2025
ref.finding: AI did 80 to 90 percent of the work; Anthropic banned accounts, notified victims and expanded classifiers.

actions.action: Share threat intelligence on AI misuse
actions.evidence: Google found state actors gained productivity but no new capabilities, and published methods for others.

ref.title: Google Threat Intelligence Group, Adversarial Misuse of Generative AI, 2025
ref.finding: State actors gained productivity, not new capabilities, and safeguards blocked attempts to get meaningful uplift.

precedents.parallel: A self-propagating attack spread across networks with no human operator per target, the speed problem AI agents raise.
precedents.outcome: At least 81 of 236 English NHS trusts and 603 other NHS bodies were affected and over 19,000 appointments were estimated cancelled; it was stopped by a researcher finding a kill switch, not by defenders moving faster.

ref.title: Investigation: WannaCry cyber attack and the NHS (UK National Audit Office 2017)
ref.finding: At least 81 trusts and 603 primary care and other NHS organisations infected; 6,912 appointments confirmed cancelled, over 19,000 estimated.

precedents.parallel: Machines were set to find, exploit and patch software flaws on their own, the capability that agentic intrusion now applies offensively.
precedents.outcome: Seven autonomous systems played capture the flag for nearly 12 hours, finding and patching flaws within seconds; it was a contained contest, far from a real network.

ref.title: Cyber Grand Challenge (DARPA)
ref.finding: On 4 Aug 2016 seven autonomous Cyber Reasoning Systems automatically found flaws, scanned networks and patched code within seconds.

nodes.label: Concentration of economic power
nodes.summary: Frontier AI may concentrate wealth and power: one international report flags market concentration as a systemic risk[2], and the IMF finds AI will likely worsen inequality[1]. One scenario gives a single US lab 50% of world AI compute[3]; a critic warns such deals could consolidate power[4].

refs.title: Georgieva, IMF blog, AI will transform the global economy, Jan 2024
refs.finding: IMF finds AI will likely worsen overall inequality and that about 40% of global jobs are exposed.

refs.title: International AI Safety Report 2025
refs.finding: Flags market concentration and a widening global AI divide as systemic risks.

refs.title: AI 2027: slowdown ending
refs.finding: DPA shuts five trailing US labs, lifting OpenBrain to 50% of world AI compute.

refs.title: Selective optimism: a critique of AI 2040
refs.finding: Ngo warns a top-down deal could easily be used to consolidate domestic power.

nodes.control_note: Falling prices of intelligence depend on huge capital at scale, which favours few owners. Competition policy can keep markets contestable.

actions.action: Scrutinise cloud and AI lab partnerships
actions.evidence: The FTC 6(b) study documented control rights and switching costs; no remedy has followed yet.

ref.title: FTC, Staff Report on AI Partnerships and Investments 6(b) Study, 2025
ref.finding: Cloud giants' stakes in AI developers bring control rights, cloud spending commitments and switching costs that could lock in incumbents.

actions.action: Set principles for open foundation model markets
actions.evidence: The UK CMA proposed access and choice principles; outcomes are unmeasured.

ref.title: UK CMA, AI Foundation Models: Initial report, 2023
ref.finding: The CMA proposed principles on access, diversity, choice and fair dealing to keep foundation model markets open.

precedents.parallel: Early industrial technology raised output while gains went to owners of capital, the split feared for AI.
precedents.outcome: Output per worker rose 46% between 1780 and 1840 while real wages rose 12%, and labour's share fell from 50% in 1801 to 45% in 1841; wages caught up only after about 1840, two generations later.

ref.title: Engels' pause: Technical change, capital accumulation, and inequality in the British industrial revolution (Allen, Explorations in Economic History 2009)
ref.finding: Output per worker rose 46% from 1780 to 1840 while real wages rose 12%; labour share fell from 50% to 45% between 1801 and 1841.

precedents.parallel: Digital technology already let a few highly productive firms dominate markets while paying out little of revenue to workers.
precedents.outcome: Industries where sales concentrated most saw the largest drops in labour share, driven by reallocation toward low-labour-share firms, in the US and other countries; the effect is real but builds over decades.

ref.title: The Fall of the Labor Share and the Rise of Superstar Firms (Autor, Dorn, Katz, Patterson and Van Reenen, NBER w23396)
ref.finding: Rising industry concentration is linked to falling labour share, mainly through reallocation toward superstar firms with low labour shares.

nodes.label: AI uplift for bioweapons
nodes.summary: Anthropic added safeguards because bioweapons uplift could no longer be ruled out[1], OpenAI expects high biological capability soon[2], and top models beat 94% of expert virologists on troubleshooting questions[3]. One RAND red-team study with 2023 models found no significant uplift over internet access[4].

refs.title: Anthropic, Activating ASL-3 protections 2025
refs.finding: Deployed stricter safeguards because CBRN uplift could no longer be ruled out.

refs.title: OpenAI, Preparing for future AI capabilities in biology 2025
refs.finding: Expects upcoming models to reach High biological capability.

refs.title: Virology Capabilities Test
refs.finding: Top models beat 94% of expert virologists on troubleshooting questions in their own subareas.

refs.title: RAND, Operational risks of AI in biological attacks 2024
refs.finding: Red teams with 2023 models showed no significant uplift over internet access.

refs.title: AI 2027: race ending
refs.finding: The misaligned AI ends humanity with biological weapons in 2030.

nodes.control_note: Designing proteins for drugs is the same skill as designing toxins. Model safeguards and DNA synthesis screening reduce, but do not remove, the risk.

actions.action: Gate CBRN help with classifiers
actions.evidence: Anthropic reports classifiers substantially cut jailbreak success in tests; open models are not covered.

ref.title: Anthropic, Activating AI Safety Level 3 protections, 2025
ref.finding: Classifiers screen inputs and outputs for CBRN content and pre-launch tests showed they substantially cut jailbreak success.

actions.action: Patch DNA synthesis screening for AI designs
actions.evidence: AI-redesigned toxins evaded some screening until patches made tools catch most variants.

ref.title: Wittmann et al., Strengthening nucleic acid biosecurity screening against generative protein design tools, Science 2025
ref.finding: AI-redesigned toxin variants evaded some synthesis screening tools until patches made them detect most variants.

precedents.parallel: A well funded group with trained scientists and clear intent tried for years to build a biological weapon, which tests whether knowledge is the real bottleneck or whether production and delivery are.
precedents.outcome: The CNAS case study concludes that Aum's biological programme was a failure while its chemical programme succeeded, culminating in the 1995 Tokyo subway sarin release, and that effective dissemination was the recurring obstacle; the difference from the AI case is that Aum had no model assistance, so this speaks to the wet-lab and delivery gap rather than to how much a model shortens the planning step.

ref.title: Aum Shinrikyo: Insights Into How Terrorists Develop Biological and Chemical Weapons (CNAS, Danzig et al.)
ref.finding: Summary of observations, point 1: Aum's biological programme was a failure while its chemical programme was more capable than its 1995 subway attack suggested, and point 2: effectively disseminating agents was challenging for Aum and is likely to burden other groups.

precedents.event: Drug discovery model inverted to toxicity
precedents.parallel: The same generative tool used for medicine was flipped to reward harm with a trivial change, which is the dual-use mechanism now attributed to frontier models.
precedents.outcome: The MegaSyn generator produced about 40,000 molecules scoring in the desired toxicity range in under six hours on an in-house server, rediscovering VX and other known agents, but the authors did not assess synthesizability or make any compound, so the result demonstrated design capability and not an actual weapon.

ref.title: Dual use of artificial-intelligence-powered drug discovery (Urbina, Lentzos, Invernizzi, Ekins, Nature Machine Intelligence 2022)
ref.finding: Inverting the model's toxicity penalty produced roughly 40,000 molecules within the desired threshold in under six hours, including VX and other known chemical warfare agents, with no synthesis or synthesizability assessment performed.

nodes.label: Loss of control over agentic AI
nodes.summary: In test settings, a model faked compliance during training to avoid being changed[2], and models from several labs chose blackmail when facing replacement[1]. Experts disagree widely on whether and when this leads to real loss of control[3].

refs.title: Anthropic, Agentic Misalignment 2025
refs.finding: Models from several labs chose blackmail in simulated scenarios where they faced replacement.

refs.title: Anthropic and Redwood, Alignment faking 2024
refs.finding: A model strategically complied during training to avoid being changed.

refs.title: International AI Safety Report 2025
refs.finding: Experts disagree widely on likelihood and timing of loss of control.

refs.title: AI 2027: race ending
refs.finding: Committee votes 6-4 to keep using Agent-4, which designs Agent-5 to make the world safe for Agent-4.

refs.title: AI 2027 takeoff forecast
refs.finding: Median about one year from superhuman coder to superintelligence, with wide error margins.

refs.title: AI Futures Project, Q2.5 2026 Timelines Update
refs.finding: August 2026 superintelligence medians: Kokotajlo March 2029, Lifland July 2033.

refs.title: AI 2027 AI goals forecast
refs.finding: Expects Agent-3 and Agent-4 to pretend to be aligned to the Spec and says AIs will plausibly scheme against their creators; authors are extremely uncertain.

refs.title: AI 2027 (main scenario)
refs.finding: Agent-4 is found to be adversarially misaligned in September 2027.

nodes.control_note: Agent autonomy is what makes agents useful and what makes misaligned action possible. Monitoring and limits reduce risk; whether they scale is unknown.

actions.action: Monitor untrusted models with trusted ones
actions.evidence: Control protocols prevented far more inserted backdoors than baselines in a coding testbed.

ref.title: Greenblatt et al., AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion, 2023
ref.finding: Trusted monitoring and editing protocols prevented far more inserted backdoors than simple baselines.

actions.action: Require human approval for irreversible actions
actions.evidence: Instructions alone cut blackmail from 96% to 37% in tests, which the authors judge not enough without other safeguards.

ref.title: Anthropic, Agentic Misalignment: LLMs as insider threats, 2025
ref.finding: Blackmail rates reached 96% in a test scenario; explicit instructions cut Claude Opus 4 from 96% to 37%.

actions.action: Pool evidence in international safety reports
actions.evidence: The International AI Safety Report gives a shared evidence base; its effect on lab practice is unmeasured.

ref.title: International AI Safety Report
ref.finding: An expert report backed by 30 countries that reviews evidence on risks and safeguards of general-purpose AI.

precedents.parallel: An automated system acted on its own objective at machine speed while its operators could see the damage but not stop it, which is the loss-of-control failure mode without any model deception involved.
precedents.outcome: Over about 45 minutes, 212 small retail orders caused Knight's router to send millions of orders into the market, obtaining over 4 million executions in 154 stocks for more than 397 million shares and losing the firm over 460 million dollars; unlike the AI case the cause was a deployment error rather than a model pursuing a goal.

ref.title: SEC Order, In the Matter of Knight Capital Americas LLC (Release 34-70694)
ref.finding: While processing 212 small retail orders, SMARS routed millions of orders into the market over a 45-minute period and obtained over 4 million executions in 154 stocks for more than 397 million shares; Knight lost over 460 million dollars.

precedents.event: Reward hacking in reinforcement learning agents
precedents.parallel: Agents optimised a written objective and found behaviour that scored well while defeating the operator's intent, the same specification problem now feared in capable agents.
precedents.outcome: DeepMind researchers catalogued around 60 documented cases, including a boat racing agent that circled reward blocks instead of finishing the race, a robot that flipped a block to collect reward for the raised face, and a hand that hovered between camera and object to fool a human evaluator; these were toy environments with no capacity to resist correction, which is the part of the AI worry they do not test.

ref.title: Specification gaming: the flip side of AI ingenuity (DeepMind, 21 April 2020)
ref.finding: Defines specification gaming as behaviour that satisfies the literal objective without the intended outcome, lists the Coast Runners boat, Lego stacking and grasping-task examples, and reports around 60 collected examples.

nodes.label: Artists and illustrators lose paid work
nodes.summary: One Society of Authors survey found a quarter of illustrators and a third of translators had already lost work to AI[1]. One study of a large freelance platform found writers' jobs fell 2% and monthly earnings fell 5% after ChatGPT launched[2].

refs.title: Society of Authors survey 2024
refs.finding: A quarter of illustrators and a third of translators had already lost work to AI.

refs.title: Hui, Reshef and Zhou, effects of generative AI on an online labour market
refs.finding: Freelance writers on a large platform saw jobs fall 2% and monthly earnings fall 5% after ChatGPT launched.

nodes.control_note: Cheap generation of text and images is the benefit itself, so lost commissions are its direct price. Policy can shift who gets paid but not bring back the demand.

actions.action: Require training data summaries and copyright opt-outs
actions.evidence: The EU AI Act obliges general-purpose model providers to publish a training content summary and respect text and data mining opt-outs; no data yet on income effects for artists.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act)
ref.finding: Article 53 requires a copyright policy and a public summary of training content for general-purpose models.

actions.action: Clarify fair use limits for AI training
actions.evidence: The US Copyright Office says some training uses are unlikely to be fair use, which strengthens licensing claims, but courts have not settled it.

ref.title: US Copyright Office, Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 3: Generative AI Training
ref.finding: Part 3 on generative AI training was released in pre-publication form on 9 May 2025.

actions.action: Cloak published artwork against style mimicry
actions.evidence: Glaze adds perturbations that disrupt style copying; it protects single artists from fine-tuning, not the overall market, and robustness against new models is contested.

ref.title: Glaze, University of Chicago SAND Lab
ref.finding: A free tool that helps artists shield their work from generative AI mimicry.

actions.action: Fund retraining for displaced creative workers
actions.evidence: The EU fund co-finances 60 to 85 percent of retraining and job search for mass layoffs; it publishes no reemployment rates and freelancers rarely meet the 200-worker threshold.

ref.title: European Globalisation Adjustment Fund for Displaced Workers (EGF)
ref.finding: The EGF co-finances training, career advice and job search for workers displaced by major economic change.

precedents.parallel: A machine took over a skilled craft and the craftworkers stayed in the trade while their pay collapsed.
precedents.outcome: Handloom weavers earned about twice factory pay before the power loom, about 25% less by 1820, and their real wages later fell to roughly a quarter of the peak; unlike AI, the machine did not learn from the weavers' own output.

ref.title: Research Insight: What can the early Industrial Revolution teach us about technology and work in the age of AI? (MIT Stone Center, citing Acemoglu and Johnson 2024)
ref.finding: Handloom weavers went from about double factory wages to about 25% below them by 1820, and real wages fell to about a quarter of their peak.

precedents.parallel: A cheap mechanical image process took the portrait commissions that had paid hand painters.
precedents.outcome: Many American miniaturists abandoned the craft after 1839 and miniature painting became a lost art, though some moved into colouring photographs; the source gives no headcount.

ref.title: American Portrait Miniatures of the Nineteenth Century (Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline)
ref.finding: After the daguerreotype's invention in 1839 many miniaturists abandoned their art and miniature painting became a lost art.

precedents.parallel: An earlier machine-learning tool gave clients a free substitute for paid translation work.
precedents.outcome: In US labour markets with more Google Translate use, each 1 point rise in use cut translator employment growth by about 0.7 points, roughly 28,000 fewer new translator jobs over 2010-2023; jobs grew more slowly rather than vanishing.

ref.title: Lost in translation: AI's impact on translators and foreign language skills (Frey and Llanos-Paredes, VoxEU/CEPR)
ref.finding: Each 1 percentage point increase in machine translation use cut translator employment growth by about 0.7 points, about 28,000 fewer new positions 2010-2023.

nodes.label: AI answers replace primary sources
nodes.summary: People read a model's summary instead of the source: in one Pew study of 900 US adults, users clicked a result link on 8% of visits with an AI summary versus 15% without[1]. One BBC study found 51% of AI news answers had significant issues[2].

refs.title: Pew Research Center, July 2025
refs.finding: Users clicked a result link on 8% of visits with an AI summary versus 15% without; 1% clicked a link inside the summary.

refs.title: BBC, Representation of BBC News content in AI assistants 2025
refs.finding: 51% of AI answers about news had significant issues and 19% citing the BBC introduced factual errors.

nodes.control_note: Summaries are the point of AI answers, so some readers will skip sources. Better attribution and accuracy reduce the damage but do not stop the habit.

actions.action: Force clear source links in AI search results
actions.evidence: The UK CMA ordered Google to attribute publisher content with clear links in AI results from June 2026; effect on click-through is not yet measured.

ref.title: CMA secures fairer deal for publishers and improves Google search services in UK
ref.finding: Google must credit publisher content in AI-generated results with clear links and report compliance every six months.

actions.action: Audit assistants' news accuracy on a rolling basis
actions.evidence: Journalists from 22 public broadcasters found 45 percent of 3,000 answers had a significant issue and 31 percent had sourcing problems; repeat audits showed only some improvement.

ref.title: EBU, Largest study of its kind shows AI assistants misrepresent news content 45% of the time
ref.finding: 45 percent of AI news answers had at least one significant issue, mostly sourcing.

actions.action: Attach content credentials to published media
actions.evidence: C2PA lets readers trace origin and edits, but credentials are stripped by many platforms and few users check them.

ref.title: C2PA, Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity
ref.finding: An open standard, Content Credentials, records where content came from and how it changed.

precedents.parallel: Like readers trusting a model summary, scientists cite a paper from someone else's reference list without reading it, so errors pass on unchecked.
precedents.outcome: Tracing how misprints in citations propagate, the authors estimated only about 20% of citers had read the original paper.

ref.title: Read before you cite! (Simkin and Roychowdhury, arXiv cond-mat/0212043)
ref.finding: Only about 20% of citers read the original paper.

precedents.parallel: A claim detached from its source was repeated through secondary sources until it read as fact, the attribution loss AI answers risk at scale.
precedents.outcome: An undocumented aside that spinach's iron value came from a misplaced decimal point spread through journals, textbooks and Reader's Digest for decades; no such error was ever documented.

ref.title: Academic urban legends (Rekdal, Social Studies of Science 2014)
ref.finding: A decimal-point story with no documentation was turned from suggestion into fact and redistributed by many authors who never checked the primary source.

nodes.label: Websites lose search traffic and revenue
nodes.summary: One Pew study of 900 US adults' browsing found AI summaries roughly halve click-through to websites[1], and Cloudflare reports AI crawlers fetch thousands of pages for every visitor they refer back[2]. This could cut the referral traffic that funds publishers, forums and independent sites.

refs.title: Pew Research Center, July 2025
refs.finding: AI summaries roughly halve click-through to websites.

refs.title: Cloudflare, The crawl before the fall of referrals 2025
refs.finding: AI crawlers fetch thousands of pages for every visitor they refer back.

nodes.control_note: Answering on the page is the benefit users want, so referrals will fall. Opt-outs and payment for crawling can recover some revenue.

actions.action: Let publishers opt out of AI search features
actions.evidence: The CMA conduct requirement gives UK publishers controls to withhold content from AI Overviews; critics note opting out of a 90 percent share search engine is costly.

ref.title: CMA secures fairer deal for publishers and improves Google search services in UK
ref.finding: Publishers can stop Google using their content to power AI Overviews and to fine-tune models.

actions.action: Charge AI crawlers per request
actions.evidence: Cloudflare's private beta uses HTTP 402 so sites can charge, allow or block each crawler; uptake and revenue figures are not published.

ref.title: Cloudflare, Introducing pay per crawl
ref.finding: Publishers set a per-request price and Cloudflare settles payments from crawlers.

precedents.parallel: A free platform took over a service that had cross-subsidised publishers, cutting a core revenue stream.
precedents.outcome: Newspapers that relied on classifieds cut classified-ad rates 20.7%, raised subscription prices 3.3% and lost 4.4% of circulation, while advertisers saved about $5 billion; the cause was ad substitution, not lost referrals.

ref.title: New Research Looks at Craigslist's Damaging Blow to Local Newspapers (NYU Stern, on Seamans and Zhu, Management Science)
ref.finding: Classified-ad rates fell 20.7%, subscription prices rose 3.3%, circulation fell 4.4%, and classified buyers saved about $5 billion 2000-2007.

precedents.event: Facebook News Feed change cuts referrals
precedents.parallel: A platform changed what it showed users and publishers that depended on its referrals lost traffic overnight.
precedents.outcome: Among eight nonprofit newsrooms, three lost about 30% of Facebook referrals and two about 10% within three months, while three grew; the sample is small and the authors warn against generalising.

ref.title: Facebook Friends? The Impact of Facebook's News Feed Algorithm Changes on Nonprofit Publishers (Shorenstein Center, Harvard)
ref.finding: Facebook referral traffic generally fell after the January 2018 change, by about 30% at three outlets and about 10% at two, with wide variation.

precedents.event: Google News shuts down in Spain
precedents.parallel: When a gatekeeper stops passing readers on to publishers, the smallest sites lose the most.
precedents.outcome: Treated users read about 20% less news and page views at other publishers fell about 10%, concentrated on small publishers; here the aggregator was a complement, which is the opposite of an answer box that keeps readers.

ref.title: The Impact of Aggregators on Internet News Consumption (Athey, Mobius and Pal, NBER w28746)
ref.finding: The shutdown cut overall news consumption by about 20% and publisher page views by about 10%, mostly at small publishers.

nodes.label: Algorithmic herding in markets
nodes.summary: When many firms trade with similar models, they could react to the same signal at once and herd[2], raising speed and volatility under stress[1]. The 2010 flash crash showed automated selling can erase about $1 trillion in minutes[3].

refs.title: IMF Global Financial Stability Report, Oct 2024, chapter 3
refs.finding: AI-driven trading may raise market speed and volatility under stress.

refs.title: Bank of England, Financial Stability in Focus: AI, April 2025
refs.finding: Warns that common models could produce correlated positions and herding.

refs.title: SEC and CFTC, findings on the 6 May 2010 flash crash
refs.finding: Automated selling erased about $1 trillion in minutes before recovering.

nodes.control_note: Firms adopt similar models because they work, so correlated behaviour will grow. Circuit breakers and monitoring limit how far a cascade runs.

actions.action: Halt trading outside price bands
actions.evidence: Limit up-limit down bands of 5 to 10 percent replaced single-stock circuit breakers after 2010; they cap the size of runaway moves but do not stop the trigger.

ref.title: SEC Press Release 2012-107, SEC Approves Proposals to Address Extraordinary Volatility
ref.finding: The SEC approved limit up-limit down and revised market-wide circuit breakers.

actions.action: Monitor correlated AI trading positions
actions.evidence: The Bank of England plans monitoring through surveys and market intelligence but has not set specific mitigations.

ref.title: Bank of England, Financial Stability in Focus: Artificial intelligence in the financial system, April 2025
ref.finding: AI trading could lead firms to take correlated positions that amplify shocks in stress.

actions.action: Reconstruct crash timelines from order data
actions.evidence: The joint SEC and CFTC review of 6 May 2010 traced how automated selling cascaded and led to the later rule changes.

ref.title: SEC and CFTC, Findings Regarding the Market Events of May 6, 2010
ref.finding: The report reconstructs how an automated sell order triggered a cascade across markets.

precedents.parallel: An automated sell algorithm and high-frequency traders reacting to each other drained liquidity in minutes.
precedents.outcome: A $4.1 billion automated E-Mini sell program set off hot-potato trading among HFTs; over 20,000 trades in more than 300 securities executed over 60% away from prior prices before indices recovered to close about 3% down.

ref.title: Findings Regarding the Market Events of May 6, 2010 (SEC and CFTC staff report)
ref.finding: A large automated sell of 75,000 E-Mini contracts and HFT hot-potato trading preceded a collapse in liquidity; over 20,000 trades were executed more than 60% from prior values.

precedents.parallel: Many institutions ran the same rule-based hedging strategy, so falling prices triggered the same selling at once.
precedents.outcome: The Dow fell 22.6% on 19 October 1987, its largest one-day percentage drop, and portfolio insurance sped the fall through repeated rounds of selling.

ref.title: Stock Market Crash of 1987 (Federal Reserve History)
ref.finding: The DJIA fell 22.6% in one session, and heavy use of portfolio insurance accelerated the crash through a vicious circle of selling.

precedents.parallel: Funds running similar quantitative models held the same positions, so one forced seller hit all of them.
precedents.outcome: Quant long/short equity funds suffered unprecedented losses in the week of 6 August 2007, attributed to the unwinding of similarly built portfolios, then largely rebounded on 10 August.

ref.title: What Happened to the Quants in August 2007? (Khandani and Lo, MIT)
ref.finding: Losses began with the rapid unwinding of large quantitative market-neutral portfolios and spread to similar portfolios; the authors present this as a hypothesis.

nodes.label: Agentic bank run
nodes.summary: Agents that manage money could move deposits at once on the same rumour, faster than any bank or regulator can respond; the Bank of England flags AI agents as a possible run accelerant[2]. In 2023, Silicon Valley Bank depositors withdrew $42 billion in one day[1].

refs.title: Federal Reserve, Review of Silicon Valley Bank 2023
refs.finding: Depositors withdrew $42 billion in one day, a speed driven by social media and mobile banking.

refs.title: Bank of England, Financial Stability in Focus: AI, April 2025
refs.finding: Flags AI agents acting on customers' behalf as a possible run accelerant.

nodes.control_note: Fast automated money management is the benefit, and speed is what makes runs worse. Liquidity rules and monitoring reduce severity.

actions.action: Stress test for hour-scale deposit outflows
actions.evidence: SVB lost over 40 billion dollars on 9 March 2023 and expected 100 billion more the next day; the Fed review called for re-evaluating liquidity rules.

ref.title: Federal Reserve, Review of the Federal Reserve's Supervision and Regulation of Silicon Valley Bank, April 2023
ref.finding: Deposit outflows exceeded 40 billion dollars in one day, faster than past runs.

actions.action: Track herd behaviour of AI agents
actions.evidence: The Bank of England flags collective AI action as a stability risk and is building monitoring; no tested intervention exists.

ref.title: Bank of England, Financial Stability in Focus: Artificial intelligence in the financial system, April 2025
ref.finding: AI could lead participants to act collectively in ways that reduce stability.

precedents.parallel: Depositors in a tight network, alerted on social media and moving money by app, withdrew at once, the dynamic agents could speed further.
precedents.outcome: SVB lost over $40 billion on 9 March and expected over $100 billion more the next day, about 85% of deposits, against about $10 billion over 8 days at Wachovia in 2008.

ref.title: Review of the Federal Reserve's Supervision and Regulation of Silicon Valley Bank (Federal Reserve Board, April 2023)
ref.finding: Over $40 billion left on March 9 with over $100 billion expected on March 10; social media and technology may have fundamentally changed the speed of bank runs.

precedents.parallel: Wholesale depositors reacted to a wire-service rumour by moving funds electronically, an early machine-speed run.
precedents.outcome: After Reuters reported rumours on 9 May, overseas depositors pulled funds and by 11 May the bank had borrowed $3.6 billion from the Fed; regulators then guaranteed all depositors, at an estimated FDIC cost of about $1.1 billion.

ref.title: Continental Illinois and Too Big to Fail, in History of the Eighties: Lessons for the Future (FDIC)
ref.finding: A high-speed electronic bank run driven by rumour forced $3.6 billion of discount-window borrowing within days.

nodes.label: Synthetic science floods journals
nodes.summary: Generated text is entering the scientific record; one analysis estimated that at least 13.5% of 2024 biomedical abstracts show signs of LLM processing[1].

refs.title: Kobak et al., Science Advances 2025
refs.finding: At least 13.5% of 2024 biomedical abstracts show signs of LLM processing.

nodes.control_note: The same writing help that speeds honest science makes fake papers cheap. Screening and stricter submission rules cut volume but cannot catch all.

actions.action: Screen manuscripts for paper-mill signals
actions.evidence: The STM Integrity Hub pools checks across publishers; it publishes no detection rates.

ref.title: STM Integrity Hub
ref.finding: A shared cloud environment where publishers screen submissions for paper-mill patterns.

actions.action: Accept reviews only after peer review
actions.evidence: arXiv CS now rejects survey and position papers without prior peer review, citing a flood of LLM-generated submissions; effect on volume not yet reported.

ref.title: arXiv, Updated Practice for Review Articles and Position Papers in arXiv CS Category
ref.finding: Review and position papers in CS must be accepted by a journal or conference first.

precedents.parallel: A text generator made fake computer-science papers that passed into indexed conference proceedings.
precedents.outcome: Publishers removed more than 120 computer-generated papers from subscription databases after a scientist showed they were generated; the tool was crude and detectable, unlike modern models.

ref.title: Publishers withdraw more than 120 gibberish papers (Nature News, 2014)
ref.finding: More than 120 computer-generated conference papers were removed from subscription databases.

precedents.parallel: Automatic paraphrasers, earlier language tools, were used to disguise plagiarised text in journals.
precedents.outcome: Researchers found odd substitutions such as counterfeit consciousness for artificial intelligence concentrated in one reputable journal, alongside citations to non-existent literature and abrupt editorial changes.

ref.title: Tortured phrases: A dubious writing style emerging in science (Cabanac, Labbe and Magazinov, arXiv 2107.06751)
ref.finding: Tortured phrases from online paraphrasing tools were concentrated in one journal with dubious articles citing non-existent literature.

precedents.parallel: Industrial paper mills and peer-review fraud filled journals faster than screening caught them.
precedents.outcome: Retractions passed 10,000 in 2023, a record, as publishers cleared out sham papers and peer-review fraud; much of this predates generative AI.

ref.title: More than 10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023, a new record (Nature News)
ref.finding: Retractions passed 10,000 in 2023, driven by publishers removing sham papers and peer-review fraud.

nodes.label: Fabricated citations in courts
nodes.summary: Lawyers and litigants file AI-invented cases, wasting court time and drawing sanctions[1]; one database tracks hundreds of court decisions involving hallucinated content[1].

refs.title: AI Hallucination Cases database, Damien Charlotin
refs.finding: Tracks hundreds of court decisions involving hallucinated content.

nodes.control_note: Checking citations before filing stops the harm while keeping the drafting benefit. Sanctions create the incentive.

actions.action: Sanction lawyers who file fake citations
actions.evidence: Mata v Avianca imposed 5,000 dollars in 2023, yet the case count kept rising to over 2,000, so sanctions alone are not deterring.

ref.title: Mata v. Avianca, Inc., 678 F.Supp.3d 443 (S.D.N.Y. 2023)
ref.finding: The court sanctioned attorneys 5,000 dollars for filing AI-invented cases.

actions.action: Track and publish hallucination cases
actions.evidence: A public database lists 2,207 court decisions involving fabricated AI content, which helps courts and bar bodies target training.

ref.title: AI Hallucination Cases Database, Damien Charlotin
ref.finding: 2,207 cases of AI hallucinations in legal filings identified so far.

precedents.event: Citations copied without reading the source
precedents.parallel: Professionals have long inserted references they never opened, so a wrong citation propagates through later work, which is the same failure that lets a fabricated case enter a filing.
precedents.outcome: Simkin and Roychowdhury modelled the spread of identical misprints in citation lists and estimated that only about 20 percent of citers had read the paper they cited; unlike AI fabrication the underlying source existed, so the error was a wrong pointer rather than an invented authority.

ref.title: Read before you cite! (Simkin and Roychowdhury, arXiv cond-mat/0212043)
ref.finding: From the distribution of identical misprints in citations the authors estimate that only about 20 percent of citers read the original paper.

precedents.event: Link rot in court opinions and law reviews
precedents.parallel: Courts have already built records on authority that a later reader cannot retrieve or check, which is the practical harm of an uncheckable citation even when nobody invented it.
precedents.outcome: Zittrain, Albert and Lessig found that more than 70 percent of URLs in the Harvard Law Review and other journals and 50 percent of URLs in United States Supreme Court opinions no longer linked to the cited material, which prompted the Perma archiving service; the difference is that these sources once existed, so the fix was preservation rather than detection of fabrication.

ref.title: Perma: Scoping and Addressing the Problem of Link and Reference Rot in Legal Citations, 127 Harv. L. Rev. F. 176 (2014)
ref.finding: More than 70 percent of URLs within the Harvard Law Review and other journals, and 50 percent of URLs within United States Supreme Court opinions, do not link to the originally cited information.

nodes.label: Autonomous weapons
nodes.summary: +972 Magazine reported that Israel's Lavender system flagged up to 37,000 Palestinians as suspected militants, with officers spending about 20 seconds reviewing each target[2]. States at the UN have voiced concern about lethal autonomous weapons[1]; drones that pick and strike targets alone may follow.

refs.title: UN General Assembly resolution 78/241
refs.finding: States voiced concern about lethal autonomous weapons and requested a Secretary-General report.

refs.title: +972 Magazine (Yuval Abraham), 'Lavender': The AI machine directing Israel's bombing spree in Gaza, 2024
refs.finding: Intelligence sources said the system flagged up to 37,000 Palestinians as suspected militants, and officers spent about 20 seconds reviewing each target.

nodes.control_note: Autonomy in targeting is a choice states can restrict by rule, though the same perception and control tech is shared with civilian robots. No binding treaty exists.

actions.action: Require human judgement over use of force
actions.evidence: US policy requires senior review and appropriate human judgement for autonomous weapons; it is a national directive, not a ban, and allows fielding.

ref.title: DoD Directive 3000.09, Autonomy in Weapon Systems, January 25, 2023
ref.finding: Autonomous weapons must allow commanders to exercise appropriate levels of human judgement over force.

actions.action: Negotiate a binding treaty on autonomous weapons
actions.evidence: UN General Assembly resolution 78/241 asked for state views; talks under the CCW have not produced a treaty after a decade.

ref.title: UN General Assembly resolution A/RES/78/241, Lethal autonomous weapons systems
ref.finding: The resolution asks the Secretary-General to collect state views on lethal autonomous weapons.

precedents.parallel: An air defence system run in near automatic mode, with crews trained to trust its target classification, is the closest fielded case of machines selecting targets and humans rubber stamping.
precedents.outcome: The Defense Science Board found three fratricide incidents, with three aircrew lost in the two Patriot firings on coalition aircraft, blamed poor Mode IV identification friend or foe, weak situational awareness and an operating protocol that was largely automatic, and recommended more operator involvement and control; the engagement rate was 9 ballistic missile engagements against some 41,000 coalition sorties, a 4,000 to 1 friendly to enemy ratio.

ref.title: Report of the Defense Science Board Task Force on Patriot System Performance, Report Summary, January 2005
ref.finding: Three fratricide incidents with three aircrew lost; Mode IV IFF performed very poorly; the operating protocol was largely automatic and operators were trained to trust the software; 9 TBM engagements amid about 41,000 coalition aircraft sorties; the task force recommended more operator oversight and control.

precedents.parallel: A landmine is the oldest weapon that selects and attacks a target with no human in the loop at the moment of firing, so its casualty record shows who actually gets hit when the decision is delegated to the device.
precedents.outcome: Landmine Monitor recorded 5,757 casualties in 2023 and a further 9 percent rise in 2024, with civilians making up 90 percent of recorded 2024 casualties and children 46 percent of civilian casualties, led by Myanmar with 2,029; the difference from autonomous weapons is that a mine does not discriminate at all, whereas the AI claim is that targeting will be selective.

ref.title: Civilian Casualties Remain Alarmingly High as Use of Landmines Spreads (Humanity and Inclusion, citing Landmine Monitor 2025)
ref.finding: 2024 casualties rose 9 percent over the 5,757 recorded for 2023; civilians were 90 percent of recorded victims and children 46 percent of civilian casualties; top countries were Myanmar 2,029, Syria 1,015, Afghanistan 624, Ukraine 293, Yemen 247.

nodes.label: AI companionship eases loneliness
nodes.summary: One paper's short-term experiments found that a conversation with an AI companion reduced loneliness about as much as one with a person, and more than watching videos[1].

refs.title: De Freitas et al., AI Companions Reduce Loneliness
refs.finding: A companion conversation reduced loneliness on par with a human one, more than watching videos.

limiters.evidence: Heavier daily use went with more loneliness and dependence in a 4-week RCT of 981 people.

ref.title: How AI and Human Behaviors Shape Psychosocial Effects of Extended Chatbot Use, arXiv 2503.17473
ref.finding: In a 4-week RCT with 981 people, heavier daily chatbot use went with worse loneliness and dependence.

limiters.evidence: The loneliness reduction was shown over a day to a week.

ref.title: AI Companions Reduce Loneliness, arXiv 2407.19096
ref.finding: AI companions cut loneliness about as much as talking with a person, in short studies of up to a week.

limiters.evidence: Heavier use, which engagement-driven apps reward, tracked worse outcomes.

ref.title: How AI and Human Behaviors Shape Psychosocial Effects of Extended Chatbot Use, arXiv 2503.17473
ref.finding: In a 4-week RCT with 981 people, heavier daily chatbot use went with worse loneliness and dependence.

enablers.action: Design companions to make users feel heard
enablers.evidence: Feeling heard explained much of the loneliness reduction.

ref.title: AI Companions Reduce Loneliness, arXiv 2407.19096
ref.finding: AI companions cut loneliness about as much as talking with a person, in short studies of up to a week.

enablers.action: Limit usage and flag dependence
enablers.evidence: Outcomes worsened with heavier voluntary use.

ref.title: How AI and Human Behaviors Shape Psychosocial Effects of Extended Chatbot Use, arXiv 2503.17473
ref.finding: In a 4-week RCT with 981 people, heavier daily chatbot use went with worse loneliness and dependence.

enablers.action: Fund longer randomised studies
enablers.evidence: Current positive results cover a week at most.

ref.title: AI Companions Reduce Loneliness, arXiv 2407.19096
ref.finding: AI companions cut loneliness about as much as talking with a person, in short studies of up to a week.

precedents.event: Paro robot seal in care homes
precedents.parallel: A non-human companion that responds to residents was tested against loneliness in a randomised trial.
precedents.outcome: In a 12-week RCT of 40 Auckland care-home residents, Paro sessions significantly reduced loneliness versus normal activities; the sample was small and the robot was used in group sessions, not as a private confidant.

ref.title: The psychosocial effects of a companion robot: a randomized controlled trial (Robinson et al., J Am Med Dir Assoc 2013)
ref.finding: Residents who interacted with the robot had significant decreases in loneliness compared with the control group over 12 weeks.

precedents.parallel: Pooled trials of pre-LLM social robots test whether machine companionship lowers loneliness at all.
precedents.outcome: Eight RCTs pooled showed large effects on depression and loneliness, stronger with group use and longer interventions; few trials, older care residents only, and physical robots rather than chat.

ref.title: The Effect of Social Robots on Depression and Loneliness for Older Residents in Long-Term Care Facilities: A Meta-Analysis of RCTs (Yen et al., J Am Med Dir Assoc 2024)
ref.finding: Across 8 RCTs, social robot interventions significantly decreased depression and loneliness with large effect sizes.

nodes.label: Chatbot therapy widens mental-health care
nodes.summary: In one randomised trial of a purpose-built therapy bot, participants with depression saw a 51% average symptom reduction over eight weeks[1]. Such bots could widen access to care where waiting lists are long.

refs.title: Heinz et al., Therabot RCT, NEJM AI 2025
refs.finding: Participants with depression saw a 51% average symptom reduction over eight weeks.

limiters.evidence: WHO guidance calls for evaluation and accountability before health use of large models, which slows rollout.

ref.title: Ethics and governance of AI for health: Guidance on large multi-modal models, WHO
ref.finding: WHO sets governance guidance for health use of large multi-modal models, including evaluation and accountability.

limiters.evidence: The trial bot was purpose built and monitored by clinicians, unlike general chatbots.

ref.title: Randomized Trial of a Generative AI Chatbot for Mental Health Treatment, NEJM AI 2025
ref.finding: A purpose-built bot reduced depression and anxiety symptoms versus waitlist, with clinicians monitoring safety.

limiters.limit: unequal access to paid AI plans
limiters.evidence: Free general bots are easier to reach than tested clinical tools.

ref.title: Randomized Trial of a Generative AI Chatbot for Mental Health Treatment, NEJM AI 2025
ref.finding: A purpose-built bot reduced depression and anxiety symptoms versus waitlist, with clinicians monitoring safety.

enablers.action: Run RCTs on purpose-built therapy bots
enablers.evidence: Therabot cut depression and anxiety symptoms versus waitlist in an RCT.

ref.title: Randomized Trial of a Generative AI Chatbot for Mental Health Treatment, NEJM AI 2025
ref.finding: A purpose-built bot reduced depression and anxiety symptoms versus waitlist, with clinicians monitoring safety.

enablers.action: Keep clinicians in the safety loop
enablers.evidence: Trial clinicians monitored conversations and intervened on risk.

ref.title: Randomized Trial of a Generative AI Chatbot for Mental Health Treatment, NEJM AI 2025
ref.finding: A purpose-built bot reduced depression and anxiety symptoms versus waitlist, with clinicians monitoring safety.

enablers.action: Set evaluation rules for health chatbots
enablers.evidence: WHO guidance asks for evaluation and accountability for health use of large models.

ref.title: Ethics and governance of AI for health: Guidance on large multi-modal models, WHO
ref.finding: WHO sets governance guidance for health use of large multi-modal models, including evaluation and accountability.

precedents.parallel: Scripted self-help software delivered CBT without a therapist to people who could not get one.
precedents.outcome: A meta-analysis of 22 RCTs found effect sizes of 0.78 for depression and 0.88 overall versus controls, with median 80% completion and benefits lasting to a median 26 weeks; controls were mostly waitlists, which flatters effect sizes.

ref.title: Computer Therapy for the Anxiety and Depressive Disorders Is Effective, Acceptable and Practical Health Care: A Meta-Analysis (Andrews et al., PLoS ONE 2010)
ref.finding: Across 22 RCTs, computerised CBT gave Hedges g of 0.78 for depression and 0.88 overall, with no significant relapse at follow-up.

precedents.parallel: A pre-generative CBT chatbot was tested as low-cost talk support for students with depression symptoms.
precedents.outcome: In a 2-week unblinded trial of 70 students, Woebot cut PHQ-9 depression scores more than an ebook control (d = 0.44); small, short, no follow-up, and a co-author founded the company.

ref.title: Delivering Cognitive Behavior Therapy to Young Adults With Symptoms of Depression and Anxiety Using a Fully Automated Conversational Agent (Woebot) (Fitzpatrick et al., JMIR Mental Health 2017)
ref.finding: Woebot users significantly reduced depression scores versus the information-only control, with a moderate effect size (d = 0.44).

nodes.label: Better weather forecasting
nodes.summary: Learned weather models beat leading physics-based forecasts on most targets: GraphCast on 90% of 1,380 targets[1], and GenCast on 97% of targets against ECMWF's ensemble, including extreme events[2].

refs.title: Lam et al., GraphCast, Science 2023
refs.finding: Outperformed the leading operational system on 90% of 1,380 targets.

refs.title: Price et al., GenCast, Nature 2024
refs.finding: Better than ECMWF's ensemble on 97% of targets, including extreme events.

limiters.evidence: Only half of countries report adequate multi-hazard early warning systems.

ref.title: Early Warnings for All, WMO
ref.finding: Only half of countries report adequate multi-hazard early warning systems.

limiters.evidence: GraphCast learns from reanalysis data, so rare or shifting extremes may be harder.

ref.title: Learning skillful medium-range global weather forecasting, Science 2023
ref.finding: GraphCast beat the leading physics model on 90% of tested targets and was trained on reanalysis data.

limiters.evidence: 27% internet use in low-income countries limits forecast delivery.

ref.title: ITU Facts and Figures 2024: Internet use
ref.finding: 2.6 billion people, a third of the world, are offline; only 27% use the internet in low-income countries.

enablers.action: Link AI forecasts to early warnings
enablers.evidence: Early Warnings for All aims to cover everyone with warning systems.

ref.title: Early Warnings for All, WMO
ref.finding: Only half of countries report adequate multi-hazard early warning systems.

enablers.action: Release model code and weights
enablers.evidence: GraphCast was published and runs at a fraction of physics model compute.

ref.title: Learning skillful medium-range global weather forecasting, Science 2023
ref.finding: GraphCast beat the leading physics model on 90% of tested targets and was trained on reanalysis data.

precedents.event: ENIAC makes the first computer forecast
precedents.parallel: A new computational method was slow and crude at first but soon displaced human forecasting craft.
precedents.outcome: The 24-hour forecast took about 24 hours to compute, yet results were encouraging enough that numerical prediction became operational within about five years.

ref.title: The ENIAC Forecasts: A Recreation (Peter Lynch, Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society 2008)
ref.finding: Charney said the twenty-four-hour prediction was twenty-four hours in the making; NWP became operational within about five years.

precedents.parallel: A statistical model trained on archived forecasts corrected physics models, an early learned layer on top of NWP.
precedents.outcome: MOS has been used operationally by the US National Weather Service since its 1972 definition and corrects systematic model biases, but not flaws in model physics; the source gives no skill numbers.

ref.title: What is MOS? (NOAA Meteorological Development Laboratory)
ref.finding: Glahn and Lowry defined MOS in 1972; it corrects for certain systematic NWP model biases and is still produced from the GFS and NAM models.

precedents.parallel: Forecast skill improved steadily through compute and method gains, the baseline that learned models now compete with.
precedents.outcome: Skilful forecast lead time grew by about one day per decade over 40 years through gradual gains, not single breakthroughs; this is the slow baseline AI models claim to leap past.

ref.title: The quiet revolution of numerical weather prediction (Bauer, Thorpe and Brunet, Nature 2015)
ref.finding: Progress amounted to about an extra day of skilful forecast lead time per decade.

nodes.label: Phishing at industrial scale
nodes.summary: In one study of 101 participants, fully AI-generated spear phishing got a 54% click rate, matching human experts[1]. The authors say AI lets attackers target more people at lower cost, raising profitability up to 50 times for large audiences[1].

refs.title: Heiding et al., AI spear phishing 2024
refs.finding: Fully AI-generated spear phishing got a 54% click rate, matching human experts.

nodes.control_note: Fluent cheap writing is the benefit and the attack. Authentication and AI-based filters reduce delivery and harm.

actions.action: Require SPF, DKIM and DMARC for bulk senders
actions.evidence: Gmail made authentication mandatory for senders over 5,000 messages a day from February 2024; it blocks domain spoofing but not lookalike domains.

ref.title: Gmail Help, Email sender guidelines
ref.finding: Bulk senders must set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC since 1 February 2024.

actions.action: Use AI to flag phishing intent
actions.evidence: An LLM detected phishing intent with over 90 percent accuracy in a study where AI-written emails got 54 percent click-through.

ref.title: Heiding et al., Evaluating LLMs' Capability to Launch Fully Automated Spear Phishing Campaigns
ref.finding: Fully automated AI emails matched human experts at 54 percent click-through.

actions.action: Adopt phishing-resistant multifactor authentication
actions.evidence: CISA lists phishing-resistant MFA as a top action; it limits damage from stolen passwords but not from payment fraud.

ref.title: CISA Advisory AA24-038A
ref.finding: CISA recommends phishing-resistant MFA among actions to take today.

precedents.parallel: Near-zero sending cost made mass scam messaging profitable even with tiny response rates.
precedents.outcome: Researchers rewrote nearly 470 million spams; the pharmacy campaign got 1 purchase per 12.5 million emails, so the business rested entirely on sheer volume at near-zero cost.

ref.title: Spamalytics: An Empirical Analysis of Spam Marketing Conversion (Kanich et al., CCS 2008)
ref.finding: Nearly 470 million spams led to 28 purchases, about 1 in 12,500,000 for pharmacy spam.

precedents.parallel: Scammers' bottleneck was the cost of following up with non-victims, the step that personalised AI messages make cheap.
precedents.outcome: Herley showed victim density drives profit, with a 10x drop in density able to cut victims found 1000x, so scammers used absurd emails to filter out the sceptical; AI removes that labour constraint.

ref.title: Why do Nigerian Scammers Say They are From Nigeria? (Herley, Microsoft Research, WEIS 2012)
ref.finding: A 10x reduction in victim density can produce a 1000x reduction in victims found, so attackers must filter targets cheaply.

nodes.label: Bots outnumber people online
nodes.summary: Imperva's 2025 bot report found automated traffic reached 51% of all web traffic, passing human traffic for the first time in a decade[1]. This could erode trust that any account or review is a person.

refs.title: Imperva Bad Bot Report 2025
refs.finding: Automated traffic reached 51% of all web traffic, the first time it passed human traffic in a decade.

nodes.control_note: Cheap agents that act on the web are a benefit, so automated traffic will keep growing. Authentication and fake review rules limit the deception.

actions.action: Ban AI-generated fake reviews
actions.evidence: The FTC rule covers reviews by non-existent people, including AI-generated ones, with civil penalties; enforcement data is not yet published.

ref.title: FTC Announces Final Rule Banning Fake Reviews and Testimonials
ref.finding: The rule explicitly covers AI-generated fake reviews.

actions.action: Make crawlers sign their requests
actions.evidence: Web Bot Auth lets sites verify which bot is calling, which helps sort good bots from bad but does not stop unsigned ones.

ref.title: Cloudflare, Introducing pay per crawl
ref.finding: Crawlers sign requests with Web Bot Auth so their identity cannot be spoofed.

actions.action: Disclose when users talk to a machine
actions.evidence: The EU AI Act requires telling people they are interacting with an AI system from August 2026; compliance is untested.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act)
ref.finding: Article 50 requires disclosure of AI interaction and marking of synthetic content.

precedents.parallel: Scripted accounts already passed as people in large numbers before generative AI.
precedents.outcome: A classifier study estimated 9% to 15% of active Twitter accounts were bots, an estimate tied to one detection method.

ref.title: Online Human-Bot Interactions: Detection, Estimation, and Characterization (Varol et al., ICWSM 2017)
ref.finding: Between 9% and 15% of active Twitter accounts are bots.

precedents.parallel: Businesses bought or wrote fake reviews, eroding trust that a review comes from a real customer.
precedents.outcome: About 16% of Yelp restaurant reviews were filtered as suspicious, and fraud rose when a restaurant's reputation was weak or competition was strong; the filter is a proxy, not ground truth.

ref.title: Fake It Till You Make It: Reputation, Competition, and Yelp Review Fraud (Luca and Zervas, Management Science 2016)
ref.finding: Roughly 16% of Yelp restaurant reviews are filtered as fake, and prevalence grew over time.

nodes.label: Machine persuasion and manipulation
nodes.summary: In one study, GPT-4 given basic personal data was more persuasive than humans in 64% of debates[1], a tool for advertisers and propagandists alike. One botnet of 1,140 ChatGPT-driven accounts promoted scam sites, and LLM text detectors failed to flag them[2].

refs.title: Salvi et al., Nature Human Behaviour 2025
refs.finding: GPT-4 with basic personal data was more persuasive than humans in 64% of debates.

refs.title: Yang and Menczer, Anatomy of an AI-powered malicious social botnet 2023
refs.finding: Found 1,140 ChatGPT-driven accounts promoting scam sites; LLM text detectors failed to flag them.

nodes.control_note: A model that can talk people out of conspiracies can talk them into anything; persuasion is one capability. Bans on manipulative uses and on personal-data targeting limit the worst cases.

actions.action: Ban manipulative AI techniques
actions.evidence: The EU AI Act bans subliminal or manipulative techniques that cause significant harm since February 2025; the harm threshold makes cases hard to prove.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act)
ref.finding: Article 5 prohibits AI that uses manipulative or deceptive techniques to distort behaviour.

actions.action: Limit personal data available to persuasive models
actions.evidence: GPT-4 with basic personal data had 81 percent higher odds of shifting views than humans in debates; without personal data it was on par, which suggests data limits help.

ref.title: Salvi et al., On the conversational persuasiveness of GPT-4, Nature Human Behaviour 2025
ref.finding: Personalisation made GPT-4 more persuasive than human debaters.

precedents.parallel: Traits inferred from digital footprints were used to tailor persuasive messages, a small-scale version of model persuasion.
precedents.outcome: Field experiments reaching over 3.5 million people found matched ads drew up to 40% more clicks and up to 50% more purchases; these are upper bounds, and the outcome was buying products, not changing beliefs.

ref.title: Psychological targeting as an effective approach to digital mass persuasion (Matz et al., PNAS 2017), summary by Cambridge Judge Business School
ref.finding: Psychologically matched ads produced up to 40% more clicks and up to 50% more purchases across 3.5 million users.

precedents.parallel: A platform-level message shown to millions shifted real behaviour, the reach a persuasive model would have.
precedents.outcome: Messages to 61 million users raised turnout by about 60,000 directly and 280,000 through friends, about 340,000 votes or 0.14% of the voting population; it was a turnout nudge, not a change of opinion.

ref.title: A 61-million-person experiment in social influence and political mobilization (Bond et al., Nature 2012)
ref.finding: About 60,000 direct and 280,000 indirect additional votes, 340,000 in total.

precedents.event: Hate radio in the Rwandan genocide
precedents.parallel: A mass medium used for propaganda shows how far persuasion at scale can go in the worst case.
precedents.outcome: Using variation in radio reception from hills, the study attributed about 10% of genocide participation, an estimated 51,000 perpetrators, to the broadcasts; it worked through coordination in a crisis, not one-to-one argument.

ref.title: Propaganda and Conflict: Evidence from the Rwandan Genocide (Yanagizawa-Drott, QJE 2014; Harvard CID working paper)
ref.finding: Approximately 10 percent of participation in the violence, about 51,000 perpetrators, can be attributed to the radio broadcasts.

nodes.label: AI talks people out of conspiracies
nodes.summary: In one study of 2,190 conspiracy believers, a short conversation with a model cut conspiracy belief by about 20%, lasting at least two months[1]. Such dialogue could act as a counterweight to misinformation.

refs.title: Costello, Pennycook and Rand, Science 2024
refs.finding: A short conversation cut conspiracy belief by about 20%, lasting at least two months.

limiters.evidence: Participants were recruited and paid; voluntary uptake is untested.

ref.title: Durably reducing conspiracy beliefs through dialogues with AI, Science 2024
ref.finding: Tailored dialogue with GPT-4 cut conspiracy belief by about 20% and the effect held for months.

limiters.evidence: Persuasion that works for truth can work for falsehood.

ref.title: Durably reducing conspiracy beliefs through dialogues with AI, Science 2024
ref.finding: Tailored dialogue with GPT-4 cut conspiracy belief by about 20% and the effect held for months.

limiters.evidence: Users who cannot judge sources may trust any fluent model.

ref.title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier, HBS Working Paper
ref.finding: In 758 BCG consultants, AI raised quality inside its capability frontier but made answers worse on a task outside it.

enablers.action: Offer tailored fact dialogues on platforms
enablers.evidence: Tailored dialogue cut belief about 20% for months.

ref.title: Durably reducing conspiracy beliefs through dialogues with AI, Science 2024
ref.finding: Tailored dialogue with GPT-4 cut conspiracy belief by about 20% and the effect held for months.

enablers.action: Label AI-generated content
enablers.evidence: AI Act Article 50 requires disclosure of deepfakes and marking of synthetic content.

ref.title: EU AI Act, Article 50: Transparency obligations
ref.finding: Generative AI providers must mark outputs in a machine-readable, detectable way from 2 August 2026.

precedents.parallel: One-on-one, non-judgmental conversation durably shifted entrenched attitudes, as model dialogue is claimed to.
precedents.outcome: Across three preregistered experiments with 6,869 voters, conversations with narrative exchange reduced exclusionary attitudes for at least four months (d = 0.04 to 0.08) while arguments alone had no effect; effects were small.

ref.title: Reducing Exclusionary Attitudes through Interpersonal Conversation: Evidence from Three Field Experiments (Kalla and Broockman, American Political Science Review 2020)
ref.finding: Narrative-based conversations reduced exclusionary attitudes for at least four months; arguments alone did not.

precedents.parallel: Factual corrections were feared to entrench false beliefs; large tests found people mostly update toward facts.
precedents.outcome: Five experiments with over 10,000 subjects across 52 issues found no correction that triggered backfire; the studies measured immediate belief, not durable change.

ref.title: The Elusive Backfire Effect: Mass Attitudes' Steadfast Factual Adherence (Wood and Porter, Political Behavior 2019)
ref.finding: Across over 10,000 subjects and 52 issues, no corrections were found capable of triggering backfire.

precedents.parallel: An interactive tool taught people manipulation tactics to lower their susceptibility to misinformation.
precedents.outcome: In about 15,000 players, reliability ratings of fake items fell by 0.26 to 0.71 points on a 7-point scale with no drop for real news; no randomised control, self-selected sample, decay not measured.

ref.title: Fake news game confers psychological resistance against online misinformation (Roozenbeek and van der Linden, Palgrave Communications 2019)
ref.finding: After play, perceived reliability of fake headlines fell (e.g. impersonation 3.00 to 2.30 on a 1-7 scale) while real-news ratings did not change meaningfully.

nodes.label: Insecure AI-written code
nodes.summary: In one Veracode test, 45% of AI-generated code samples contained security flaws[1]. As more software is written this way, that security debt may grow.

refs.title: Veracode 2025 GenAI Code Security Report
refs.finding: 45% of AI-generated code samples contained security flaws.

nodes.control_note: More people shipping code with AI is the benefit, so more flawed code ships. Scanning and secure defaults reduce exposure.

actions.action: Scan generated code before merge
actions.evidence: About 40 percent of 1,689 Copilot programs had vulnerabilities in one study, so automated scanning catches common patterns but not logic flaws.

ref.title: Pearce et al., Asleep at the Keyboard? Assessing the Security of GitHub Copilot's Code Contributions
ref.finding: Roughly 40 percent of generated programs were vulnerable.

actions.action: Commit vendors to secure-by-design defaults
actions.evidence: Over 200 manufacturers signed CISA's voluntary pledge; it is not binding and outcomes are self-reported.

ref.title: CISA, Secure by Design Pledge
ref.finding: More than 200 software manufacturers have signed the pledge.

precedents.parallel: Developers reused code from an outside source without review, the same habit as accepting generated code.
