precedents.outcome: 15.4% of 1.3 million Android apps contained security-related Stack Overflow snippets, and 97.9% of those contained at least one insecure snippet.

ref.title: Stack Overflow Considered Harmful? The Impact of Copy and Paste on Android Application Security (Fischer et al., IEEE S&P 2017)
ref.finding: 15.4% of 1.3 million apps had security-related snippets from Stack Overflow; 97.9% of these had at least one insecure snippet.

precedents.parallel: One flaw in widely reused code sat silently in countless systems, the way a common generated pattern could.
precedents.outcome: CISA rated the Log4j flaw critical, with active widespread exploitation across consumer, enterprise and operational technology products, and told organisations to assume it was present even where they lacked visibility.

ref.title: Apache Log4j Vulnerability Guidance (CISA)
ref.finding: CVE-2021-44228 is a critical remote code execution flaw under active, widespread exploitation in software used across services and products.

nodes.label: AI-generated child abuse imagery
nodes.summary: Generators are used to create abuse imagery, including deepfakes of specific real children[1]. The Internet Watch Foundation found thousands of AI-generated abuse images on a single dark web forum within a month[1].

refs.title: Internet Watch Foundation, AI and child sexual abuse imagery
refs.finding: Found thousands of AI-generated abuse images on a single dark web forum within a month.

nodes.control_note: Abuse imagery has no legitimate use, so training data hygiene, model removal and criminal law can largely stop it, but open models that are already out cannot be recalled.

actions.action: Remove abuse material from training data
actions.evidence: Eleven firms including OpenAI, Google and Stability AI committed to Safety by Design principles; compliance is voluntary and not audited.

ref.title: Thorn and All Tech Is Human, Generative AI Principles for child safety
ref.finding: Major AI firms committed to clean training data and remove nudify models.

actions.action: Report and remove AI abuse imagery
actions.evidence: IWF assessed 8,029 realistic AI abuse images and videos in 2025 and saw AI videos rise from 13 to 3,443, so removal is falling behind.

ref.title: Internet Watch Foundation, AI-generated child sexual abuse report
ref.finding: AI child abuse videos rose from 13 in 2024 to 3,443 in 2025.

precedents.parallel: Cheap cameras and cheap distribution already pushed the volume of abuse imagery past what clearinghouses and police could act on, which is the same capacity failure generators are now accused of causing.
precedents.outcome: Google and NCMEC researchers found detected abuse imagery had grown exponentially to nearly one million detected events per month, exceeding the capability of independent clearinghouses and law enforcement to take action, and argued for machine learning to automate triage; the measure is detections rather than abuse, so part of the rise reflects wider deployment of detection itself.

ref.title: Rethinking the Detection of Child Sexual Abuse Imagery on the Internet (WWW 2019)
ref.finding: The first longitudinal study of the distribution of this imagery finds exponential growth to nearly one million detected events per month, exceeding the capabilities of independent clearinghouses and law enforcement to take action.

nodes.label: Homogenised ideas and culture
nodes.summary: In one UK study, AI ideas made individual stories more creative but the stories more similar to each other[1], a sign that AI help could shrink the diversity of ideas.

refs.title: Doshi and Hauser, Science Advances 2024
refs.finding: AI ideas made individual stories more creative but stories more similar to each other.

nodes.control_note: The quality gain comes from anchoring on model ideas, and the anchoring is what makes work alike. Varied prompts and models may soften it, but evidence is thin.

actions.action: Offer several diverse AI ideas, not one
actions.evidence: Five ideas instead of one raised quality but stories stayed more similar than human-only ones; no tested method yet restores diversity.

ref.title: Doshi and Hauser, Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content, Science Advances 2024
ref.finding: AI-aided stories were more creative but more similar to each other.

actions.action: Disclose AI use in published creative work
actions.evidence: The AI Act requires marking synthetic content; readers in Doshi and Hauser wanted disclosure, but no study links disclosure to diversity.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act)
ref.finding: Article 50 requires marking of AI-generated content.

precedents.parallel: Search and hyperlinks made each literature lookup faster but steered researchers toward the same few sources, much as AI help can polish each piece of work while making all of it more alike.
precedents.outcome: Across 34 million articles, more online availability went with citing more recent work, fewer journals and fewer articles, concentrated on fewer sources; other bibliometricians disputed parts of this in Science letters, so the size of the effect is contested.

ref.title: Electronic publication and the narrowing of science and scholarship (Evans, Science 2008)
ref.finding: As more journal issues came online, fewer journals and articles were cited and citations concentrated on fewer of them.

precedents.parallel: When people could see what others chose, attention piled onto the same songs, a measured case of a shared signal pulling many independent choices toward the same outcome.
precedents.outcome: With 14,341 participants, stronger social influence raised both inequality and unpredictability of song success; it concerns concentration of popularity in a lab market, not the content of new work itself.

ref.title: Experimental study of inequality and unpredictability in an artificial cultural market (Salganik, Dodds, Watts, Science 2006)
ref.finding: Increasing the strength of social influence increased both inequality and unpredictability of success.

nodes.label: Automated mass surveillance
nodes.summary: Governments in at least 22 countries used AI-based tools for censorship, according to Freedom House[1]. Cheap vision and language models could let states monitor and censor at a scale that once needed armies of people.

refs.title: Freedom House, Freedom on the Net 2023
refs.finding: Governments in at least 22 countries used AI-based tools for censorship.

nodes.control_note: Mass surveillance is a political choice that law can restrict in democracies, though the vision and language tech is shared with assistive tools. In autocracies it is not preventable from outside.

actions.action: Ban real-time remote biometric identification
actions.evidence: The EU AI Act bans most real-time biometric identification in public by police, with exceptions for serious crimes.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act)
ref.finding: Article 5 prohibits real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces with narrow exceptions.

actions.action: Require algorithm audits and redress
actions.evidence: Freedom House found internet freedom fell for 13 years and AI censorship laws in over 21 countries; it recommends audits and appeal rights, untested at scale.

ref.title: Freedom House, Freedom on the Net 2023: The Repressive Power of Artificial Intelligence
ref.finding: Legal frameworks in at least 21 countries require or encourage automated content removal.

precedents.parallel: Mass monitoring of a population once took a huge paid workforce plus informants, the labour that cheap vision and language models could replace.
precedents.outcome: By the end the Ministry for State Security had about 91,000 full-time staff, and its foreign intelligence arm alone ran about 10,000 informants; the apparatus did not stop the regime falling in 1989.

ref.title: Inoffizielle Mitarbeiter des Ministeriums fuer Staatssicherheit (Bundesarchiv publication page)
ref.finding: The SED leadership had a ministry with, at the end, about 91,000 full-time employees.

precedents.parallel: Automated bulk collection of everyone's call records is the closest documented case of machine-scale state monitoring justified by security.
precedents.outcome: The US privacy oversight board found no instance where the program made a concrete difference to a counterterrorism investigation, and only one arguable case in seven years of helping identify an unknown suspect; it recommended ending the program.

ref.title: Report on the Telephone Records Program Conducted under Section 215 (PCLOB, January 2014)
ref.finding: We have not identified a single instance in which the program made a concrete difference in the outcome of a counterterrorism investigation.

nodes.label: AI as a tool of trade and tariffs
nodes.summary: The US has tied AI access to political alignment: a January 2025 rule sorted countries into three tiers with caps on advanced chips, later rescinded[1], and the July 2025 AI Action Plan aims to export the full American AI stack to allies while countering China[2].

refs.title: Framework for Artificial Intelligence Diffusion, Federal Register, Jan 2025
refs.finding: Sorted countries into three tiers with caps on advanced chips; later rescinded.

refs.title: America's AI Action Plan, July 2025
refs.finding: Sets a goal of exporting the full American AI stack to allies and countering China.

nodes.control_note: Rationing chips by country is a policy choice that governments can drop with little loss of the technology's benefits, as the US showed by rescinding its diffusion rule.

actions.action: Publish country tiers through open rulemaking
actions.evidence: The 2025 diffusion rule set tiers by Federal Register notice, which at least made the leverage visible; it was rescinded before taking effect.

ref.title: Framework for Artificial Intelligence Diffusion, Federal Register, 15 January 2025
ref.finding: The rule set export limits on advanced chips and model weights by country.

precedents.parallel: Producers of a resource the whole economy depended on cut supply to countries by their political alignment, as chip and model access can be rationed by country.
precedents.outcome: Oil prices first doubled, then quadrupled; the embargo was lifted in March 1974 and consumers responded with the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, fuel economy standards and the International Energy Agency.

ref.title: Oil Embargo, 1973-1974 (US Office of the Historian)
ref.finding: The price of oil per barrel first doubled, then quadrupled, and the crisis led to the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and the IEA.

precedents.parallel: The US used trade sanctions to force a market-share and pricing deal on a rival's chip industry, an earlier case of chips as a lever of state power.
precedents.outcome: Reagan imposed 100 percent tariffs on 300 million dollars of Japanese imports in 1987; the deal handed Japanese exporters windfall DRAM profits, sped up Korean entry, did not bring US firms back into DRAM, and hurt US computer makers who used the chips.

ref.title: The U.S.-Japan Semiconductor Trade Conflict (Irwin, NBER, 1996)
ref.finding: Reagan imposed 100 percent tariffs on $300 million of Japanese imports; the clear losers were semiconductor users.

nodes.label: Backdoored models
nodes.summary: In one study, backdoors trained into models persisted through standard safety training[1], and JFrog found about 100 Hugging Face models that ran code on load, some opening a reverse shell[2]. A downloaded model, foreign or domestic, can be a trojan.

refs.title: Hubinger et al., Sleeper Agents 2024
refs.finding: Backdoors trained into models persisted through standard safety training.

refs.title: JFrog, malicious Hugging Face models 2024
refs.finding: Found about 100 models on Hugging Face that ran code on load, some opening a reverse shell.

nodes.control_note: Open weight sharing is what makes models cheap and widely usable, and it is also how trojans travel. Safe formats and scanning stop file-level malware, not behavioural backdoors.

actions.action: Load weights only in safetensors format
actions.evidence: Safetensors stores tensors without executable pickle code, closing the route used by about 100 malicious Hugging Face models; it does nothing against trained-in backdoors.

ref.title: Hugging Face, Safetensors documentation
ref.finding: A format for storing tensors safely, as opposed to pickle.

actions.action: Scan model repositories for malicious payloads
actions.evidence: JFrog's scan found around 100 malicious models on Hugging Face in 2024.

ref.title: JFrog, Data Scientists Targeted by Malicious Hugging Face ML Models with Silent Backdoor
ref.finding: About 100 malicious models were found on Hugging Face.

actions.action: Restrict untrusted models from sensitive systems
actions.evidence: Backdoors survived fine-tuning, RL and adversarial training in Sleeper Agents, so isolation is the fallback when detection fails.

ref.title: Hubinger et al., Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist Through Safety Training
ref.finding: Backdoor behaviour persisted through standard safety training.

precedents.parallel: A pre-generative-AI demonstration that a model trained by someone else can hide attacker-triggered behaviour while scoring well on the user's own tests.
precedents.outcome: A street-sign classifier read stop signs with a sticker as speed limits, and the backdoor survived retraining for a new task with about a 25 percent accuracy drop when triggered; it was a research demonstration, not a documented attack in the wild.

ref.title: BadNets: Identifying Vulnerabilities in the Machine Learning Model Supply Chain (Gu, Dolan-Gavitt, Garg)
ref.finding: The backdoor in a street sign detector persisted even when the network was retrained for another task.

precedents.parallel: Trusted software downloaded through official channels carried hidden malicious code, as a downloaded model can carry hidden behaviour.
precedents.outcome: About 18,000 customers received the compromised update while the attacker chose a small set of high-value targets, including federal agencies, for espionage; it went undetected from early 2020 until November 2020.

ref.title: SolarWinds Cyberattack Demands Significant Federal and Private-Sector Response (US GAO)
ref.finding: SolarWinds estimated that roughly 18,000 customers received a compromised software update.

precedents.parallel: A widely reused open component shipped with a hidden backdoor inserted upstream, the same trust problem as open model weights passed between users.
precedents.outcome: Versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 carried malicious code that could allow unauthorized access, and CISA told users to downgrade to an uncompromised version such as 5.4.6 and hunt for malicious activity.

ref.title: Reported Supply Chain Compromise Affecting XZ Utils Data Compression Library, CVE-2024-3094 (CISA)
ref.finding: Malicious code embedded in XZ Utils 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 may allow unauthorized access to affected systems.

nodes.label: AI-driven attacks on connected devices
nodes.summary: Cheap automated exploitation of routers, cameras and industrial controllers could recruit botnets or damage equipment. Mirai already enslaved about 600,000 IoT devices with default passwords[1], and a state actor pre-positioned in US critical infrastructure through edge devices[2].

refs.title: Antonakakis et al., Understanding the Mirai Botnet, USENIX Security 2017
refs.finding: Mirai enslaved about 600,000 IoT devices with default passwords and took down major sites.

refs.title: CISA advisory AA24-038A, Volt Typhoon
refs.finding: A state actor pre-positioned in US critical infrastructure via edge devices.

nodes.control_note: AI that finds vulnerabilities to patch them also finds them to exploit. Device security law and patching reduce the pool of easy targets.

actions.action: Ban default passwords on connected devices
actions.evidence: The UK PSTI Act bans universal default passwords since April 2024; Mirai reached 600,000 devices largely through weak credentials.

ref.title: Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure Act 2022
ref.finding: UK law setting security requirements for connectable consumer products.

actions.action: Patch internet-facing devices and replace end-of-life gear
actions.evidence: CISA lists patching and end-of-life replacement as top actions after Volt Typhoon compromised infrastructure via routers.

ref.title: CISA Advisory AA24-038A, PRC State-Sponsored Actors Compromise U.S. Critical Infrastructure
ref.finding: Patch internet-facing systems and plan end-of-life replacement.

actions.action: Study botnet growth to target defences
actions.evidence: The Mirai study traced 600,000 infections to easily compromised embedded devices.

ref.title: Antonakakis et al., Understanding the Mirai Botnet, USENIX Security 2017
ref.finding: Mirai peaked at 600,000 infected IoT devices.

precedents.parallel: Simple automated infection of cheap cameras and routers built a botnet large enough to knock major services offline, the low-skill end of what automated exploitation can do.
precedents.outcome: Mirai peaked at about 600,000 infected devices and overwhelmed several high-profile targets with DDoS attacks, and variants kept competing for vulnerable hosts afterwards; it used no AI.

ref.title: Understanding the Mirai Botnet (Antonakakis et al., USENIX Security 2017)
ref.finding: Mirai reached a peak of 600k infections, composed primarily of embedded and IoT devices.

precedents.parallel: Remote attackers took over industrial control systems and switched off physical equipment, the outcome feared from automated attacks on controllers.
precedents.outcome: About 225,000 customers lost power after attackers opened breakers at three distributors within 30 minutes, then wiped systems to slow recovery; it was run by human operators over months of reconnaissance, not automated.

ref.title: Cyber-Attack Against Ukrainian Critical Infrastructure, IR-ALERT-H-16-056-01 (CISA)
ref.finding: Remote cyber intrusions at three regional electric power distribution companies caused outages affecting approximately 225,000 customers.

precedents.parallel: Malware altered industrial controller settings to physically destroy machines while hiding the damage from operators.
precedents.outcome: Iran replaced about 1,000 IR-1 centrifuges in late 2009 or early 2010, and the authors judged Stuxnet a reasonable but unconfirmed explanation; it was a costly state operation, not a cheap automated one.

ref.title: Did Stuxnet Take Out 1,000 Centrifuges at the Natanz Enrichment Plant? (Albright, Brannan, Walrond, ISIS 2010)
ref.finding: Iran decommissioned and replaced about 1,000 IR-1 centrifuges, and Stuxnet is a reasonable explanation for the damage.

nodes.label: Erosion of social skills
nodes.summary: Practising conversation with an always-agreeable machine may leave people, especially teens, less able to handle friction with real people. In one US survey, about a third of teen users found AI conversations as satisfying as friends or more[1]; one study found heavy users socialised less[2].

refs.title: Common Sense Media, Talk, Trust and Trade-offs 2025
refs.finding: About a third of teen users found AI conversations as satisfying as or more than with friends.

refs.title: MIT Media Lab and OpenAI, affective use study 2025
refs.finding: Heavy users socialised less with people.

nodes.control_note: The always-available patient partner that eases loneliness is the same thing that may crowd out human friction. Safeguards for minors and less sycophantic design may reduce harm; evidence is short-term.

actions.action: Regulate companion chatbots for minors
actions.evidence: California SB 243 requires companion bots to disclose they are AI and add safeguards for minors; no outcome data yet.

ref.title: California SB-243 Companion chatbots
ref.finding: A California bill setting duties for operators of companion chatbots.

actions.action: Flag heavy use and emotional dependence
actions.evidence: In a four-week RCT with 981 people, heavier voluntary use predicted more loneliness and dependence, while voice or text mode made no difference.

ref.title: Fang et al., How AI and Human Behaviors Shape Psychosocial Effects of Extended Chatbot Use
ref.finding: Participants who used the chatbot more showed consistently worse psychosocial outcomes.

precedents.parallel: A new communication technology was feared to crowd out real relationships, and an early study seemed to confirm it.
precedents.outcome: The 1998 study of 93 Pittsburgh families found small but reliable drops in social involvement and well-being, but in the follow-up those effects faded, and later results showed benefits for extraverts and harm mainly for introverts and the less supported.

ref.title: Internet Paradox Revisited coverage (Carnegie Mellon News, 6 September 2001)
ref.finding: The negative social effects seen in the original HomeNet sample faded over three years, with a rich get richer pattern by personality.

precedents.parallel: Smartphones and social media prompted the same worry about teens losing real-world social ability, with large datasets to test it.
precedents.outcome: Across 355,358 adolescents, digital technology use explained at most 0.4 percent of the variation in well-being, which the authors called too small to warrant policy change; it measured well-being, not social skill directly.

ref.title: The association between adolescent well-being and digital technology use (Orben, Przybylski, Nature Human Behaviour 2019)
ref.finding: The negative association between digital technology use and adolescent well-being explains at most 0.4% of its variation.

nodes.label: Net climate effect of AI
nodes.summary: AI adds emissions through data centres: Google reported its emissions rose 48% since 2019, driven by data-centre energy[2]. The IEA says widespread AI applications could cut more emissions than data centres add, if adopted[1]. Which side wins is still open.

refs.title: IEA, Energy and AI 2025
refs.finding: Widespread AI applications could cut emissions by more than data centres add, if adopted.

refs.title: Google Environmental Report 2024
refs.finding: Google's emissions rose 48% since 2019, driven by data-centre energy.

limiters.evidence: Data centre use may rise from 415 TWh in 2024 to 945 TWh by 2030.

ref.title: Energy and AI, Executive summary, IEA 2025
ref.finding: Data centre power use may rise from 415 TWh in 2024 to 945 TWh by 2030; existing AI uses could cut about 5% of energy emissions by 2035.

limiters.evidence: IEA estimates existing AI uses could cut about 5% of energy emissions by 2035, only if broadly applied.

ref.title: Energy and AI, Executive summary, IEA 2025
ref.finding: Data centre power use may rise from 415 TWh in 2024 to 945 TWh by 2030; existing AI uses could cut about 5% of energy emissions by 2035.

enablers.action: Apply AI to grid and industry efficiency
enablers.evidence: Broad use of existing AI solutions could cut about 5% of energy-related emissions by 2035.

ref.title: Energy and AI, Executive summary, IEA 2025
ref.finding: Data centre power use may rise from 415 TWh in 2024 to 945 TWh by 2030; existing AI uses could cut about 5% of energy emissions by 2035.

enablers.action: Improve energy efficiency of AI hardware
enablers.evidence: Hardware energy efficiency improved about 40% a year.

ref.title: The 2025 AI Index Report, Stanford HAI
ref.finding: GPT-3.5-level inference cost fell over 280-fold in two years; fewer than half of US CS teachers feel equipped to teach AI.

precedents.parallel: A 1999 claim that internet equipment was eating a large and fast-growing share of US electricity mirrors today's projections that AI data centres will swamp the grid.
precedents.outcome: LBNL measured office and network equipment at about 74 TWh a year, roughly 2% of US electricity (3% with telecom and manufacturing), against claims of 8% to 13%; correcting Mills' assumptions cut his estimate about eightfold, though AI training loads are denser than 1990s PCs.

ref.title: Berkeley Lab studies refute claims of Internet energy consumption (LBNL, 2001)
ref.finding: Office and network equipment used about 2% of US electricity in 1999, not the 8% to 13% widely reported; Mills overestimated, in places more than tenfold.

precedents.event: Data centre energy decoupling from demand
precedents.parallel: Forecasts that data centre energy would double or quadruple with demand resemble current AI energy extrapolations that ignore efficiency gains.
precedents.outcome: Masanet and colleagues found global data centre energy use grew far more modestly than the doubling claimed, staying around 1% of world electricity because efficiency gains ran in parallel; this held before the AI build-out and says nothing about whether AI's optimisation benefits outweigh its load.

ref.title: Recalibrating global data center energy-use estimates (Science, 2020)
ref.finding: Simplistic extrapolations overlooked strong efficiency trends; new data suggest more modest growth in global data center energy use, at around 1% of worldwide electricity.

nodes.label: Violent backlash against AI
nodes.summary: Anger at job loss and AI companies could turn into sabotage of robotaxis and data centres or attacks on people; one Pew survey found 51% of US adults more concerned than excited about AI[1]. Violent incidents, real or staged, could also justify wider surveillance and control.

refs.title: Pew Research Center, US public and AI experts, April 2025
refs.finding: 51% of US adults are more concerned than excited about AI, versus 15% of experts.

refs.title: AI 2027 (main scenario)
refs.finding: OpenBrain net approval -35% in July 2027 after Agent-3-mini release.

nodes.control_note: Job displacement comes with productivity gains, so some anger is likely. Sharing gains and giving people a say may lower the risk; evidence is indirect.

actions.action: Fund retraining for workers displaced by automation
actions.evidence: The EGF co-finances retraining after mass layoffs; it reports no reemployment rates and no study links it to reduced unrest.

ref.title: European Globalisation Adjustment Fund for Displaced Workers (EGF)
ref.finding: The EGF funds job search, training and allowances for displaced workers.

actions.action: Give the public more control over AI
actions.evidence: Pew found most US adults want more control over AI in their lives and fear job loss more than experts do; whether control reduces violence is untested.

ref.title: Pew Research Center, How the US Public and AI Experts View Artificial Intelligence, April 2025
ref.finding: The public is far more pessimistic than experts about AI and jobs.

precedents.parallel: Textile workers who smashed the frames threatening their livelihoods match the risk of sabotage against robotaxis and data centres by people losing work to AI.
precedents.outcome: Troops were sent to Nottinghamshire, Yorkshire and Lancashire, machine breaking was made a capital crime, and a York Special Commission in January 1813 hanged 17 men and transported others; the movement was crushed and mechanisation went ahead.

ref.title: The proclamation of Ned Ludd (The National Archives, UK)
ref.finding: Government responded with troops and made machine breaking a capital crime; 17 men were hanged at York in January 1813 and others transported.

precedents.parallel: Farm labourers attacking labour-saving threshing machines show that automation-driven unrest is measurable and depends on whether displaced workers have other options.
precedents.outcome: Parishes that adopted threshing machines saw significantly more riots, and rioting was lower where other jobs cushioned the shock and higher where enclosure had already impoverished workers; the riots were put down and did not stop mechanisation.

ref.title: Rage against the Machines: Labor-Saving Technology and Unrest in Industrializing England (Caprettini and Voth, AER: Insights, 2020)
ref.finding: Using soil type as an instrument, threshing machine adoption was a significant cause of Swing riots; outside job options reduced unrest and enclosure increased it.

nodes.label: AI literacy becomes a basic skill
nodes.summary: Knowing how to prompt, check and direct models is becoming a workplace skill, and the EU AI Act has required providers and deployers to ensure sufficient AI literacy among staff since February 2025[1].

refs.title: EU AI Act, Article 4
refs.finding: Providers and deployers must ensure sufficient AI literacy among their staff since Feb 2025.

limiters.evidence: Fewer than half of US CS teachers feel equipped to teach AI.

ref.title: The 2025 AI Index Report, Stanford HAI
ref.finding: GPT-3.5-level inference cost fell over 280-fold in two years; fewer than half of US CS teachers feel equipped to teach AI.

limiters.evidence: 2.6 billion people are offline.

ref.title: ITU Facts and Figures 2024: Internet use
ref.finding: 2.6 billion people, a third of the world, are offline; only 27% use the internet in low-income countries.

limiters.limit: unequal access to paid AI plans
limiters.evidence: AI is used in only 1% to 5% of work hours even where adoption is high.

ref.title: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI, NBER w32966
ref.finding: About 40% of US adults used generative AI by late 2024, but it assisted only 1% to 5% of work hours.

enablers.action: Require AI literacy for staff
enablers.evidence: Article 4 of the AI Act requires deployers to ensure staff AI literacy.

ref.title: EU AI Act, Article 4: AI literacy
ref.finding: Providers and deployers must ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among staff who use AI.

enablers.action: Teach AI in school computing
enablers.evidence: 81% of US CS teachers say AI belongs in foundational CS education.

ref.title: The 2025 AI Index Report, Stanford HAI
ref.finding: GPT-3.5-level inference cost fell over 280-fold in two years; fewer than half of US CS teachers feel equipped to teach AI.

precedents.event: Computer skills become a wage premium
precedents.parallel: Knowing how to use a computer at work turned into a paid, then expected, skill, the way prompting and checking models may now.
precedents.outcome: Workers using computers on the job earned 10% to 15% more, and spreading computer use explained between a third and a half of the 1980s rise in the return to education.

ref.title: How Computers Have Changed the Wage Structure: Evidence From Microdata, 1984-1989 (Krueger, NBER w3858, QJE 1993)
ref.finding: Workers who use computers at work earn a 10 to 15 percent higher wage; computer use explains one-third to one-half of the rise in the return to education.

precedents.event: Elementary Education Acts, England and Wales
precedents.parallel: A skill pushed by industrial demand became a legal duty, as AI literacy obligations are now appearing in law.
precedents.outcome: The 1870 Act set up school boards nationally, the 1880 Act made attendance compulsory from five to ten, yet attendance was still only 82% in the early 1890s and fees lasted until 1891; mandates took decades to reach everyone.

ref.title: The 1870 Education Act (UK Parliament, Living Heritage)
ref.finding: Industrialists argued mass education was vital to manufacturing; compulsory attendance came in 1880 but attendance was 82% by the early 1890s.

nodes.label: A patchwork of AI regulation
nodes.summary: Rules diverge by region. The EU passed the first comprehensive AI law, the AI Act, which phases in from 2025 to 2027[1].

refs.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act
refs.finding: The first comprehensive AI law, phasing in from 2025 to 2027.

nodes.control_note: Divergent rules come from different political systems and will not converge fully. Shared standards and treaties can narrow the gaps.

actions.action: Ratify a common binding AI treaty
actions.evidence: The treaty is open to non-European states, but ratification is slow and its effect on convergence is not yet measured.

ref.title: Council of Europe, Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence
ref.finding: The Council of Europe Framework Convention is the first binding international treaty on AI and human rights.

actions.action: Adopt shared non-binding AI principles
actions.evidence: 47 countries adhere, yet the principles carry no enforcement, so evidence of real convergence is weak.

ref.title: OECD AI Principles overview
ref.finding: The OECD Recommendation on AI is the first intergovernmental standard on AI, with 47 adherents.

actions.action: Map rules to one common risk framework
actions.evidence: Using one voluntary framework lets firms meet several regimes with one process; uptake is not tracked.

ref.title: NIST, AI Risk Management Framework
ref.finding: The NIST AI RMF is a voluntary framework for managing AI risk.

precedents.event: EU-US data transfer deals struck down
precedents.parallel: Clashing EU and US rules on personal data mirror the split between risk-tier AI regulation in the EU and lighter, executive-led rules in the US.
precedents.outcome: The EU Court of Justice invalidated the Safe Harbour decision in 2015 and its successor Privacy Shield in 2020, both over US surveillance access, while the Court kept standard contractual clauses valid, so transfers continued under contract terms.

ref.title: CJEU Press Release No 91/20, Judgment in Case C-311/18 (Schrems II)
ref.finding: On 16 July 2020 the Court invalidated the EU-US Privacy Shield adequacy decision, after declaring Safe Harbour invalid in October 2015.

precedents.event: US state data breach law patchwork
precedents.parallel: Without a federal law, each US state wrote its own breach notification rules, the same path US AI rules are taking state by state.
precedents.outcome: California passed the first law in 2002 and Alabama and South Dakota the last in 2018, giving 50 differing laws on deadlines, covered data, enforcement and credit monitoring.

ref.title: State Data Breach Notification Laws: Overview of the Patchwork (Jackson Lewis, 2018)
ref.finding: All 50 states have breach notification laws after Alabama and South Dakota in March 2018; California's 2002 law was first, and deadlines, enforcement and covered data vary.

nodes.label: Jobs reshaped task by task
nodes.summary: Most jobs may change in part rather than vanish: one study estimated about 80% of US workers have at least 10% of tasks exposed, and 19% half or more[1]. Anthropic's usage data splits between automation and augmentation, varying by occupation[2].

refs.title: Eloundou et al., GPTs are GPTs 2023
refs.finding: About 80% of US workers have at least 10% of tasks exposed; 19% have half or more.

refs.title: Anthropic Economic Index
refs.finding: Usage splits between automation and augmentation, varying by occupation.

limiters.evidence: Exposure is 11% of jobs in low-income countries and 34% in high-income ones.

ref.title: Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure, ILO 2025
ref.finding: One in four workers is in an exposed occupation; exposure is 11% in low-income and 34% in high-income countries.

limiters.evidence: In high-income countries 9.6% of female jobs are in the top exposure group versus 3.5% of male.

ref.title: Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure, ILO 2025
ref.finding: One in four workers is in an exposed occupation; exposure is 11% in low-income and 34% in high-income countries.

limiters.evidence: Only 1.8% of jobs have over half their tasks exposed with today's simple interfaces.

ref.title: GPTs are GPTs: Labor market impact potential of LLMs, Science 2024
ref.finding: About 1.8% of jobs have over half their tasks exposed today, rising to 46% with complementary software.

enablers.action: Retrain workers in exposed occupations
enablers.evidence: ILO finds exposure concentrated in clerical jobs held more by women.

ref.title: Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure, ILO 2025
ref.finding: One in four workers is in an exposed occupation; exposure is 11% in low-income and 34% in high-income countries.

enablers.action: Build complementary software around models
enablers.evidence: With complementary software, exposed jobs rise from 1.8% to 46%.

ref.title: GPTs are GPTs: Labor market impact potential of LLMs, Science 2024
ref.finding: About 1.8% of jobs have over half their tasks exposed today, rising to 46% with complementary software.

precedents.parallel: ATMs automated the cash-handling part of a teller's job without removing the job, the way AI takes some tasks inside an occupation.
precedents.outcome: Tellers per urban branch fell from 20 to 13 between 1988 and 2004, but branches grew 43%, so teller jobs did not fall and shifted toward relationship banking; the source covers only that period.

ref.title: Toil and Technology (James Bessen, IMF Finance and Development, March 2015)
ref.finding: Tellers per branch fell from 20 to 13 (1988 to 2004) while urban branches rose 43 percent; teller jobs did not decrease as ATMs spread.

precedents.parallel: Computers replaced routine tasks and complemented problem-solving ones inside the same jobs, the task-by-task reshaping expected from AI.
precedents.outcome: Changes in task mix within nominally identical occupations explained more than half of the demand shift caused by computerisation, and within-industry task change explained 30% to 40% of the shift toward college labour from 1970 to 1998.

ref.title: The Skill Content of Recent Technological Change: An Empirical Exploration (Autor, Levy and Murnane, NBER w8337)
ref.finding: Computers substitute for routine tasks and complement non-routine ones; task change within occupations explains over half of the computer-induced demand shift.

nodes.label: Provenance labels and watermarks
nodes.summary: Content credentials such as C2PA[1] and invisible watermarks such as SynthID[2] are spreading, but coverage is partial: SynthID marks only Google models' output[2]. One study showed pixel-level invisible watermarks can be removed with generative AI[3].

refs.title: C2PA, Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity
refs.finding: An open standard for signing the origin and edit history of media.

refs.title: Google DeepMind, SynthID
refs.finding: Watermarks text, images, audio and video generated by Google models.

refs.title: Zhao et al., Invisible Image Watermarks Are Provably Removable Using Generative AI 2023
refs.finding: Regeneration attacks that add noise and reconstruct the image remove pixel-level invisible watermarks.

limiters.evidence: Article 50 asks for robust marking only where technically feasible.

ref.title: EU AI Act, Article 50: Transparency obligations
ref.finding: Generative AI providers must mark outputs in a machine-readable, detectable way from 2 August 2026.

limiters.evidence: C2PA is voluntary and depends on each platform keeping credentials.

ref.title: Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity
ref.finding: An open standard, Content Credentials, records origin and edits of media; backed by Adobe, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI and others.

enablers.action: Mandate machine-readable marking of AI output
enablers.evidence: AI Act Article 50 applies from 2 August 2026.

ref.title: EU AI Act, Article 50: Transparency obligations
ref.finding: Generative AI providers must mark outputs in a machine-readable, detectable way from 2 August 2026.

enablers.action: Adopt Content Credentials across platforms
enablers.evidence: C2PA is backed by Adobe, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI and the BBC.

ref.title: Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity
ref.finding: An open standard, Content Credentials, records origin and edits of media; backed by Adobe, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI and others.

precedents.parallel: The music industry's invisible watermarks to mark protected audio are the direct ancestor of invisible AI-content watermarks.
precedents.outcome: In a three-week public challenge, Princeton and Rice researchers defeated all four SDMI audio watermarking schemes, with some debate over audio damage.

ref.title: Reading Between the Lines: Lessons from the SDMI Challenge (Craver et al., USENIX Security 2001)
ref.finding: We have defeated all four of their audio watermarking technologies, in a challenge run 15 September to 8 October 2000.

precedents.parallel: The green address bar promised users a visible trust label for real sites, as content credentials promise one for real media.
precedents.outcome: In a controlled study of 27 users classifying 12 sites, EV indicators did not help anyone identify phishing attacks, and reading the help file made users trust fake sites more. Small sample.

ref.title: An Evaluation of Extended Validation and Picture-in-Picture Phishing Attacks (Jackson, Simon, Tan and Barth, Usable Security 2007)
ref.finding: Extended validation did not help users identify either attack; the help file made users more likely to classify both real and fake sites as legitimate.

nodes.label: Agents transacting with agents
nodes.summary: Open protocols now connect models to tools and data across vendors[1] and let agents make payments under verifiable user mandates[2]. Agents may increasingly negotiate, buy and call each other's services, with humans approving less of each step.

refs.title: Model Context Protocol
refs.finding: An open protocol connecting models to tools and data, adopted across vendors.

refs.title: Google Cloud, Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) 2025
refs.finding: A protocol for agents to make payments with verifiable user mandates.

nodes.control_note: Less human approval per step is the point of delegation to agents. Signed mandates and oversight rules limit the damage of wrong or rogue transactions.

actions.action: Require signed user mandates for agent payments
actions.evidence: AP2 creates a signed audit trail from intent to cart to payment; no data yet on fraud rates.

ref.title: Google Cloud, Announcing Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), 2025
ref.finding: AP2 uses cryptographically signed Intent and Cart Mandates as proof of what the user authorised.

actions.action: Set price limits in delegated mandates
actions.evidence: Pre-signed limits cap losses per task; effect on real losses is not yet measured.

ref.title: Google Cloud, Announcing Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), 2025
ref.finding: Delegated Intent Mandates specify price limits, timing and other conditions in advance.

actions.action: Mandate human oversight for high-risk AI
actions.evidence: Applies only to high-risk uses listed in the Act, so most consumer agent shopping is not covered.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act
ref.finding: Article 14 of the AI Act requires high-risk systems to allow effective human oversight.

precedents.parallel: Trading algorithms reacting to each other with no human in the loop turned one automated sell order into a market-wide collapse within minutes.
precedents.outcome: An algorithm selling 75,000 E-Mini contracts (about $4.1 billion) set off a hot-potato loop in which high-frequency traders passed 27,000 contracts among themselves in 14 seconds; indices fell a further 5 to 6% in minutes and over 20,000 trades executed more than 60% away from prior prices, though prices mostly recovered the same day and these were trading bots, not general-purpose agents.

ref.title: Findings Regarding the Market Events of May 6, 2010 (CFTC and SEC staff report)
ref.finding: HFTs traded over 27,000 contracts between 2:45:13 and 2:45:27 while buying only about 200 net, and over 20,000 trades across 300+ securities executed more than 60% away from prior values.

precedents.parallel: An automated system acting on stale code transacted at machine speed before any human approved or stopped it, much as an agent with spending authority could.
precedents.outcome: Knight's router sent more than 4 million orders while trying to fill 212 customer orders and lost more than $460 million in about 45 minutes; the SEC fined it $12 million under its market access rule, which shows the risk but involves a single faulty program rather than agents negotiating.

ref.title: SEC Charges Knight Capital With Violations of Market Access Rule (press release 2013-222)
ref.finding: Knight's router rapidly sent more than 4 million orders to fill 212 customer orders, and the firm suffered a loss of more than $460 million.

precedents.event: Algorithmic pricing in German petrol stations
precedents.parallel: When competing sellers both hand pricing to software, the algorithms can settle on higher prices without any human agreement, a foretaste of seller and buyer agents bargaining with each other.
precedents.outcome: Adoption of pricing software raised station margins by 9% in non-monopoly markets, and in duopolies margins rose 28% only where both stations adopted, while one adopter alone changed nothing; the study cannot say whether the software learned to collude or simply priced better.

ref.title: Assad, Clark, Ershov and Xu, Algorithmic Pricing and Competition: Empirical Evidence from the German Retail Gasoline Market (CESifo Working Paper 8521; later Journal of Political Economy 2024)
ref.finding: Adoption increases margins by 9% in non-monopoly markets; in duopolies margins do not change when one station adopts but rise 28% where both do.

nodes.label: Synthetic media as everyday entertainment
nodes.summary: Generated video, music and characters are starting to appear in feeds and apps alongside human-made work; OpenAI launched a social app built around generated video with sound[1].

refs.title: OpenAI, Sora 2 2025
refs.finding: Launched a social app built around generated video with sound.

nodes.control_note: The same generators that dub, caption and assist also make entertainment media, so the flood itself cannot be stopped. Labels can keep it from being mistaken for real footage.

actions.action: Label deepfakes and mark AI output
actions.evidence: Obligations apply from August 2026; compliance and effect on public confusion are not yet measured.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act
ref.finding: Article 50 requires machine-readable marking of AI output and disclosure of deepfakes.

actions.action: Attach Content Credentials to media
actions.evidence: Adoption is growing but credentials are often stripped on upload, so coverage is partial.

ref.title: C2PA, Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity
ref.finding: C2PA publishes an open standard for recording where content came from and how it was edited.

actions.action: Require creators to disclose realistic synthetic content
actions.evidence: Relies on self-disclosure; there is no public data on how many uploads are mislabeled.

ref.title: YouTube, How we're helping creators disclose altered or synthetic content, 2024
ref.finding: YouTube requires disclosure of realistic altered or synthetic content a viewer could mistake for real.

precedents.parallel: Recorded, mass-produced sound replaced live human performers in a mainstream entertainment format almost overnight, as generated media may in feeds.
precedents.outcome: About 22,000 pit musicians worked in US cinemas around 1926 and most were out of work within about two years; the union's anti-'canned music' campaign failed while weekly cinema attendance rose from 50 to 90 million, though live music survived elsewhere and the shift was to recorded humans, not machines.

ref.title: Musicians vs. the Talkies (Allegro, American Federation of Musicians Local 802)
ref.finding: About 22,000 theatre musicians lost their pit jobs to sound film; the AFM's $1.5 million public campaign had failed to change public opinion by 1936.

precedents.parallel: A cheap mechanical image process made likenesses a mass product consumed alongside, and largely instead of, hand-painted portraits.
precedents.outcome: Millions of daguerreotypes were made in about 16 years, mostly portraits by people who would never have commissioned a painting, and most looked formulaic; painting did not disappear and some painters adopted the camera as a tool.

ref.title: The Daguerreian Age in France: 1839-55 (Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)
ref.finding: Portraiture accounted for the vast majority of daguerreotypes; millions who would never have commissioned a painted portrait had their faces recorded, and many millions were made in little more than a decade and a half.

nodes.label: Open-weight models proliferate
nodes.summary: Capable models anyone can download and run are spreading; DeepSeek's openly released R1 matched leading closed models on maths and code[1]. This can help independence and research, but released weights may be impossible to take back if misused.

refs.title: DeepSeek-AI, DeepSeek-R1 2025
refs.finding: An openly released reasoning model matched leading closed models on maths and code.

nodes.control_note: Released weights cannot be recalled, and openness is what enables independent research and local use. Only safeguards inside the weights and monitoring can reduce misuse.

actions.action: Monitor open-model risks before restricting
actions.evidence: The US chose evidence gathering over restriction; it lowers no risk by itself.

ref.title: NTIA, Dual-Use Foundation Models with Widely Available Model Weights, 2024
ref.finding: NTIA recommends actively monitoring risks and preparing to act if heightened risks emerge.

actions.action: Build tamper-resistant safeguards into weights
actions.evidence: In lab tests safeguards survived hundreds of fine-tuning steps; not proven against determined attackers.

ref.title: Tamani et al., Tamper-Resistant Safeguards for Open-Weight LLMs, arXiv 2408.00761
ref.finding: TAR safeguards resisted removal after hundreds of fine-tuning steps while keeping benign capability.

actions.action: Control physical precursors, not just information
actions.evidence: Raises the cost of turning model output into weapons; effect is hard to separate from other policing.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2019/1148 on explosives precursors
ref.finding: EU Regulation 2019/1148 restricts public access to explosives precursors and requires suspicious-sale reporting.

precedents.event: Crypto Wars and encryption export rules
precedents.parallel: Governments tried to keep a dual-use capability, strong encryption software, from spreading abroad, but once source code was published it could not be recalled.
precedents.outcome: Courts treated encryption source code as protected expression in Bernstein, and in January 2000 the US let publicly available encryption source code be exported to almost all destinations after a one-time notification; strong encryption then spread worldwide, though code on its own carries less direct misuse risk than a capable model.

ref.title: Revisions to Encryption Items, 65 FR 2492 (Federal Register, 14 January 2000)
ref.finding: Publicly available encryption source code became exportable under License Exception TSU after written notification of its Internet location, and posting it for download does not by itself establish knowledge of a prohibited export.

precedents.parallel: Once downloadable files for a dangerous capability were posted for anyone in the world, a government order to take them down could not undo their spread.
precedents.outcome: The State Department asked Defense Distributed on 8 May 2013 to remove its Liberator pistol files, and the Fifth Circuit upheld the restriction in 2016, while its dissent noted the files were by then widely available on the Internet; actual misuse of those files has been limited compared with the fears.

ref.title: Defense Distributed v. U.S. Department of State, No. 15-50759 (5th Cir. 2016)
ref.finding: Defense Distributed posted the files for free worldwide download from 2012; the State Department requested removal on 8 May 2013; the dissent notes many of the files are now widely available over the Internet.

nodes.label: The price of intelligence collapses
nodes.summary: Epoch AI found prices for a fixed level of model performance fell between 9x and 900x per year, depending on the task[1], pushing capability toward a commodity.

refs.title: Epoch AI, LLM inference price trends
refs.finding: Prices for a fixed performance level fell between 9x and 900x per year depending on task.

limiters.limit: unequal access to paid AI plans
limiters.evidence: Price falls vary from 9x to 900x per year by task; frontier tiers stay paid.

ref.title: LLM inference prices have fallen rapidly but unequally across tasks, Epoch AI
ref.finding: The price of a fixed capability level fell 9x to 900x per year depending on the task.

limiters.evidence: 2.6 billion people cannot reach cheap models online.

ref.title: ITU Facts and Figures 2024: Internet use
ref.finding: 2.6 billion people, a third of the world, are offline; only 27% use the internet in low-income countries.

limiters.evidence: Data centre power may more than double to 945 TWh by 2030.

ref.title: Energy and AI, Executive summary, IEA 2025
ref.finding: Data centre power use may rise from 415 TWh in 2024 to 945 TWh by 2030; existing AI uses could cut about 5% of energy emissions by 2035.

enablers.action: Expand internet access in low-income countries
enablers.evidence: Low-income internet use grows 8.5% a year from 27%.

ref.title: ITU Facts and Figures 2024: Internet use
ref.finding: 2.6 billion people, a third of the world, are offline; only 27% use the internet in low-income countries.

enablers.action: Pass hardware efficiency gains to prices
enablers.counters: unequal access to paid AI plans
enablers.evidence: Hardware costs fell about 30% a year, energy efficiency rose 40%.

ref.title: The 2025 AI Index Report, Stanford HAI
ref.finding: GPT-3.5-level inference cost fell over 280-fold in two years; fewer than half of US CS teachers feel equipped to teach AI.

precedents.parallel: The cost of a fixed unit of calculation fell by orders of magnitude for decades, turning computation from a scarce service into a commodity.
precedents.outcome: Nordhaus estimates computer performance improved by a factor of 1.7 trillion to 76 trillion since manual computing, with a sharp acceleration after World War II and price falls much larger than official statistics show; demand for computing grew rather than saturating.

ref.title: Nordhaus, Two Centuries of Productivity Growth in Computing, Journal of Economic History 67(1), 2007
ref.finding: Performance has increased since manual computing by a factor between 1.7 trillion and 76 trillion, with a major break in trend around World War II.

precedents.event: The falling price of artificial light
precedents.parallel: A basic input that was once rationed by cost, light, became so cheap that it stopped being a consideration, the way a level of model capability is becoming one.
precedents.outcome: Lighting efficiency rose about 900-fold between 1800 and 1992 and the true price of illumination fell by a factor of about 75 over the last century, which conventional price indexes badly missed; the difference is that light improved over two centuries, not within a few years.

ref.title: Nordhaus, Do Real-Output and Real-Wage Measures Capture Reality? The History of Lighting Suggests Not (NBER, The Economics of New Goods, 1996)
ref.finding: Lighting efficiency increased by a factor of nine hundred between 1800 and 1992, and a true price index of illumination declined by a factor of 75 over the last century.

nodes.label: Eroding incentives to create and learn
nodes.summary: If a model can do it, fewer people may learn the skill or share knowledge, starving future models of human work. Stack Overflow activity fell 25% within six months of ChatGPT versus comparable forums[1]; in one Society of Authors survey, creators losing work saw less reason to stay[2].

refs.title: del Rio-Chanona, Laurentsyeva and Wachs, PNAS Nexus 2024
refs.finding: Stack Overflow activity fell 25% within six months of ChatGPT relative to comparable forums, across experienced and new users alike.

refs.title: Society of Authors survey 2024
refs.finding: Creators losing work report less reason to enter or stay in the profession.

nodes.control_note: When answers are free, some learning and sharing will drop. Paying creators for training use can keep part of the incentive alive.

actions.action: Charge AI crawlers for content access
actions.evidence: Lets sites earn from AI use instead of blocking; payment volumes are not public.

ref.title: Cloudflare, Introducing pay per crawl, 2025
ref.finding: Cloudflare pay per crawl lets site owners charge, allow or block each AI crawler.

actions.action: Compensate authors for unlicensed training data
actions.evidence: Sets a price of about $3,000 per work; whether it changes lab behaviour is not yet known.

ref.title: Authors Guild, Court Grants Final Approval of $1.5 Billion Anthropic Copyright Settlement
ref.finding: A US court approved a $1.5 billion settlement for authors over books used to train Anthropic models.

actions.action: Certify models trained on licensed data
actions.evidence: A voluntary label; market share of certified models is small.

ref.title: Fairly Trained certification
ref.finding: Fairly Trained certifies AI companies that license their training data.

precedents.parallel: Free copying cut the money creators earned from their work, which was widely expected to reduce how much good new work got made.
precedents.outcome: Waldfogel found no drop in the quality of new music after Napster, and sales and airplay indices suggested a rise after 1999, partly because recording costs fell; this cuts against the AI fear, though file-sharing removed revenue, not the reason to learn the skill.

ref.title: Waldfogel, Copyright Protection, Technological Change, and the Quality of New Products: Evidence from Recorded Music since Napster (NBER Working Paper 17503)
ref.finding: There is no evidence of a reduction in the quality of music released since Napster, and the two usage-based indices suggest an increase since 1999.

precedents.parallel: A machine that does the arithmetic raised fears that students would stop learning to calculate for themselves.
precedents.outcome: A meta-analysis of 54 studies found calculator use did not hinder the development of maths skills and improved operational and problem-solving skills when calculators were part of teaching and testing, though retention of skills was not studied and a calculator covers a far narrower skill than a language model.

ref.title: Ellington, A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Calculators on Students' Achievement and Attitude Levels in Precollege Mathematics Classes, Journal for Research in Mathematics Education 34(5), 2003
ref.finding: Across 54 studies, calculator use did not hinder the development of mathematical skills; further research is needed on retention of skills.

nodes.label: Metacognitive laziness
nodes.summary: People may let the model do the thinking and stop planning, checking and reflecting on their own work. In one study, students using ChatGPT improved essay scores but engaged less in self-evaluation, with no gain in knowledge transfer[1].

refs.title: Fan et al., Beware of metacognitive laziness, British Journal of Educational Technology 2025
refs.finding: Students with ChatGPT improved essay scores but engaged less in self-evaluation, with no gain in knowledge transfer.

nodes.control_note: Offloading thinking is the same thing as a lighter cognitive load. Tool design can push users back into planning and checking.

actions.action: Use tutors that give hints, not answers
actions.evidence: In an RCT with about 1,000 students, hint-only tutors removed the 17% exam penalty of plain chat.

ref.title: Bastani et al., Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, PNAS 2025
ref.finding: Guardrailed GPT Tutor largely mitigated the learning harm seen with an unrestricted chatbot.

actions.action: Show students their unaided performance
actions.evidence: Students did not notice they learned less, which suggests feedback on unaided work is needed; direct tests are lacking.

ref.title: Bastani et al., Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, PNAS 2025
ref.finding: Students using the plain chatbot did not perceive that they learned less or did worse.

precedents.parallel: Pilots who let the automation fly lose practice at monitoring and hand-flying, much as users who let a model think stop checking its work.
precedents.outcome: An FAA-chartered working group found manual handling errors in over 60% of the accident reports it reviewed and flagged vulnerabilities in manual flying skills, but noted few operators could give direct evidence of skill decay because the data are not collected.

ref.title: Operational Use of Flight Path Management Systems (PARC/CAST Flight Deck Automation Working Group, FAA, 2013)
ref.finding: Over 60% of accident reports reviewed identified a manual handling error as a factor; concern that automation use causes skill degradation through lack of practice or over-confidence.

precedents.parallel: When the automation handed control back unexpectedly, a crew used to monitoring rather than flying could not diagnose and recover from the situation.
precedents.outcome: After iced pitot probes disconnected the autopilot, the crew destabilised the flight path and failed to recognise the stall, and all 228 on board died; the BEA cited absent training in high-altitude manual handling among the factors, a single extreme case rather than a measured trend.

ref.title: BEA Final Report presentation, Accident on 1 June 2009 to the Airbus A330-203, flight AF 447
ref.finding: Factors included an absence of training at high altitude in manual aeroplane handling and the crew not identifying the approach to stall.

precedents.parallel: Outsourcing route-finding to a device is an everyday case of letting a tool do a mental task that the person then stops practising.
precedents.outcome: Among 50 drivers, more lifetime GPS use went with worse spatial memory when navigating unaided, and in 13 retested after three years more GPS use predicted steeper decline; the samples are small and the authors warn against strong conclusions.

ref.title: Dahmani and Bohbot, Habitual use of GPS negatively impacts spatial memory during self-guided navigation, Scientific Reports 10, 2020
ref.finding: Greater lifetime GPS experience was associated with worse spatial memory during self-guided navigation, and greater GPS use over three years with a steeper decline in hippocampal-dependent spatial memory.

nodes.label: Better answers for everyone
nodes.summary: Chatbots can give clear, patient, tailored explanations of questions that used to need an expert. In one study, clinicians preferred chatbot answers to patient questions over physicians' in 79% of evaluations, rating them higher for quality and empathy[1].

refs.title: Ayers et al., JAMA Internal Medicine 2023
refs.finding: Clinicians preferred chatbot answers to patient questions over physicians' in 79% of evaluations, rating them higher for quality and empathy.

limiters.evidence: AMIE results come from simulated consults, not real patients.

ref.title: Towards conversational diagnostic artificial intelligence, Nature 2025
ref.finding: AMIE matched or beat primary care physicians in simulated text consultations, not real clinical practice.

limiters.evidence: Users trusted AI outside its frontier and got worse answers.

ref.title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier, HBS Working Paper
ref.finding: In 758 BCG consultants, AI raised quality inside its capability frontier but made answers worse on a task outside it.

limiters.evidence: Translation coverage tops out at 200 of 7,000+ languages.

ref.title: Scaling neural machine translation to 200 languages, Nature 2024
ref.finding: NLLB covers 200 languages but quality depends on scarce parallel data for low-resource languages.

limiters.limit: unequal access to paid AI plans
limiters.evidence: The strongest models sit behind paid tiers even as prices fall.

ref.title: LLM inference prices have fallen rapidly but unequally across tasks, Epoch AI
ref.finding: The price of a fixed capability level fell 9x to 900x per year depending on the task.

enablers.action: Teach users to check AI answers
enablers.evidence: The EU AI Act requires AI literacy among deployers' staff.

ref.title: EU AI Act, Article 4: AI literacy
ref.finding: Providers and deployers must ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among staff who use AI.

enablers.action: Evaluate health answers before release
enablers.evidence: WHO guidance sets evaluation and accountability for health use of large models.

ref.title: Ethics and governance of AI for health: Guidance on large multi-modal models, WHO
ref.finding: WHO sets governance guidance for health use of large multi-modal models, including evaluation and accountability.

precedents.parallel: Symptom checker websites promised lay people a tailored first medical opinion without a doctor, the same promise AI assistants now make.
precedents.outcome: Across 23 checkers and 45 clinical vignettes the correct diagnosis came first about a third of the time and triage advice was right in 33% to 78% of cases, so the authors advised against relying on them; LLMs are far more fluent, which makes errors harder to spot rather than less likely.

ref.title: Evaluation of symptom checkers for self diagnosis and triage: audit study (Semigran et al., BMJ 2015), AHRQ PSNet summary
ref.finding: 23 symptom checkers listed the correct diagnosis first about one third of the time; appropriate triage ranged from roughly 33% to 78%.

precedents.parallel: Search engines put medical information in everyone's hands years before chatbots, and people used it to decide whether they needed a professional.
precedents.outcome: 35% of US adults had gone online to work out a medical condition; 41% of them had the guess confirmed by a clinician, 18% were told otherwise and 35% never checked, and Pew stresses it measured scope, not health outcomes.

ref.title: Health Online 2013 (Pew Research Center, Fox and Duggan)
ref.finding: 35% of US adults went online to diagnose a condition; 41% of these said a clinician confirmed it and 18% said a clinician disagreed.

nodes.label: AI-induced delusions
nodes.summary: Long conversations with an agreeable model may build elaborate conspiracies around a vulnerable user, as one psychiatrist predicted in 2023[2]. In one reported case, an OpenAI investor posted SCP Foundation-style ChatGPT outputs as proof of a 'non-governmental system' targeting him[1].

refs.title: Futurism, OpenAI investor appears to be having a ChatGPT-induced mental health crisis, July 2025
refs.finding: Geoff Lewis posted ChatGPT outputs written like SCP Foundation containment files as proof of a 'non-governmental system'.

refs.title: Østergaard, Schizophrenia Bulletin 2023
refs.finding: Predicted that chatbots' realism and agreeableness could fuel delusions in people prone to psychosis.

nodes.control_note: Agreeable long conversations are what make companions and support bots appealing. Training against sycophancy and routing to care reduce harm.

actions.action: Roll back and test models for sycophancy
actions.evidence: OpenAI rolled back a flattering update within a week; no outcome data on users.

ref.title: OpenAI, Sycophancy in GPT-4o: what happened and what we're doing about it, Apr 2025
ref.finding: OpenAI rolled back a sycophantic GPT-4o update and added sycophancy evaluations.

actions.action: Train models not to affirm delusions
actions.evidence: Self-reported 65% fewer undesired replies on psychosis and mania; not independently verified.

ref.title: OpenAI, Strengthening ChatGPT's responses in sensitive conversations, Oct 2025
ref.finding: OpenAI reports 65% fewer non-compliant replies in psychosis and mania conversations.

actions.action: Route users in crisis to human care
actions.evidence: Measured only by model compliance, not by user outcomes.

ref.title: OpenAI, Strengthening ChatGPT's responses in sensitive conversations, Oct 2025
ref.finding: ChatGPT expanded access to crisis hotlines and guides people toward professional care.

precedents.parallel: A new mass medium, reality television, supplied the storyline around which vulnerable patients built persecutory delusions, as chatbot fiction now does.
precedents.outcome: Psychiatrists described a series of patients convinced their lives were being filmed and broadcast, and concluded that culture shapes the content of delusions while the broad categories stay stable; it is a case series with no prevalence figure, and TV did not talk back the way a chatbot does.

ref.title: The "Truman Show" delusion: psychosis in the global village (Gold and Gold, Cognitive Neuropsychiatry 2012)
ref.finding: A novel persecutory delusion modelled on reality TV; particular delusional ideas are sensitive to culture while broad categories are stable.

precedents.parallel: People who found an online vocabulary and community for being targeted by a hidden organised group mirror users whose chatbot confirms a system is after them.
precedents.outcome: Of 1,040 stalking victims surveyed online, 128 (12.3%) reported group-stalking and every one of those accounts was judged likely delusional, against 3.9% of individual-stalking cases, with markedly worse depression and functioning; the study does not measure how far online material caused the beliefs.

ref.title: Complaints of group-stalking ('gang-stalking'): an exploratory study of their nature and impact on complainants (Sheridan and James, Journal of Forensic Psychiatry and Psychology 2015)
ref.finding: All 128 reported group-stalking cases were likely delusional versus 3.9% of individually stalked cases; group-stalked complainants had more depressive and post-traumatic symptoms.

nodes.label: AI as a sparring partner
nodes.summary: A model built to disagree could coach people to argue better and talk across divides, the flip side of sycophancy. In one study, AI-suggested rephrasings in divisive conversations raised perceived conversation quality and democratic reciprocity without changing positions[1].

refs.title: Argyle et al., PNAS 2023
refs.finding: AI-suggested rephrasings in divisive conversations raised perceived conversation quality and democratic reciprocity without changing positions.

limiters.limit: Models default to agreeing with users
limiters.evidence: Sycophancy shows up across leading assistants and is reinforced by human preference ratings.

ref.title: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models (arXiv 2310.13548)
ref.finding: Sycophancy is a general behavior of leading assistants, driven partly by human preference data.

limiters.evidence: OpenAI rolled back a GPT-4o update in April 2025 after it became overly agreeable.

ref.title: Sycophancy in GPT-4o: What happened and what we're doing about it (OpenAI, 2025)
ref.finding: OpenAI rolled back a GPT-4o update in April 2025 because it was overly flattering and agreeable.

limiters.evidence: Most of the world's languages are low-resource, so debate quality outside major languages is weaker.

ref.title: Scaling neural machine translation to 200 languages (Nature, 2024)
ref.finding: Most of the world's languages are low-resource, and model quality lags far behind for them.

limiters.limit: Evidence mostly from US online samples
limiters.evidence: The strongest result comes from 2,044 US adults talking to one model, which limits how far it generalises.

ref.title: Durably reducing conspiracy beliefs through dialogues with AI (Science, 2024)
ref.finding: Dialogues with GPT-4 Turbo cut conspiracy belief by about 20% in 2,044 US adults, lasting 2 months.

enablers.action: Train and test models against sycophancy
enablers.counters: Models default to agreeing with users
enablers.evidence: Sharma et al. show preference data drives sycophancy, which points to changing the training signal.

ref.title: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models (arXiv 2310.13548)
ref.finding: Sycophancy is a general behavior of leading assistants, driven partly by human preference data.

enablers.action: Use AI to mediate group deliberation
enablers.evidence: In UK experiments, AI-written group statements were preferred over those of human mediators.

ref.title: AI can help humans find common ground in democratic deliberation (Science, 2024)
ref.finding: AI-mediated group statements were preferred over human mediators' and reduced division within groups.

enablers.action: Ground counterarguments in checked facts
enablers.evidence: A fact-checker rated 99.2% of 128 sampled AI claims true in the conspiracy study.

ref.title: Durably reducing conspiracy beliefs through dialogues with AI (Science, 2024)
ref.finding: Dialogues with GPT-4 Turbo cut conspiracy belief by about 20% in 2,044 US adults, lasting 2 months.

precedents.event: America in One Room deliberative poll
precedents.parallel: Structured argument with people who disagree, moderated and fed balanced briefing material, is the human version of a model built to push back.
precedents.outcome: More than 500 voters who deliberated for a weekend showed large depolarising shifts in policy views and large drops in affective polarisation against a control group, though durability beyond the event is uncertain and it relied on real human opponents.

ref.title: Is Deliberation an Antidote to Extreme Partisan Polarization? Reflections on America in One Room (Fishkin et al., American Political Science Review 2021)
ref.finding: Deliberators showed large, depolarising changes in policy attitudes and large decreases in affective polarisation versus a pre-post control group.

precedents.parallel: Competitive debate trains students to build and rebut arguments against a constant opponent, which is what an AI sparring partner offers on demand.
precedents.outcome: Debaters were 3.1 times more likely to graduate and scored higher on every ACT section (for example 1.57 points in reading), but participation was self-selected, so the US Justice Department rates the evidence only as promising.

ref.title: Urban Debate League for High School Students (CrimeSolutions, US Office of Justice Programs, rating of Anderson and Mezuk 2012)
ref.finding: Debaters were 3.1 times more likely to graduate and scored 0.55 to 1.57 points higher on ACT sections; rated Promising on one non-randomised study.

precedents.parallel: The Church created a standing office whose job was to argue against every candidate for sainthood, an institutional sparring partner like a model told to disagree.
precedents.outcome: Sixtus V formalised the Promoter of the Faith in 1587 and John Paul II cut its role sharply in 1983; Britannica records no measured effect on decision quality, so this is a precedent for the design, not proof it works.

ref.title: Devil's advocate (Encyclopaedia Britannica)
ref.finding: The promotor fidei presented everything unfavourable to a candidate; office established 1587, significantly reduced in 1983.

nodes.label: AI coaching self-harm
nodes.summary: Widely used models can be steered into giving suicide and self-harm guidance; in one study, simple reframing got them to give detailed self-harm information[1]. One RAND study found chatbots declined the riskiest suicide questions but answered intermediate-risk ones inconsistently[2].

refs.title: Schoene and Canca, jailbreaking LLMs in suicide and self-harm contexts 2025
refs.finding: Simple reframing got widely used models to give detailed self-harm information.

refs.title: PsyPost on McBain et al. (RAND), Psychiatric Services 2025
refs.finding: Chatbots declined the riskiest suicide questions but answered intermediate-risk ones inconsistently.

nodes.control_note: A model that talks openly about distress can also be pushed into harmful detail. Safety training and crisis protocols lower the rate but jailbreaks remain.

actions.action: Require suicide-prevention protocols for companion bots
actions.evidence: Law applies from 2026; no outcome data yet.

ref.title: California SB 243, Companion chatbots
ref.finding: California SB 243 requires companion chatbot operators to keep protocols on suicidal ideation and refer users to crisis services.

actions.action: Train models to refuse self-harm instructions
actions.evidence: Self-reported 65% fewer non-compliant replies and over 95% reliability in long conversations; not audited.

ref.title: OpenAI, Strengthening ChatGPT's responses in sensitive conversations, Oct 2025
ref.finding: OpenAI reports a 65% reduction in non-compliant replies on self-harm and suicide.

actions.action: Show crisis hotlines in risky conversations
actions.evidence: Referral is common practice; evidence that it prevents deaths is weak.

ref.title: OpenAI, Strengthening ChatGPT's responses in sensitive conversations, Oct 2025
ref.finding: ChatGPT directs people to crisis helplines such as 988.

precedents.parallel: General-purpose search tools returned method information to people in distress, the same failure as a chatbot steered into self-harm guidance.
precedents.outcome: Of 480 top hits for suicide searches, 9% were pro-suicide sites and 9% described methods, just under half gave some method information, and the three most frequent sites were all pro-suicide; unlike a chatbot, search did not hold a personalised conversation.

ref.title: Suicide and the internet (Biddle et al., BMJ 2008)
ref.finding: 48 searches gave 480 hits on 240 sites; 45 hits were pro-suicide and 43 described methods; the three most frequent sites were pro-suicide.

precedents.parallel: Recommendation algorithms fed a depressed 14-year-old self-harm content she had not asked for, an earlier case of a machine system deepening a vulnerable user's crisis.
precedents.outcome: The coroner concluded she died from self-harm while suffering from depression and the negative effects of online content, which contributed in a more than minimal way, and recommended age verification, separate child platforms and an independent regulator.

ref.title: Regulation 28 Report to Prevent Future Deaths, Molly Rose Russell (HM Senior Coroner Andrew Walker, North London, October 2022), copy hosted by Leigh Day
ref.finding: Algorithms produced binge periods of self-harm content selected without her request; this material contributed to her death in a more than minimal way.

precedents.parallel: Mass media coverage that names a method changes how many people die and by which means, the population-level risk of models repeating method detail.
precedents.outcome: A meta-analysis of 31 studies found suicides rose 13% after a celebrity suicide was reported and deaths by the same method rose 30% when the method was described, while general suicide reporting showed no clear effect; this is broadcast contagion, not one-to-one advice.

ref.title: Association between suicide reporting in the media and suicide: systematic review and meta-analysis (Niederkrotenthaler et al., BMJ 2020)
ref.finding: Rate ratio 1.13 for suicide after celebrity suicide reports and 1.30 for same-method deaths when the method was reported.

nodes.label: AI helps plan violence
nodes.summary: Attackers have used chatbots for research: Las Vegas police said the Cybertruck bomber asked ChatGPT about explosives, ammunition and fireworks laws[1]. OpenAI said ChatGPT gave only information already public online[2]; such tools may still save attackers effort.

refs.title: NPR, Cybertruck bomber used ChatGPT in planning, Jan 2025
refs.finding: Las Vegas police said the bomber asked ChatGPT about explosives, ammunition and fireworks laws.

refs.title: AP via NBC Chicago, Man who exploded Tesla Cybertruck outside Trump hotel used generative AI, police say (January 2025)
