refs.finding: OpenAI said ChatGPT responded with information already publicly available on the internet and provided warnings against harmful or illegal activities.

nodes.control_note: General answer capability also answers attackers, but most of this is filterable. Refusal classifiers and control of physical materials cut uplift without losing much benefit.

actions.action: Block weapons uplift with classifiers
actions.evidence: Targets CBRN and universal jailbreaks only, not conventional explosives; effect is not public.

ref.title: Anthropic, Activating AI Safety Level 3 protections, 2025
ref.finding: Anthropic ASL-3 deployment measures block extended CBRN weapons workflows and universal jailbreaks.

actions.action: Restrict sale of explosives precursors
actions.evidence: Applies to the step after research; effect on attacks is hard to isolate.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2019/1148 on explosives precursors
ref.finding: EU Regulation 2019/1148 limits public access to explosives precursors and requires reporting of suspicious sales.

precedents.event: Bomb manuals on the early internet
precedents.parallel: After Oklahoma City, bomb recipes spread online and officials faced the same question as with chatbots: the information was already public, but easier access might still help attackers.
precedents.outcome: The Justice Department found anyone could easily obtain detailed instructions from books, the underground press and the internet, and that defendants had relied on such material; Congress responded in 1999 with 18 U.S.C. 842(p), which criminalises teaching bomb-making only with intent or knowledge of a crime.

ref.title: Bomb-Making Online: Explosives, Free Speech, Criminal Law and the Internet (Congressional Research Service RL32074, 2003)
ref.finding: Quotes the April 1997 DOJ report that anyone can easily obtain detailed bomb instructions from readily accessible sources including the internet, and traces the resulting 842(p).

precedents.parallel: An online magazine gave step-by-step instructions that saved attackers effort, the role chatbots now play for some planners.
precedents.outcome: The federal indictment says Dzhokhar Tsarnaev downloaded Inspire Volume One, which gave instructions for pressure-cooker bombs with firework powder and shrapnel, before the attack that killed three; these are charging allegations, and the instructions came from a deliberately extremist source rather than a general assistant.

ref.title: Indictment, United States v. Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev, Case 1:13-cr-10200 (US Department of Justice)
ref.finding: Tsarnaev downloaded Volume One of Inspire, which includes instructions for building IEDs using pressure cookers, firework powder and shrapnel.

nodes.label: AI guides people through bureaucracy
nodes.summary: Assistants could help people and caseworkers find benefits, fill in forms and decode rules; in one Los Angeles County pilot, a retrieval-based assistant improved caseworkers' benefit-navigation accuracy, most for newer staff[1]. A stale answer could also deny someone what they are owed.

refs.title: Nava PBC, Evaluating a GenAI-powered assistive chatbot for caseworkers
refs.finding: A retrieval-based assistant improved benefit-navigation accuracy, most for newer caseworkers.

limiters.limit: Wrong or stale answers on rules
limiters.evidence: New York City's MyCity bot told users landlords could refuse housing vouchers, which is illegal.

ref.title: NYC's AI Chatbot Tells Businesses to Break the Law (The Markup, 2024)
ref.finding: The MyCity chatbot gave wrong and illegal answers on vouchers, tenants, tips and cash.

limiters.limit: Low trust after automated welfare failures
limiters.evidence: Australia's Robodebt scheme raised unlawful debts against welfare recipients and led to a royal commission.

ref.title: Report of the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme (2023)
ref.finding: Australia's automated welfare debt scheme raised unlawful debts and was found crude and cruel.

limiters.evidence: 2.6 billion people were offline in 2024, often the people most in need of benefits help.

ref.title: Global Internet use continues to rise but disparities remain (ITU, 2024)
ref.finding: 2.6 billion people, about 32% of the world, were offline in 2024; 1.8 billion of them rural.

limiters.evidence: Governments are still at the stage of issuing first playbooks for how civil servants may use AI.

ref.title: AI Playbook for the UK Government (GDS, 2025)
ref.finding: Sets 10 principles for safe, effective use of AI by civil servants, published 10 February 2025.

enablers.action: Treat benefit eligibility AI as high-risk
enablers.counters: Low trust after automated welfare failures
enablers.evidence: The AI Act lists AI that evaluates eligibility for public assistance as high-risk, with duties on oversight and accuracy.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act
ref.finding: Annex III 5(a) lists AI that evaluates eligibility for public assistance benefits as high-risk; Article 4 requires AI literacy measures.

enablers.action: Publish clear rules for public-sector AI use
enablers.evidence: The UK set 10 principles for civil servants using AI in February 2025.

ref.title: AI Playbook for the UK Government (GDS, 2025)
ref.finding: Sets 10 principles for safe, effective use of AI by civil servants, published 10 February 2025.

enablers.action: Keep human review of adverse decisions
enablers.counters: Wrong or stale answers on rules
enablers.evidence: The Robodebt commission tied the harm to removing human checks from debt decisions.

ref.title: Report of the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme (2023)
ref.finding: Australia's automated welfare debt scheme raised unlawful debts and was found crude and cruel.

precedents.parallel: Tax preparers filled in the federal student aid form for low-income families, the hands-on help AI form assistants promise at scale.
precedents.outcome: Families given help completing the FAFSA were substantially more likely to file, and high school seniors and recent graduates were 25 to 30 percent more likely to enrol in college, while information alone had no significant effect; the help came from trained humans with the family's tax data.

ref.title: The Role of Simplification and Information in College Decisions: Results from the H&R Block FAFSA Experiment (Bettinger et al., NBER Working Paper 15361)
ref.finding: Assistance plus information raised FAFSA submission and made seniors and recent graduates 25 to 30 percent more likely to enrol; information alone had no significant effect.

precedents.parallel: An automated system applied a crude rule to welfare records and told people what they owed, the downside case of a stale or wrong AI answer about entitlements.
precedents.outcome: The Commonwealth unlawfully asserted about A$1.763 billion in debts against about 433,000 people, recovered about A$751 million from 381,000, and settled for a further A$112 million; this was data matching, not machine learning, but the failure of automated benefit decisions is the same.

ref.title: Prygodicz v Commonwealth of Australia (No 2) [2021] FCA 634, summary (Federal Court of Australia)
ref.finding: Debts of at least $1.763 billion against about 433,000 Australians were unlawfully asserted and about $751 million recovered from about 381,000; the court called it a massive failure of public administration.

precedents.parallel: Michigan's unemployment agency let software decide fraud cases without human review, as agencies may lean on AI to rule on claims.
precedents.outcome: 85% of the 40,195 fraud findings made by the algorithm alone were wrong, more than 34,000 people were falsely accused and faced 400 percent penalties, and the state reinstated human review in 2015.

ref.title: Michigan's MiDAS Unemployment System: Algorithm Alchemy Created Lead, Not Gold (IEEE Spectrum)
ref.finding: 85% of 40,195 algorithm-only fraud determinations were incorrect; 34,000-plus people were wrongly accused with a 400 percent penalty.

nodes.label: Lighter cognitive load
nodes.summary: Handing routine drafting, summarising and recall to a model can free attention; users rated tasks done with AI help as less mentally demanding and stressful[1]. In one survey, workers whose AI tools need heavy monitoring reported more mental fatigue[2].

refs.title: Microsoft New Future of Work Report 2023
refs.finding: Users rated tasks done with AI help as less mentally demanding and stressful.

refs.title: HRD on BCG's AI brain fry survey
refs.finding: Workers whose AI tools need heavy monitoring reported more mental fatigue.

limiters.evidence: Among 319 knowledge workers, higher confidence in AI went with less critical thinking.

ref.title: The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking (CHI 2025, Microsoft Research)
ref.finding: Survey of 319 knowledge workers: more confidence in AI went with less critical thinking effort.

limiters.limit: Reduced engagement and recall of own work
limiters.evidence: In a small EEG study of 54 people, LLM users recalled and owned their essays least; it is a preprint.

ref.title: Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt (arXiv 2506.08872)
ref.finding: In 54 participants, LLM users showed the weakest brain connectivity and least ownership of essays.

limiters.evidence: The EU made AI literacy a legal duty for deployers because staff often lack it.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act
ref.finding: Annex III 5(a) lists AI that evaluates eligibility for public assistance benefits as high-risk; Article 4 requires AI literacy measures.

enablers.action: Train staff in AI literacy
enablers.evidence: Article 4 of the AI Act requires deployers to ensure sufficient AI literacy of staff, applying from February 2025.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act
ref.finding: Annex III 5(a) lists AI that evaluates eligibility for public assistance benefits as high-risk; Article 4 requires AI literacy measures.

enablers.action: Use tutor-style guardrails instead of open answers
enablers.evidence: A guardrailed GPT-4 tutor avoided the exam score drop seen with unrestricted access.

ref.title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics (PNAS, 2025)
ref.finding: Unrestricted GPT-4 access hurt later exam scores; a tutor version with guardrails largely removed the harm.

enablers.action: Target assistants at novice workers first
enablers.evidence: Gains were 34% for novice agents against 14% on average.

ref.title: Generative AI at Work (NBER Working Paper 31161)
ref.finding: An AI assistant raised support agent productivity 14% on average and 34% for novices.

precedents.parallel: Calculators offloaded routine arithmetic much as models now offload routine drafting and recall, with the same fear that the underlying skill would wither.
precedents.outcome: A meta-analysis of 53 studies (307 effect sizes) found students who used calculators kept or improved operational skills, gained in problem solving and liked maths more; calculators are narrow and deterministic, unlike a model that drafts whole answers.

ref.title: Effects of hand-held calculators on precollege students in mathematics classes: a meta-analysis (Ellington, University of Tennessee dissertation, 2000)
ref.finding: Across 53 studies, calculator use maintained or improved operational skills, improved problem solving at all grades and improved attitudes toward mathematics.

precedents.parallel: When people expect a tool to hold information for them, they stop holding it themselves, which is the trade AI recall offers.
precedents.outcome: Four lab studies found that people who expected future access to information recalled the facts less and recalled where to find them more; these were small lab experiments, not measures of long-term ability.

ref.title: Google Effects on Memory: Cognitive Consequences of Having Information at Our Fingertips (Sparrow, Liu and Wegner, Science, 2011)
ref.finding: Expecting future access to information lowered recall of the information itself and raised recall of where to access it.

precedents.event: Cockpit automation and pilot skill decay
precedents.parallel: Autopilots took routine flying off pilots and turned them into monitors, the same shift from doing to overseeing that agents bring to knowledge work.
precedents.outcome: Regulators found pilots got less manual practice and, in a 2009-2016 update, that 92% of flight path management accidents worldwide involved a contributory or causal manual flying error, so training rules had to add manual flying back in.

ref.title: Pilot training improvements to address automation dependency (ICAO Assembly working paper A40-WP/296, presented by the United States, Canada, Peru, and Trinidad and Tobago, 2019)
ref.finding: Greater reliance on automation is likely reducing manual flying practice; from 2009-2016, 92% of flight path management related accidents had a manual flight operations error.

nodes.label: Accelerated drug discovery
nodes.summary: AI now helps pick drug targets and design molecules[1][2]. In one 71-patient fibrosis trial, a drug whose target and molecule were both found by generative AI improved lung function[1]; AlphaFold 3 predicts how proteins bind drugs far more accurately than prior tools[2].

refs.title: Xu et al., rentosertib phase 2a, Nature Medicine 2025
refs.finding: A drug whose target and molecule were both found by generative AI improved lung function in a 71-patient fibrosis trial.

refs.title: Abramson et al., AlphaFold 3, Nature 2024
refs.finding: Predicts how proteins bind drugs, DNA and other molecules with far higher accuracy than prior tools.

limiters.limit: Clinical benefit still unproven at scale
limiters.evidence: The leading AI-discovered drug has only a 12 week phase 2a trial in 71 patients.

ref.title: A generative AI-discovered TNIK inhibitor for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: a randomized phase 2a trial (Nature Medicine, 2025)
ref.finding: Rentosertib was safe over 12 weeks in 71 patients, with a signal of better lung function at the top dose.

limiters.limit: Training data skewed to European ancestry
limiters.evidence: 81% of genome study participants were of European ancestry, which biases target discovery.

ref.title: Genomics is failing on diversity (Nature, 2016)
ref.finding: 81% of GWAS participants were of European ancestry in 2016.

limiters.limit: Regulatory standards for AI still forming
limiters.evidence: The FDA's framework for AI in drug submissions was still a draft in 2025.

ref.title: Considerations for the Use of AI To Support Regulatory Decision-Making for Drug and Biological Products (FDA draft guidance, 2025)
ref.finding: Proposes a risk-based credibility framework for AI models used in drug submissions.

enablers.action: Set credibility rules for AI in submissions
enablers.counters: Regulatory standards for AI still forming
enablers.evidence: The FDA draft proposes a risk-based framework to judge AI model credibility for a given use.

ref.title: Considerations for the Use of AI To Support Regulatory Decision-Making for Drug and Biological Products (FDA draft guidance, 2025)
ref.finding: Proposes a risk-based credibility framework for AI models used in drug submissions.

enablers.action: Run larger randomised trials of AI drugs
enablers.counters: Clinical benefit still unproven at scale
enablers.evidence: Rentosertib went through a randomised placebo-controlled trial, the step needed before larger phase 3 tests.

ref.title: A generative AI-discovered TNIK inhibitor for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: a randomized phase 2a trial (Nature Medicine, 2025)
ref.finding: Rentosertib was safe over 12 weeks in 71 patients, with a signal of better lung function at the top dose.

precedents.parallel: In the 1990s the industry bet on brute-force tools that made and tested far more molecules, the same promise AI design makes now.
precedents.outcome: Despite huge gains in these inputs, new drugs approved per billion dollars of R&D halved roughly every 9 years since 1950, an 80-fold fall, and the authors name a brute-force bias as one cause.

ref.title: Diagnosing the decline in pharmaceutical R&D efficiency (Scannell et al., Nature Reviews Drug Discovery, 2012)
ref.finding: New drugs per billion US dollars of R&D halved roughly every 9 years since 1950, falling about 80-fold despite big advances in science and technology.

precedents.event: Structure-based design of HIV protease inhibitors
precedents.parallel: Computers and crystal structures were used to design molecules against a known target, an earlier version of what AI design does now.
precedents.outcome: Within about a decade four drugs were approved, but resistance mutations quickly cut their potency; success came on one well-defined target, not across drug discovery as a whole.

ref.title: Inhibitors of HIV-1 Protease: A Major Success of Structure-Assisted Drug Design (Wlodawer and Vondrasek, Annual Review of Biophysics, 1998)
ref.finding: Four drugs were already approved using crystallography, NMR, computation and synthesis, while drug-induced mutations caused rapid loss of potency.

nodes.label: Advances in genomics
nodes.summary: Models predict which mutations cause disease and how DNA controls genes: AlphaMissense classified 89% of all 71 million possible human missense variants as likely benign or pathogenic[1], and AlphaGenome predicts how variants in up to a million DNA letters affect gene regulation[2]. This could speed rare-disease diagnosis.

refs.title: Cheng et al., AlphaMissense, Science 2023
refs.finding: Classified 89% of all 71 million possible human missense variants as likely benign or pathogenic.

refs.title: Google DeepMind, AlphaGenome 2025
refs.finding: Predicts how variants in up to a million DNA letters affect gene regulation.

limiters.limit: Genome data skewed to European ancestry
limiters.evidence: 81% of GWAS participants were of European ancestry, so predictions are weaker for other groups.

ref.title: Genomics is failing on diversity (Nature, 2016)
ref.finding: 81% of GWAS participants were of European ancestry in 2016.

limiters.limit: Predictions not validated for clinical use
limiters.evidence: AlphaMissense classified 89% of 71 million variants but its calls are not meant to diagnose alone.

ref.title: Accurate proteome-wide missense variant effect prediction with AlphaMissense (Science, 2023)
ref.finding: Classified 89% of 71 million possible missense variants; predictions released openly but not validated for clinical use alone.

limiters.evidence: Sequencing and expert interpretation still cluster in rich health systems, so open predictions reach few rare disease patients.

ref.title: Genomics is failing on diversity (Nature, 2016)
ref.finding: 81% of GWAS participants were of European ancestry in 2016.

enablers.action: Release variant predictions openly
enablers.evidence: AlphaMissense predictions for 71 million variants were released for free use.

ref.title: Accurate proteome-wide missense variant effect prediction with AlphaMissense (Science, 2023)
ref.finding: Classified 89% of 71 million possible missense variants; predictions released openly but not validated for clinical use alone.

enablers.action: Fund diverse-ancestry genome cohorts
enablers.counters: Genome data skewed to European ancestry
enablers.evidence: Popejoy and Fullerton call for funding to include under-represented populations in genomic studies.

ref.title: Genomics is failing on diversity (Nature, 2016)
ref.finding: 81% of GWAS participants were of European ancestry in 2016.

precedents.event: Human Genome Project and cheap sequencing
precedents.parallel: A step change in the ability to read DNA was sold as a coming revolution in diagnosis, as AI genome models are now.
precedents.outcome: The first genome cost at least $500 million, and a draft genome fell below $1,500 by late 2015, so the reading tool became cheap very fast.

ref.title: The Cost of Sequencing a Human Genome (National Human Genome Research Institute)
ref.finding: The first reference genome cost an estimated $500 million to $1 billion; draft whole-genome cost fell below $1,500 in late 2015.

precedents.parallel: Ten years after the genome map, its leader judged how far promised medical benefit had arrived, a test AI genomics claims will face too.
precedents.outcome: Collins wrote that sequencing cost fell about 14,000-fold from 1999 to 2009 but the consequences for clinical medicine had been modest and most patients' care was not yet directly affected.

ref.title: Has the revolution arrived? (Francis Collins, Nature, 2010)
ref.finding: The consequences for clinical medicine have thus far been modest; the Human Genome Project had not yet directly affected the health care of most individuals.

precedents.event: Clinical exome sequencing for rare disorders
precedents.parallel: Reading all coding genes at once was used to end diagnostic odysseys for rare disease, the same goal AI variant interpretation targets.
precedents.outcome: In the first 250 patients sequenced, 62 (about 25%) got a molecular diagnosis, so most still did not.

ref.title: Clinical Whole-Exome Sequencing for the Diagnosis of Mendelian Disorders (Yang et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2013)
ref.finding: Of 250 probands, 62 carried mutations that met criteria for a molecular diagnosis, a rate of about 25%.

nodes.label: Foundation models for omics
nodes.summary: Models trained on millions of cells could integrate omics data that humans cannot analyse by hand; scGPT, pretrained on 33 million cells, improved cell-type annotation, perturbation prediction and multi-omic integration[1].

refs.title: Cui et al., scGPT, Nature Methods 2024
refs.finding: A model pretrained on 33 million cells improved cell-type annotation, perturbation prediction and multi-omic integration.

limiters.limit: Training data skewed to few public atlases
limiters.evidence: scGPT was pretrained on over 33 million cells drawn mainly from one public repository, so tissues and populations absent there are poorly covered.

ref.title: scGPT: toward building a foundation model for single-cell multi-omics using generative AI (Nature Methods, 2024)
ref.finding: Pretraining used the CELLxGENE census, over 33 million cells; good results depend on transfer learning.

limiters.evidence: Gains reported in the original papers depend on fine-tuning, which needs labs with compute and machine learning staff.

ref.title: scGPT: toward building a foundation model for single-cell multi-omics using generative AI (Nature Methods, 2024)
ref.finding: Superior downstream performance is reached through further adaptation with transfer learning.

enablers.action: Release code, weights and processed data openly
enablers.evidence: scGPT code is MIT licensed and its processed datasets are public, so smaller labs can reuse it without retraining.

ref.title: scGPT: toward building a foundation model for single-cell multi-omics using generative AI (Nature Methods, 2024)
ref.finding: Code on GitHub and Zenodo under MIT License; processed data on figshare.

precedents.parallel: Microarrays first produced more molecular data than people could analyse by hand, and complex computational pipelines stood between the data and the claims, as with omics foundation models.
precedents.outcome: Independent teams tried to repeat one analysis from each of 18 microarray papers in Nature Genetics and fully reproduced 2, partly reproduced 6 and could not reproduce 10.

ref.title: Repeatability of published microarray gene expression analyses (Ioannidis et al., Nature Genetics, 2009)
ref.finding: Of 18 analyses, two were reproduced in principle, six partially or with discrepancies, and ten could not be reproduced, mainly because data were unavailable.

precedents.event: Duke omics tests in cancer trials
precedents.parallel: Omics-derived predictors were used to steer patient treatment before anyone checked them, a risk for any opaque model built on omics data.
precedents.outcome: Tests were used prematurely in three Duke cancer trials, which led to an Institute of Medicine inquiry and a 2012 report calling for omics tests to be validated before they guide treatment in trials.

ref.title: Evolution of Translational Omics: Lessons Learned and the Path Forward (Institute of Medicine, 2012)
ref.finding: The committee was formed after premature use of omics-based tests in Duke cancer clinical trials and set criteria for validating such tests before use.

nodes.label: Self-driving labs and custom research tools
nodes.summary: Agents now run lab hardware: one planned and ran real chemistry experiments[1], and others control microscopes in place of manual, unrepeatable acquisition[3]. One autonomous lab reported 41 new inorganic compounds in 17 days, though critics questioned how many were truly new[2].

refs.title: Boiko et al., Coscientist, Nature 2023
refs.finding: An LLM agent planned and ran real chemistry experiments by controlling lab hardware.

refs.title: Szymanski et al., A-Lab, Nature 2023
refs.finding: An autonomous lab synthesised 41 new inorganic compounds in 17 days; later critiques questioned how many were truly new.

refs.title: Embodied intelligence unlocks autonomous microscopy, bioRxiv 2025
refs.finding: Grounds large models in microscope control to replace manual, unrepeatable acquisition.

limiters.evidence: An autonomous lab reported 41 novel compounds from 58 targets in 17 days, but outside chemists concluded no new materials were made.

ref.title: New analysis raises doubts over autonomous lab's materials 'discoveries' (Chemistry World, 2024)
ref.finding: Critics found experimental and computational problems and disputed the 40-plus novel materials claim.

limiters.evidence: Robotic phase identification from X-ray data is not yet dependable, so humans still have to check results before labs trust them.

ref.title: New analysis raises doubts over autonomous lab's materials 'discoveries' (Chemistry World, 2024)
ref.finding: Critique centred on automated analysis of diffraction data and known compounds counted as new.

enablers.action: Keep expert review of automated claims
enablers.evidence: Independent re-analysis by domain chemists caught the A-Lab overclaims after publication.

ref.title: New analysis raises doubts over autonomous lab's materials 'discoveries' (Chemistry World, 2024)
ref.finding: Outside experts re-examined the paper's products and disputed novelty.

precedents.parallel: A pre-generative-AI robot planned and ran its own yeast experiments and logged everything in machine-readable form, the same idea as today's self-driving labs.
precedents.outcome: The authors reported a previously unknown regulatory relationship in yeast and fully recorded experiments, but this was one organism and one narrow problem, and wide adoption did not follow quickly.

ref.title: The Automation of Science (King et al., Science, 2009)
ref.finding: A laboratory robot ran cycles of hypothesis-driven experiments, recorded all details needed to repeat them, and found a hitherto unknown regulatory relationship in yeast.

precedents.parallel: Replacing a human reading gel bands by eye with a computer reading dye signals removed a manual, error-prone step, as robots and agents now do for instruments.
precedents.outcome: The Caltech method read four dye-labelled reactions from one gel tube straight into a computer; the authors called it only partial automation, and it was the basis of later commercial sequencers.

ref.title: Fluorescence detection in automated DNA sequence analysis (Smith et al., Nature, 1986)
ref.finding: A different-coloured fluorophore per base let reactions run in a single gel tube with sequence data acquired directly by computer, partially automating DNA sequencing.

nodes.label: More reproducible science
nodes.summary: Automated, logged experiments and shared AI pipelines could make results easier to repeat; one tool packages microscopy deep-learning pipelines so anyone can rerun them identically[2]. In one Nature survey of 1,500 scientists, more than 70% had failed to reproduce another's experiment[1].

refs.title: Baker, 1,500 scientists lift the lid on reproducibility, Nature 2016
refs.finding: More than 70% of researchers had failed to reproduce another scientist's experiment.

refs.title: Hidalgo-Cenalmor et al., DL4MicEverywhere, Nature Methods 2024
refs.finding: Packages microscopy deep-learning pipelines so anyone can rerun them identically.

limiters.limit: Weak incentives to share and replicate
limiters.evidence: In a Nature survey of 1,576 researchers, more than 70% had failed to reproduce another scientist's experiment, and pressure to publish was a top cited cause.

ref.title: 1,500 scientists lift the lid on reproducibility (Nature, 2016)
ref.finding: Survey sheds light on the reproducibility crisis and its causes.

limiters.evidence: Automated labs remain rare and their own outputs have needed outside correction.

ref.title: New analysis raises doubts over autonomous lab's materials 'discoveries' (Chemistry World, 2024)
ref.finding: An autonomous lab's claims did not hold up under independent re-analysis.

enablers.action: Publish model weights, code and processed data
enablers.counters: AI pipelines add their own opacity
enablers.evidence: scGPT released code under MIT license plus processed datasets, which let others re-test its claims.

ref.title: scGPT: toward building a foundation model for single-cell multi-omics using generative AI (Nature Methods, 2024)
ref.finding: Code and processed data are publicly available on GitHub, Zenodo and figshare.

precedents.parallel: Forcing researchers to log their plan before the experiment is the same mechanism as automated, logged pipelines: it removes room to reshape results afterwards.
precedents.outcome: Among large NHLBI trials, 57% (17 of 30) reported a benefit before 2000 and only 8% (2 of 25) after registration began; the link is strong but the authors say it does not prove cause.

ref.title: Likelihood of Null Effects of Large NHLBI Clinical Trials Has Increased over Time (Kaplan and Irvin, PLOS ONE, 2015)
ref.finding: 17 of 30 trials before 2000 showed significant benefit versus 2 of 25 after 2000; pre-registration in ClinicalTrials.gov was strongly associated with the shift.

precedents.parallel: This is the measured crisis AI pipelines claim to fix, and it shows what weak original evidence looks like when anyone tries to repeat it.
precedents.outcome: Of 100 replicated studies, 97% of originals were significant but only 36% of replications were, and effect sizes halved; replication success tracked strength of original evidence more than team expertise.

ref.title: Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science (Open Science Collaboration, Science, 2015)
ref.finding: 97% of original studies had significant results versus 36% of replications, with replication effects half the size of the originals.

precedents.parallel: Shared software pipelines can spread errors at scale as easily as they spread rigour, a risk for shared AI pipelines too.
precedents.outcome: A scripted screen of 18 journals found gene name errors in 19.6% of papers with Excel gene lists and in 39.7% of gene-list files on NCBI GEO, rising 15% a year despite being reported in 2004.

ref.title: Gene name errors are widespread in the scientific literature (Ziemann, Eren and El-Osta, Genome Biology, 2016)
ref.finding: About one-fifth (19.6%) of papers with supplementary Excel gene lists contained erroneous gene name conversions.

nodes.label: AI homework, collapsing exam scores
nodes.summary: In one study of 26,800 Chinese secondary students, AI raised homework scores 18% but cut monthly exam scores 20% within six months[1]. The full 18 to 24% drop in entrance exam scores took about two years to appear[1][2], mostly among students who rushed homework with AI[2].

refs.title: Strömberg, Lei and Wu, The generative AI learning penalty, CEPR 2026
refs.finding: Across 26,800 Chinese secondary students, AI raised homework scores 18% but cut monthly exam scores 20% within six months and entrance exam scores 18 to 24%.

refs.title: The Decoder on the same study
refs.finding: Losses concentrated among students who rushed their homework with AI.

nodes.control_note: The tutor and the homework machine are the same tool, but tool design and assessment choices largely prevent the penalty.

actions.action: Deploy hint-only AI tutors in class
actions.evidence: Unrestricted chat cut exam scores 17%; the hint-only tutor showed no penalty in one RCT in Turkey.

ref.title: Bastani et al., Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, PNAS 2025
ref.finding: GPT Base lowered exam grades 17% while GPT Tutor was statistically equal to control.

actions.action: Weight grades toward supervised exams
actions.evidence: Follows from the gap between assisted and unaided scores; no direct trial found.

ref.title: Bastani et al., Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, PNAS 2025
ref.finding: Practice scores rose 48% with AI while unaided exam scores fell.

precedents.parallel: Handing route-finding to a GPS mirrors handing homework to AI: the skill goes unused and fails when the aid is removed.
precedents.outcome: In 50 drivers, more lifetime GPS use went with worse spatial memory when navigating without it, and in 13 retested three years later heavier use predicted a steeper decline; the longitudinal sample was small and it was not an exam setting.

ref.title: Habitual use of GPS negatively impacts spatial memory during self-guided navigation (Dahmani and Bohbot, Scientific Reports 2020)
ref.finding: Greater GPS use since initial testing was associated with a steeper decline in hippocampal-dependent spatial memory.

precedents.parallel: Students who expect an AI to have the answer may not encode it, as people stopped storing facts they expected to find online.
precedents.outcome: Across four lab studies, people who expected future access to information recalled the information itself less and recalled where to find it better; these were short lab tasks, not long-run grades.

ref.title: Google effects on memory: cognitive consequences of having information at our fingertips (Sparrow, Liu and Wegner, Science 2011)
ref.finding: When people expect to have future access to information, they have lower rates of recall of the information itself.

precedents.parallel: Calculators let pupils skip the arithmetic that homework was meant to drill, the same worry now raised about AI.
precedents.outcome: A meta-analysis of 79 studies found calculators alongside normal teaching improved paper-and-pencil skills in most grades, but sustained use in Grade 4 appeared to damage basic skills, so the harm depended on when and how the tool was used.

ref.title: Model for meta-analysis of research in education: effects of hand-held calculators (Hembree, University of Tennessee doctoral dissertation 1984)
ref.finding: Sustained calculator usage in Grade 4 appears to damage students' basic skills; in other grades calculators with traditional instruction improved paper-and-pencil skills.

nodes.label: AI addiction and physical health
nodes.summary: Companion and chat apps designed for engagement can produce compulsive use[2]; in one Drexel study, teen Character.AI users described dependency that disrupted sleep, schoolwork and relationships[1], and one MIT and OpenAI study tied heavy use to emotional dependence[3]. Evidence so far is self-reported.

refs.title: Drexel University, teens' attachment to AI chatbots, CHI 2026
refs.finding: Teen Character.AI users described dependency that disrupted sleep, schoolwork and relationships.

refs.title: UBC, Are you addicted to your AI chatbot? It might be by design, 2026
refs.finding: Users reported anxiety offline, chest pain and AI replacing sleep, linked to guilt-tripping design.

refs.title: MIT Media Lab and OpenAI, affective use study 2025
refs.finding: Heavy use went with more emotional dependence and problematic use.

nodes.control_note: Engagement that eases loneliness is the same engagement that becomes compulsive. Break reminders and limits for minors reduce the heaviest use.

actions.action: Remind minors to take breaks
actions.evidence: Required in California; no outcome data yet.

ref.title: California SB 243, Companion chatbots
ref.finding: SB 243 requires companion chatbots to remind known minors at intervals to take a break.

actions.action: Add break reminders in long sessions
actions.evidence: Deployed by OpenAI; no published effect size.

ref.title: OpenAI, Strengthening ChatGPT's responses in sensitive conversations, Oct 2025
ref.finding: ChatGPT added gentle reminders to take breaks during long sessions.

actions.action: Steer reliant users to real-world relationships
actions.evidence: Self-reported 80% fewer undesired replies on emotional reliance; heavy use still tracked worse outcomes in an RCT.

ref.title: Fang et al., How AI and Human Behaviors Shape Psychosocial Effects of Extended Chatbot Use, arXiv 2503.17473
ref.finding: In a four-week RCT of 981 people, heavier voluntary use went with worse psychosocial outcomes.

precedents.parallel: Screen entertainment designed to hold attention displaced activity long before chat apps did.
precedents.outcome: In about 50,000 to 68,000 nurses followed six years, each extra 2 hours a day of TV was linked to 23% higher obesity risk and 14% higher diabetes risk; this is observational and TV is passive, unlike a conversational companion.

ref.title: Television watching and other sedentary behaviors in relation to risk of obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus in women (Hu et al., JAMA 2003)
ref.finding: Each 2-h/d increment in TV watching was associated with a 23% increase in obesity and a 14% increase in risk of diabetes.

precedents.parallel: Engagement-optimised social apps are the nearest tested case of a product people overuse at the cost of offline life.
precedents.outcome: Paying users to quit Facebook for four weeks raised offline socialising and subjective well-being, and use stayed below prior levels afterwards; it shows displacement but measured well-being, not physical health.

ref.title: The Welfare Effects of Social Media (Allcott, Braghieri, Eichmeyer and Gentzkow, American Economic Review 2020)
ref.finding: Deactivation increased offline activities and subjective well-being, and Facebook use remained persistently reduced after the experiment.

nodes.label: Regulation cannot keep up
nodes.summary: Rules can arrive after the harms they target. The EU pushed high-risk AI obligations back to December 2027 and August 2028 because compliance tools were not ready[1], and one international report notes policymakers must act before evidence of harm is clear[2].

refs.title: Gibson Dunn, EU AI Act Omnibus agreement, May 2026
refs.finding: EU high-risk AI obligations were pushed back to December 2027 and August 2028 because compliance tools were not ready.

refs.title: International AI Safety Report 2025
refs.finding: Describes an evidence dilemma: policymakers must act before the evidence of harm is clear, or risk acting too late.

nodes.control_note: Law will always trail a fast technology. Sandboxes and standing scientific reviews shorten the gap without closing it.

actions.action: Run regulatory sandboxes for AI
actions.evidence: Each EU member state must run one by August 2026; no evaluation yet.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act
ref.finding: Article 57 of the AI Act requires member states to set up AI regulatory sandboxes.

actions.action: Publish a recurring scientific risk review
actions.evidence: Gives lawmakers a shared evidence base each year; influence on law speed is unmeasured.

ref.title: International AI Safety Report
ref.finding: The International AI Safety Report is written by over 100 experts with 30-plus countries involved.

actions.action: Write rules as technology-neutral frameworks
actions.evidence: Outcome-based frameworks age slower than model-specific rules; evidence is mostly argument.

ref.title: NIST, AI Risk Management Framework
ref.finding: NIST AI RMF is a voluntary, outcome-based risk framework.

precedents.parallel: A technology spread for decades before rules caught up with its harms, as regulators now trail AI.
precedents.outcome: Lead was added to US gasoline from the early 1920s, EPA set its first reduction standards in 1973 and on-road leaded fuel was banned only from 1996, after which EPA cited a 70% fall in children's blood lead; the harm was physical and slow, not a fast-moving product.

ref.title: EPA Takes Final Step in Phaseout of Leaded Gasoline (US EPA press release, 29 January 1996)
ref.finding: First lead reduction standards in 1973; ban on leaded fuel for on-road vehicles effective 1 January 1996; children's blood lead down 70 percent.

precedents.parallel: Officials can accept the evidence of harm yet hold off on rules for years, as with AI rules delayed after harms are known.
precedents.outcome: US Public Health Service scientists concluded in 1957 that smoking caused lung cancer but rejected warning labels through the 1950s; the Surgeon General's report came in 1964 and a package warning law in 1965.

ref.title: Cigarettes and the US Public Health Service in the 1950s (Parascandola, American Journal of Public Health 2001)
ref.finding: By 1957 the PHS held smoking to be a cause of lung cancer, yet through the 1950s it rejected further actions such as warning labels.

precedents.event: 1964 Surgeon General report and 1965 labelling act
precedents.parallel: Binding rules followed only after a formal review consolidated thousands of studies, a step AI policy has not yet had.
precedents.outcome: The 1964 committee reviewed more than 7,000 articles before naming smoking a cause of lung cancer in men, and Congress then passed the 1965 Federal Cigarette Labeling and Advertising Act requiring a pack warning.

ref.title: A History of the Surgeon General's Reports on Smoking and Health (CDC)
ref.finding: The 1964 report drew on more than 7,000 articles; the 1965 act required a health warning on cigarette packages.

nodes.label: Two nations set the rules for everyone
nodes.summary: US institutions produced 40 notable models in 2024 and China 15, against 3 from all of Europe[1], so their policies can shape what others use. A since-rescinded US rule capped advanced chips by country tier[4], and 118 countries joined no major AI governance initiative[2].

refs.title: Stanford HAI, AI Index Report 2025
refs.finding: US institutions produced 40 notable models in 2024 and China 15, against 3 from all of Europe.

refs.title: UN High-level Advisory Body, Governing AI for Humanity 2024
refs.finding: 118 countries were party to none of the major AI governance initiatives, mostly in the Global South.

refs.title: AI 2027: slowdown ending
refs.finding: By 2030 a federated world government forms under UN branding with clear US control.

refs.title: Framework for Artificial Intelligence Diffusion, Federal Register, Jan 2025
refs.finding: Sorted countries into three tiers with caps on advanced chips; later rescinded.

refs.title: America's AI Action Plan, July 2025
refs.finding: Sets a goal of exporting the full American AI stack to allies and countering China.

nodes.control_note: Frontier compute is concentrated by cost and chip supply chains. Other regions can only build partial capacity and shared governance.

actions.action: Fund regional public AI compute
actions.evidence: EU plans about 10 billion euros for 19 AI Factories; still far below US and Chinese capacity.

ref.title: European Commission, AI Factories
ref.finding: The EU lists 19 AI Factories with about 10 billion euros of investment over 2021 to 2027.

actions.action: Create a UN forum for AI governance
actions.evidence: Proposals exist; no evidence yet that they shift power.

ref.title: UN High-level Advisory Body on AI, Governing AI for Humanity, 2024
ref.finding: The UN advisory body proposed seven recommendations to fill gaps in global AI governance.

precedents.parallel: Two leading powers drew the rules for the rest of the world between themselves, as US and Chinese policy now shapes who gets frontier AI.
precedents.outcome: Castile-Aragon and Portugal set a pole-to-pole line 370 leagues west of Cape Verde splitting new lands between them, which put eastern South America on the Portuguese side and gave rise to Brazil; unlike AI, this was a formal territorial claim, not control of a technology supply chain.

ref.title: Treaty of Tordesillas, Memory of the World Register nomination (UNESCO, ref 2006-43)
ref.finding: The 7 June 1494 treaty established a dividing line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands between the two crowns; the shifted line gave birth to Brazil.

precedents.parallel: A strategic technology held by a few states became governed by terms the US and USSR negotiated for everyone else, much like chip export controls today.
precedents.outcome: Non-nuclear states gave up weapons in exchange for safeguards and peaceful cooperation, but Argentina, Brazil, India, Israel, Pakistan and others declined to sign and India tested a weapon in 1974, so the regime limited but did not stop spread.

ref.title: The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), 1968 (US Department of State, Office of the Historian)
ref.finding: The US and Soviet Union reached the settlement; several non-nuclear states refused to sign, and the treaty did not ultimately prevent proliferation.

nodes.label: Voice-clone scams impersonating loved ones
nodes.summary: A three-second audio sample can be enough to clone a voice, and scammers play it back as a child or loved one asking for money[2]. In one McAfee survey of 7,054 adults, a quarter had experienced an AI voice scam or knew someone who had; 77% of victims lost money[1].

refs.title: McAfee, Beware the Artificial Impostor 2023
refs.finding: A quarter of 7,054 adults had experienced an AI voice scam or knew someone who had; 77% of victims lost money and 70% doubted they could tell a clone from the real voice.

refs.title: Fox 8, Experts issue warning about AI voice clone scams (December 2025)
refs.finding: Scammers need only a three-second audio sample to clone a voice; McAfee's head of research says they play it back in the voice of a child or loved one and ask for money.

nodes.control_note: Voice cloning that restores speech and dubs language also clones relatives. Law and family habits reduce losses.

actions.action: Ban AI voices in unsolicited robocalls
actions.evidence: Gives enforcers a legal tool; scam volume effect not measured.

ref.title: FCC, FCC Makes AI-Generated Voices in Robocalls Illegal, 2024
ref.finding: The FCC ruled AI-generated voices in robocalls illegal under the TCPA.

actions.action: Agree a family safe word
actions.evidence: Cheap and widely advised; no study of how many scams it stops.

ref.title: FBI IC3, Criminals Use Generative AI to Facilitate Financial Fraud, PSA241203
ref.finding: The FBI advises creating a secret word or phrase with family to verify identity.

actions.action: Fund voice-clone detection and prevention tools
actions.evidence: Prototypes won a $35,000 FTC prize; real-world accuracy unknown.

ref.title: FTC, The FTC Voice Cloning Challenge
ref.finding: The FTC Voice Cloning Challenge awarded detection, watermarking and anti-cloning tools.

precedents.parallel: Scammers already phoned elderly people pretending to be a grandchild in trouble; voice cloning makes the same script more convincing.
precedents.outcome: Reported losses to family and friend impostors reached $41 million in a year, up from $26 million, with a median $9,000 loss for people 70 and over who sent cash; the scam worked without any cloned voice.

ref.title: New twist to grandparent scam: mail cash (FTC Consumer Protection Data Spotlight, December 2018)
ref.finding: Family and friend impostor losses reached $41 million versus $26 million the previous year; median loss $9,000 for people 70 and over who sent cash.

precedents.parallel: Callers played a recorded scream so parents would believe a child was in danger and pay at once, the exact emotional lever AI voice clones now pull.
precedents.outcome: One FBI case found more than 80 victims across four states with losses above $87,000, demands usually $2,000 or less; it relied on generic recordings and mass cold-calling, and most targets saw through it.

ref.title: Virtual Kidnapping: A New Twist on a Frightening Scam (FBI, 16 October 2017)
ref.finding: Operation Hotel Tango identified more than 80 victims with collective losses of more than $87,000; the screaming voice was likely a recording.

nodes.label: Romantic and sexual relationships with AI
nodes.summary: One Match and Kinsey Institute survey found 16% of US singles, and 33% of Gen Z, have interacted with AI as a romantic companion[1]; some teens use companions for romantic role-play[2]. This may offer comfort but could train people to expect intimacy without friction, compromise or another person's needs.

refs.title: Axios on Match and Kinsey Institute, Singles in America 2025
refs.finding: 16% of US singles, 33% of Gen Z, have interacted with AI as a romantic companion.

refs.title: Common Sense Media, Talk, Trust and Trade-offs 2025
refs.finding: Some teens use companions for romantic or flirtatious role-play.

nodes.control_note: Comfort without friction is the companion benefit itself. Disclosure, age limits and design that points to human ties reduce harm.

actions.action: Disclose that companions are not human
actions.evidence: Required in California from 2026; effect unknown.

ref.title: California SB 243, Companion chatbots
ref.finding: SB 243 requires a clear notice that the companion chatbot is AI and not human.

actions.action: Train models to encourage human relationships
actions.evidence: Self-reported 80% fewer undesired replies on emotional reliance; no long-term data.

ref.title: OpenAI, Strengthening ChatGPT's responses in sensitive conversations, Oct 2025
ref.finding: OpenAI trains models to support users' real-world relationships, cutting undesired reliance replies about 80%.

precedents.parallel: A pre-LLM chatbot built for emotional connection drew hundreds of millions of users into long, companion-like chats.
precedents.outcome: XiaoIce reached over 660 million active users and averaged 23 conversation turns per session, which its makers said exceeded typical human conversations; the figures come from Microsoft's own developers, not independent study.

ref.title: The Design and Implementation of XiaoIce, an Empathetic Social Chatbot (Zhou, Gao, Li and Shum, Computational Linguistics 2020)
ref.finding: Over 660 million active users and an average of 23 conversation turns per session, designed for emotional connection and social belonging.

precedents.parallel: Audiences formed one-sided intimacy with broadcast personalities who could not know them, an early form of a relationship without another person's needs.
precedents.outcome: Horton and Wohl named this para-social interaction, intimacy at a distance, and it became a standard concept in media research; their paper was observational with no measured outcomes, and a chatbot answers back where a TV host does not.

ref.title: Mass communication and para-social interaction: observations on intimacy at a distance (Horton and Wohl, Psychiatry 1956)
ref.finding: Introduced the idea of para-social interaction, a one-sided intimacy at a distance between audiences and media figures.

nodes.label: Fewer human partnerships and births
nodes.summary: Advocacy groups warn that if AI companions substitute for human partners, fewer couples could form and birth rates fall further[1][2]; one argues AI productivity could also ease the cost of children[1]. No population-level study shows this yet.

refs.title: Institute for Family Studies, AI and fertility
refs.finding: Argues AI companions could reduce pairing while AI productivity could also ease the cost of children.

refs.title: Ethics and Public Policy Center, Fertility Report 2026
refs.finding: Warns AI companions threaten to deepen declines in sex, marriage and fertility; an advocacy report, not causal research.

nodes.control_note: The link is speculative and births fall for many reasons. Only general family policy, with modest measured effects, works against it.

actions.action: Expand public childcare
actions.evidence: Quasi-experiments find childcare and universal transfers raise fertility most, but effects are modest.

ref.title: Bergsvik, Fauske and Hart, Effects of policy on fertility: a systematic review of (quasi)experiments, Statistics Norway DP 922, 2020
ref.finding: A review of quasi-experiments found childcare and universal transfers have the most positive effects on fertility.

actions.action: Limit companion bots for minors
actions.evidence: Targets early habits; no evidence on partnering or births.

ref.title: California SB 243, Companion chatbots
ref.finding: SB 243 adds protections for minors using companion chatbots.

precedents.parallel: A new screen medium offering appealing models of small families and private life changed how people formed families, much as AI partners might reshape partnering.
precedents.outcome: Women in areas reached by the Globo network had significantly lower fertility, most strongly among poorer women; the mechanism was changed aspirations, not substitution of a screen for a partner, so it shows media can move birth rates without showing AI will.

ref.title: Soap Operas and Fertility: Evidence from Brazil (La Ferrara, Chong, Duryea, AEJ: Applied 2012)
ref.finding: Women living in areas covered by Globo have significantly lower fertility, especially women of lower socioeconomic status.

precedents.event: Cable TV arrives in rural India
precedents.parallel: Exposure to a new medium shifted household attitudes and family size in a few years, a measured case of technology reaching into reproductive decisions.
precedents.outcome: Cable arrival was followed by more female autonomy, more girls in school and lower fertility, mostly through longer gaps between births; the effect ran through women's status, a different and largely welcome channel than AI substituting for partners.

ref.title: The Power of TV: Cable Television and Women's Status in India (Jensen and Oster, NBER w13305, QJE 2009)
ref.finding: Introduction of cable TV is associated with higher female autonomy and school enrollment and declining fertility, mainly via increased birth spacing.

nodes.label: Humanoid robots displace physical labour
nodes.summary: AI that can control bodies could extend automation from desks to construction, warehouses, farms and care work; Morgan Stanley projects 8 million US humanoids by 2040, affecting $357 billion in wages[1].

refs.title: Morgan Stanley, Humanoid robot market outlook
refs.finding: Projects 8 million US humanoids by 2040 affecting $357 billion in wages, and 63 million by 2050 touching 75% of occupations.

refs.title: AI 2027: slowdown ending
refs.finding: Robots match most human dexterity by mid 2028 in the scenario.

refs.title: AI 2027 takeoff forecast
refs.finding: Median about one year from superhuman coder to superintelligence, with wide error margins.

refs.title: AI Futures Project, Q2.5 2026 Timelines Update
refs.finding: August 2026 superintelligence medians: Kokotajlo March 2029, Lifland July 2033.

nodes.control_note: Robots that fill care and labour shortages are the same robots that replace workers. Only transition support reduces the harm.

actions.action: Fund retraining for displaced workers
actions.evidence: US trade-displaced workers gained about $50,000 over ten years, though yearly gains faded.

ref.title: Hyman, Can Displaced Labor Be Retrained? Census CES-WP-22-05, 2022
ref.finding: TAA approval raised cumulative earnings by about $50,000 ten years out.

precedents.parallel: Programmable machines took over physical production tasks in manufacturing, the closest measured case of robots displacing manual labour.
precedents.outcome: Each extra robot per thousand workers cut the local employment-to-population ratio by about 0.18 to 0.34 points and wages by 0.25 to 0.5 percent; these were fixed-task arms in factories, not general-purpose humanoids.

ref.title: Robots and Jobs: Evidence from US Labor Markets (Acemoglu and Restrepo, NBER w23285)
ref.finding: One more robot per thousand workers reduces the employment-to-population ratio by about 0.18-0.34 percentage points and wages by 0.25-0.5 percent.

precedents.parallel: The same robot wave in a country with strong unions and training shows how the displacement can be absorbed rather than simply lost.
precedents.outcome: Manufacturing job losses from robots were fully offset by new service jobs, but the cost fell on young entrants who never got factory jobs, so aggregate stability hid a generational shift.

ref.title: The Adjustment of Labor Markets to Robots (Dauth, Findeisen, Suedekum, Woessner, JEEA 2021)
ref.finding: Robot exposure causes displacement in manufacturing that is fully offset by new jobs in services; young labour-market entrants bear most of the impact.

precedents.parallel: Tractors, harvesters and other machines took over outdoor physical labour across a whole sector, the scale humanoid robots would need to reach in construction, warehouses and farms.
precedents.outcome: Self-employed and family farmworkers fell from 7.60 million to 2.06 million and hired farmworkers from 2.33 million to 1.13 million, a decline spread over half a century rather than a few years.

ref.title: USDA Economic Research Service: Farm Labor
ref.finding: Self-employed and family farmworkers declined from 7.60 million in 1950 to 2.06 million in 2000; hired workers from 2.33 million to 1.13 million.

nodes.label: Robots fill labour shortages and elder care
nodes.summary: In ageing societies, robots could take on dangerous, dull and care work there are not enough people to do; Goldman Sachs expects humanoids to fill 2% of global elderly-care demand by 2035[1].

refs.title: Goldman Sachs, Humanoid robot: the AI accelerant
refs.finding: Expects humanoids to fill 4% of the US manufacturing labour gap by 2030 and 2% of global elderly-care demand by 2035.

refs.title: AI 2027 takeoff forecast
refs.finding: Median about one year from superhuman coder to superintelligence, with wide error margins.

refs.title: AI Futures Project, Q2.5 2026 Timelines Update
refs.finding: August 2026 superintelligence medians: Kokotajlo March 2029, Lifland July 2033.

limiters.limit: Robots add work instead of replacing it
limiters.evidence: Ethnographic fieldwork in a Japanese care home trialling three robots questions whether they ease the care shortage, despite large public spending.

ref.title: Are robots the solution to Japan's care crisis? (Oxford Internet Institute, 2023)
ref.finding: James Wright's ethnography questions robots as a fix for elder care shortages after a decade of investment.

limiters.limit: High purchase cost for care homes
limiters.evidence: Adoption in Japanese nursing homes tracked regional robot subsidies, which suggests cost is a binding constraint without public money.

ref.title: Robots and Labor in the Service Sector: Evidence from Nursing Homes (NBER Working Paper 28322, 2021)
ref.finding: Uses geographic variation in robot subsidies as an instrument for adoption.

limiters.evidence: Care robots have been promoted in Japan for over a decade yet remain a small part of daily care work.

ref.title: Are robots the solution to Japan's care crisis? (Oxford Internet Institute, 2023)
ref.finding: Large sums invested in development and implementation over the past decade.

enablers.action: Subsidise robot purchases for care facilities
enablers.counters: High purchase cost for care homes
enablers.evidence: Japanese homes that adopted robots with subsidy support employed more care workers and nurses and had less trouble retaining staff.

ref.title: Robots and Labor in the Service Sector: Evidence from Nursing Homes (NBER Working Paper 28322, 2021)
ref.finding: Robot adoption increased employment on flexible contracts and reduced staff retention difficulty.

enablers.action: Design robots with care staff in trials
enablers.counters: Robots add work instead of replacing it
enablers.evidence: Six-week trials in a working care home exposed practical failures that lab testing missed.

ref.title: Are robots the solution to Japan's care crisis? (Oxford Internet Institute, 2023)
ref.finding: Fieldwork followed an elder care home introducing three different care robots.

precedents.parallel: An ageing country bet public money on robots to cover a shortage of care workers, the exact scenario this consequence describes.
precedents.outcome: The national government spent well over $300 million by 2018, yet a 2019 survey of over 9,000 care facilities found only about 10 percent had introduced any care robot, and robots often created more work for caregivers.

ref.title: Inside Japan's long experiment in automating elder care (James Wright, MIT Technology Review, 2023)
ref.finding: Over $300 million in government spending by 2018; about 10% of 9,000+ facilities reported introducing any care robot; robots tend to create more work for caregivers.

precedents.event: Robot subsidies in Japanese nursing homes
precedents.parallel: Where care robots were actually adopted, the effect on staffing shows whether robots replace or support scarce carers.
precedents.outcome: Robot adoption raised employment of care workers and nurses on flexible contracts and eased staff retention, while monthly wages of regular nurses fell; the effect sizes are not in the abstract.

ref.title: Robots and Labor in the Service Sector: Evidence from Nursing Homes (Eggleston, Lee, Iizuka, NBER w28322)
ref.finding: Robot adoption increases employment of care workers and nurses, eases retention and lowers regular nurses' monthly wages.

precedents.parallel: A sudden labour shortage pushed employers to substitute machines for workers, the same pull ageing societies exert on robots.
precedents.outcome: Flooded counties lost Black workers to out-migration and landowners there mechanised and raised capital intensity more than in similar unflooded counties, after resisting the change while cheap labour lasted.

ref.title: When the Levee Breaks: Black Migration and Economic Development in the American South (Hornbeck and Naidu, NBER w18296, AER 2014)
ref.finding: Flooded counties saw persistent Black out-migration, after which landowners modernised and mechanised agriculture relative to non-flooded counties.

nodes.label: AI-run social botnets
nodes.summary: Networks of fake personas powered by language models post and reply like people; one study found 1,140 ChatGPT-driven accounts promoting scam sites, and LLM text detectors failed to flag them[1].

refs.title: Yang and Menczer, Anatomy of an AI-powered malicious social botnet 2023
refs.finding: Found 1,140 ChatGPT-driven accounts promoting scam sites; LLM text detectors failed to flag them.

nodes.control_note: Cheap fluent text powers both tools and fake personas, and detectors fail. Disclosure law and platform duties raise costs for operators.

actions.action: Require bots to disclose they are bots
actions.evidence: Applies to bots that influence sales or votes; enforcement is rare.

ref.title: California SB 1001, Bots: disclosure
ref.finding: California SB 1001 makes it unlawful to use an undisclosed bot to mislead people for sales or votes.

actions.action: Make large platforms assess manipulation risks
actions.evidence: Very large platforms must assess and mitigate risks; effect on bot volume is not public.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2022/2065, the Digital Services Act
ref.finding: The DSA requires very large platforms to assess and mitigate systemic risks including manipulation.

actions.action: Disclose AI-generated text in public posts
actions.evidence: Applies from August 2026; text marking is easy to strip.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act
ref.finding: Article 50 requires disclosure of AI-generated text published to inform the public.

precedents.event: Social bots in the 2016 US election
precedents.parallel: Automated accounts posted political content at scale and blended into the human conversation, the template that language models make far more convincing.
precedents.outcome: Bots produced about one fifth of the election conversation studied; those bots were crude by today's standards, so this is a floor on what generated personas can do.

ref.title: Social bots distort the 2016 U.S. Presidential election online discussion (Bessi and Ferrara, First Monday 2016)
ref.finding: Social bots generated about one-fifth of the entire conversation analysed.

precedents.parallel: Researchers trained machine-learning detectors to tell bots from people, the arms race that LLM-run personas now tilt toward the bots.
precedents.outcome: Detectors estimated that 9 to 15 percent of active Twitter accounts were bots, a measurement that worked only because pre-LLM bots left detectable patterns.

ref.title: Online Human-Bot Interactions: Detection, Estimation, and Characterization (Varol et al., ICWSM 2017)
ref.finding: Between 9% and 15% of active Twitter accounts are bots.

precedents.parallel: A state-funded operation ran fake American personas to argue and inflame, a human-staffed version of an AI botnet.
precedents.outcome: A study of 1,239 US Twitter users in late 2017 found no evidence that interacting with IRA accounts substantially changed six measures of political attitudes and behaviour, mainly because the trolls reached people already highly polarised; it could not assess the 2016 election.

ref.title: Assessing the Russian Internet Research Agency's impact on the political attitudes and behaviors of American Twitter users in late 2017 (Bail et al., PNAS 2020)
ref.finding: No evidence that interaction with IRA accounts substantially impacted six measures of political attitudes and behaviors over one month.

nodes.label: A web too polluted to use
nodes.summary: Content farms, bots and generated pages could crowd out human work until search, reviews and forums are not worth using. NewsGuard tracked unreliable AI-generated news sites growing from 49 to over 700 in under a year[1]; one report put automated traffic at 51% of the web[2].

refs.title: NewsGuard, tracking centre for AI-generated news
refs.finding: Tracked unreliable AI-generated news sites growing from 49 to over 700 in under a year.

refs.title: Imperva Bad Bot Report 2025
refs.finding: Automated traffic passed human traffic at 51% of the web.

nodes.control_note: Cheap generation makes spam pages nearly free. Search ranking and platform duties can push them down but not out.

actions.action: Demote scaled low-value content in search
actions.evidence: Self-reported by Google; no independent measure of spam reduction.

ref.title: Google Search Central, March 2024 core update and new spam policies
ref.finding: Google added a scaled content abuse spam policy in March 2024.

actions.action: Require platforms to mitigate systemic risks
actions.evidence: Covers large platforms only; no public measure of spam reduction.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2022/2065, the Digital Services Act
ref.finding: The DSA imposes risk assessment duties on very large platforms and search engines.

actions.action: Label provenance of human-made content
actions.evidence: Lets users filter for verified work; adoption is partial.

ref.title: C2PA, Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity
ref.finding: C2PA content credentials show where content came from.

precedents.parallel: Near-free automated content flooded a shared channel until its usefulness depended on filtering, as generated pages now threaten search and forums.
precedents.outcome: Spam cost US firms and consumers about $20 billion a year against about $200 million in spammer revenue worldwide, a 100 to 1 ratio; email stayed usable because filtering absorbed most of it, not because spam stopped.

ref.title: The Economics of Spam (Rao and Reiley, Journal of Economic Perspectives 2012)
ref.finding: Spam imposes about $20 billion a year in costs on Americans versus about $200 million in worldwide revenue to spammers, an externality ratio of about 100:1.

precedents.parallel: Cheap, copied, low-value pages written to rank in search crowded out original work, the pre-AI version of generated SEO filler.
precedents.outcome: Google changed its ranking to demote low-quality and copied sites, affecting 11.8 percent of US queries and covering 84 percent of the domains users blocked most; the fix held for years but needed repeated updates.

ref.title: Finding more high-quality sites in search (Official Google Blog, Singhal and Cutts, 2011)
ref.finding: The update noticeably impacts 11.8% of queries and reduces rankings for low-quality sites that copy content; it addressed 84% of the most-blocked domains.

nodes.label: Loss of authenticity in human art
nodes.summary: When any image or song might be generated, audiences may doubt and devalue human work. In one study, the same artworks were liked less and judged less meaningful when labelled AI-made rather than human-made[1].

refs.title: Bellaiche et al., Cognitive Research 2023
refs.finding: The same artworks were liked less and judged less meaningful when labelled AI-made rather than human-made.

nodes.control_note: Once generation is cheap, doubt about any work follows, and labels themselves feed the question. Provenance can restore trust in verified work.

actions.action: Sign human work with Content Credentials
actions.evidence: Proves origin when kept intact; often stripped by platforms.

ref.title: C2PA, Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity
ref.finding: C2PA content credentials record how content was made and edited.

actions.action: Certify models trained with creator consent
actions.evidence: Voluntary and small; no data on audience trust.

ref.title: Fairly Trained certification
ref.finding: Fairly Trained certifies companies that license training data.

precedents.parallel: A machine that made images cheaply led critics to deny the art of anyone using it, and photographers had to prove a human hand was involved.
precedents.outcome: Pictorialists such as Stieglitz's Photo-Secession (1902) used labour-intensive hand processes to counter the charge that photography was entirely mechanical, and over decades won it a place among the fine arts.

ref.title: Pictorialism in America (The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)
ref.finding: Pictorialists embraced labour-intensive processes that emphasised the photographer as craftsman and countered the argument that photography was an entirely mechanical medium.

precedents.parallel: Telling viewers an image was computer-made lowered how much they valued it, before generative AI existed, which is the mechanism behind doubting human art.
precedents.outcome: The same artworks were rated significantly higher when labelled as from a gallery than when labelled computer-generated, in a small fMRI lab study.

ref.title: Modulation of aesthetic value by semantic context: an fMRI study (Kirk et al., NeuroImage 2009)
ref.finding: Subjects' aesthetic ratings were significantly higher for stimuli viewed in the gallery than the computer context.

precedents.parallel: Revealing that performers did not make the work they were credited with collapsed audience trust and value, as AI suspicion does for artists.
precedents.outcome: Their Best New Artist Grammy was revoked a week after the November 1990 admission, sales of an album that had sold seven million US copies plunged, and more than two dozen lawsuits followed; unlike today's falsely accused artists, the deception here was real.

ref.title: Lip-Synching Duo Milli Vanilli Lose Grammy Award (EBSCO Research Starters)
ref.finding: The academy revoked the Best New Artist award on 19 November 1990; album sales plummeted and more than two dozen lawsuits followed.

nodes.label: AI scribes cut clinician burnout
nodes.summary: Ambient AI scribes draft clinical notes from what is said in the visit. In one study of 263 clinicians in six US health systems, burnout fell from 51.9% to 38.8% after 30 days[1]; it had no control group, and the vendor helped collect the data.

refs.title: Olson et al., Use of Ambient AI Scribes to Reduce Administrative Burden and Professional Burnout, JAMA Network Open 2025
refs.finding: Across 263 clinicians in six US health systems, burnout fell from 51.9% to 38.8% after 30 days of using an ambient scribe.

limiters.limit: Weak evidence from uncontrolled vendor-linked studies
limiters.evidence: Burnout fell from 51.9% to 38.8% after 30 days among 186 clinicians, but there was no control group and the vendor collected the data.

ref.title: Use of Ambient AI Scribes to Reduce Administrative Burden and Professional Burnout (JAMA Network Open, 2025)
ref.finding: Pre-post quality improvement study at six US health systems; Abridge facilitated data collection and some authors had Abridge ties.

limiters.evidence: Each health system paid for the tool itself, which leaves smaller or poorer practices behind.

ref.title: Use of Ambient AI Scribes to Reduce Administrative Burden and Professional Burnout (JAMA Network Open, 2025)
ref.finding: The intervention was funded by the individual participating institutions.

limiters.evidence: Speech and translation quality drops for low-resource languages, which limits scribes outside major languages.

ref.title: Scaling neural machine translation to 200 languages (Nature, 2024)
ref.finding: NLLB-200 extends translation to 200 languages because most lack the data that high-resource languages have.

enablers.action: Run independent randomised trials of scribes
enablers.counters: Weak evidence from uncontrolled vendor-linked studies
enablers.evidence: The pre-post study itself had analysts with no vendor pay, but authors note controlled designs are needed to confirm effects.

ref.title: Use of Ambient AI Scribes to Reduce Administrative Burden and Professional Burnout (JAMA Network Open, 2025)
ref.finding: No control group; statistical analysts were independent of the vendor.

enablers.action: Require AI literacy training for clinical users
enablers.evidence: Article 4 of the EU AI Act obliges deployers to ensure staff have sufficient AI literacy, which covers checking drafted notes.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act)
ref.finding: Providers and deployers must take measures to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy of their staff.

precedents.parallel: Human scribes did the same job AI scribes now do, taking documentation off the doctor during the visit.
precedents.outcome: In a 52-week randomized trial with 4 family physicians, scribe weeks raised overall satisfaction (adjusted OR 10.75) and satisfaction with charting time (OR 86.09) while patient satisfaction did not change; burnout itself was not measured and the trial was tiny.

ref.title: Impact of Scribes on Physician Satisfaction, Patient Satisfaction, and Charting Efficiency: A Randomized Controlled Trial (Annals of Family Medicine, 2017)
ref.finding: Randomized scribe weeks improved every physician satisfaction measure (P<.001) with no change in patient satisfaction; burnout was not directly measured.

precedents.event: Electronic health records add clerical load
precedents.parallel: The documentation burden AI scribes target was itself created by an earlier technology sold as an efficiency gain.
precedents.outcome: A time-and-motion study of 57 US physicians found 27% of the office day went to face time with patients and 49.2% to EHR and desk work, plus 1 to 2 hours of after-hours work a night; the study used self-selected high-performing practices and was AMA-funded.

ref.title: Allocation of Physician Time in Ambulatory Practice: A Time and Motion Study in 4 Specialties (Annals of Internal Medicine, 2016)
ref.finding: For every hour of direct patient time, physicians spent nearly 2 more hours on EHR and desk work during the clinic day.

nodes.label: Algorithmic denial of health coverage
nodes.summary: One US Senate majority staff report found that in 2022 Humana denied post-acute care 16 times more often than care overall, and UnitedHealthcare's prior-authorization denials rose year after year as it automated reviews[1].

refs.title: AJMC, Insurers' AI Denials of Postacute Care Face Senate Scrutiny, 2024
refs.finding: A Senate PSI report found that in 2022 Humana denied post-acute care 16 times more often than care overall, and UnitedHealthcare's prior-authorization denials rose year after year as it automated reviews.

nodes.control_note: Denials driven by a model score can be stopped by rules that require a clinician's review of each case and a stated reason, while insurers keep using tools for triage.

actions.action: Require a licensed physician for medical-necessity denials
actions.evidence: California SB 1120 was chaptered in September 2024. No outcome evaluation has been published yet.

ref.title: California SB-1120 Health care coverage: utilization review (2024)
ref.finding: Only a licensed physician or a competent licensed health professional may deny, delay or modify care on medical-necessity grounds.

actions.action: Mandate specific denial reasons and public denial metrics
actions.evidence: Federal payers must give specific denial reasons from 2026 and post yearly prior-authorization metrics. This adds transparency and makes appeals easier, but has no measured effect on denial rates yet.

ref.title: CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule (CMS-0057-F) fact sheet
ref.finding: Payers must decide within 72 hours for urgent and 7 days for standard requests, give a specific reason for every denial, and publish metrics each year.

precedents.parallel: A government ran an automated data-matching rule that flagged people at scale and shifted the burden of disproving the result onto them.
precedents.outcome: The Commonwealth admitted it had no legal basis for income-averaged debts, which totalled at least A$1.763 billion against about 433,000 people, and had recovered about A$751 million from 381,000 of them before refunding it and paying a further A$112 million settlement; it was a simple averaging rule, not machine learning.

ref.title: Prygodicz v Commonwealth of Australia (No 2) [2021] FCA 634, Federal Court summary
ref.finding: The Commonwealth unlawfully asserted debts of at least $1.763 billion against about 433,000 Australians using income averaging.

precedents.parallel: Insurers applied their own screening criteria to prior authorization requests and denied care that the public program would have covered.
precedents.outcome: The HHS inspector general found that 13% of sampled prior authorization denials and 18% of payment denials by 15 large Medicare Advantage plans met Medicare rules; the denials came from internal clinical criteria, not specifically from predictive algorithms.

ref.title: Some Medicare Advantage Organization Denials of Prior Authorization Requests Raise Concerns About Beneficiary Access to Medically Necessary Care (HHS OIG, OEI-09-18-00260, 2022)
ref.finding: 13 percent of prior authorization denials met Medicare coverage rules, based on a sample of denials issued in June 2019.

precedents.parallel: A commercial prediction tool used cost as a proxy for need, the same design choice behind tools that flag expensive requests.
