precedents.outcome: At a given risk score Black patients were considerably sicker than White patients, and fixing the proxy would raise the share of Black patients getting extra help from 17.7% to 46.5%; this tool allocated extra care rather than denying coverage.

ref.title: Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations (Science, 2019)
ref.finding: Predicting health costs instead of illness produced large racial bias in who was selected for additional care.

nodes.label: Health chatbots fail real patients
nodes.summary: Alone, LLMs identified the right conditions in about 95% of cases, yet in one UK lab study of fictional scenarios, 1,298 participants using them found the relevant conditions in under 34.5% of cases, no better than a control group[1].

refs.title: Bean et al., Clinical knowledge in LLMs does not translate to human interactions, arXiv 2025
refs.finding: Alone, the LLMs identified the right conditions in about 95% of cases, but the 1,298 participants using them found the relevant conditions in under 34.5% of cases, no better than the control group.

nodes.control_note: The gap sits in how people talk to the model, so it comes with any public health chatbot. Testing with real users finds it, but it does not remove it.

actions.action: Test health chatbots with real users before release
actions.evidence: In a study of 1,298 people, the models alone named the condition in 94.9% of cases, but people using them did so in under 34.5%. Simulated-patient tests did not predict this failure, so benchmark scores are a weak proxy. This is one lab study of fictional scenarios.

ref.title: Bean et al., Clinical knowledge in LLMs does not translate to human interactions (arXiv 2504.18919)
ref.finding: Participants with LLMs did no better than controls, and simulated interactions did not predict the failures with real people.

precedents.parallel: Earlier consumer self-diagnosis tools promised to let laypeople judge their own symptoms with an algorithm.
precedents.outcome: Across 23 symptom checkers and 45 vignettes, the correct diagnosis came first in 34% of evaluations and triage advice was right in 57%, falling to 33% for self-care cases; like the AI study, it used standardized vignettes, not real patients.

ref.title: Evaluation of symptom checkers for self diagnosis and triage: audit study (BMJ, 2015)
ref.finding: Symptom checkers listed the correct diagnosis first in 34% of evaluations and gave appropriate triage advice in 57%.

precedents.parallel: A widely deployed clinical prediction model looked strong in its developer's testing and weak once checked in a real hospital.
precedents.outcome: In 38,455 Michigan hospitalizations the model had an AUC of 0.63 against a developer-reported 0.76 to 0.83, missed 67% of sepsis cases and alerted on 18% of all patients; this is a clinician-facing tool, not a patient chatbot.

ref.title: External Validation of a Widely Implemented Proprietary Sepsis Prediction Model in Hospitalized Patients (JAMA Internal Medicine, 2021)
ref.finding: The model showed poor discrimination (AUC 0.63) and missed 1,709 of 2,552 sepsis cases at the alert threshold.

nodes.label: Brain implants restore speech
nodes.summary: AI decoders turn neural signals from people with paralysis into text or a speaking avatar: one participant with ALS reached 62 words per minute[1], and a woman paralysed by a stroke about 78[2]. So far the results come from single trial participants with surgical implants.

refs.title: Willett et al., A high-performance speech neuroprosthesis, Nature 2023
refs.finding: A participant with ALS reached 62 words per minute with a 23.8% word error rate on a 125,000-word vocabulary.

refs.title: Metzger et al., A high-performance neuroprosthesis for speech decoding and avatar control, Nature 2023
refs.finding: A woman with paralysis after a stroke reached about 78 words per minute of decoded text, with a speaking avatar.

limiters.evidence: Both landmark BrainGate2 speech studies report one participant each, and the authors say results must be confirmed in more people.

ref.title: An Accurate and Rapidly Calibrating Speech Neuroprosthesis (NEJM, 2024)
ref.finding: This study involved a single participant; whether similar results can be expected in future users is uncertain.

limiters.evidence: The system needed a 5 cm craniotomy, two skull-mounted pedestals wired by HDMI to a cart of computers, and a researcher to connect it.

ref.title: An Accurate and Rapidly Calibrating Speech Neuroprosthesis (NEJM, 2024)
ref.finding: A researcher's assistance was required to connect and launch the system.

limiters.evidence: The 2023 system had a 23.8% word error rate on a large vocabulary, which the authors call too high for everyday use, and array longevity needs more demonstration.

ref.title: A high-performance speech neuroprosthesis (Nature, 2023)
ref.finding: A 24% word error rate is probably not yet sufficiently low for everyday use.

enablers.action: Cut decoder calibration time
enablers.evidence: Calibration fell to 30 minutes of data for 99.6% accuracy on 50 words, versus about 17 hours in earlier work.

ref.title: An Accurate and Rapidly Calibrating Speech Neuroprosthesis (NEJM, 2024)
ref.finding: 99.6% accuracy with a 50-word vocabulary on the first day after 30 minutes of calibration.

enablers.action: Raise electrode count per implant
enablers.evidence: Offline analysis found doubling electrodes cut word error rate by a factor of about 0.57.

ref.title: A high-performance speech neuroprosthesis (Nature, 2023)
ref.finding: Doubling the electrode count cuts word error rate by nearly half.

enablers.action: Share neural datasets and decoder code openly
enablers.evidence: The Stanford team published 10,850 sentences of neural data on Dryad and decoder code on GitHub.

ref.title: A high-performance speech neuroprosthesis (Nature, 2023)
ref.finding: All neural data needed to reproduce the findings are publicly available on Dryad.

precedents.parallel: An earlier generation of implanted brain-computer interfaces decoded motor intent in a handful of people with paralysis.
precedents.outcome: Two people with tetraplegia from brainstem stroke reached and grasped objects with a robotic arm, and one drank coffee unaided for the first time in nearly 15 years, succeeding on 4 of 6 attempts; over a decade later such systems are still not a routine clinical product.

ref.title: Reach and grasp by people with tetraplegia using a neurally controlled robotic arm (Nature, 2012)
ref.finding: Participant T2 touched targets in 95.6% of trials and grasped them in 62.2%; S3 drank from a bottle on 4 of 6 attempts.

precedents.parallel: A surgically implanted neural prosthesis that translates signals for the brain went from small trials to mass use.
precedents.outcome: About 736,900 devices had been implanted worldwide by December 2019; they give useful but not normal hearing, results vary, and the path from FDA approval to scale took decades.

ref.title: Cochlear Implants (NIH National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders)
ref.finding: As of December 2019 approximately 736,900 registered devices had been implanted worldwide; an implant does not restore normal hearing.

nodes.label: AI detectors flag non-native writers
nodes.summary: Detectors used to police cheating can wrongly flag non-native English writing: in one study, seven detectors flagged 61.22% of 91 TOEFL essays as AI-generated, against near-zero for 88 US eighth-graders' essays[1]. False accusations can land on those students.

refs.title: Liang et al., GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers, Patterns/arXiv 2023
refs.finding: Seven detectors misclassified 61.3% of TOEFL essays by non-native writers as AI-generated, against near-zero for essays by US eighth-graders.

nodes.control_note: The harm comes from using detectors to punish students. Schools can stop doing that and lose little, because the detectors are unreliable anyway.

actions.action: Disable AI-text detectors in grading tools
actions.evidence: Vanderbilt turned off Turnitin's detector. It noted that even a 1% false-positive rate across its 75,000 papers a year would flag about 750 students wrongly.

ref.title: Vanderbilt University, Guidance on AI Detection and Why We're Disabling Turnitin's AI Detector (2023)
ref.finding: Vanderbilt disabled the detector, citing opacity, bias against non-native writers and doubts that detection works.

actions.action: Never use a detector score as sole evidence
actions.evidence: OpenAI's own classifier caught only 26% of AI text and flagged 9% of human text. OpenAI withdrew it in July 2023 and said it should not be a primary decision tool.

ref.title: OpenAI, New AI classifier for indicating AI-written text
ref.finding: The classifier was withdrawn on 20 July 2023 for low accuracy, at a 26% true-positive and 9% false-positive rate.

actions.action: Audit detectors on non-native writing samples
actions.evidence: Seven detectors often misclassified TOEFL essays by non-native writers as AI-generated. The test sets were small.

ref.title: Liang et al., GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers, Patterns 2023
ref.finding: The detectors frequently misclassified TOEFL essays by non-native English authors as AI-generated.

precedents.parallel: An automated detector run by a test provider flagged non-native English speakers as cheats, and authorities acted on the flags.
precedents.outcome: ETS voice recognition and listeners labelled 97% of 58,458 UK tests invalid or questionable, 25,115 people faced Home Office action, at least 11,356 left the UK, and 3,714 won first-tier appeals; the NAO found the error rate could not be determined because there was no pilot or control group.

ref.title: Investigation into the response to cheating in English language tests (National Audit Office, 2019)
ref.finding: ETS identified 97% of all UK tests as invalid or questionable using voice recognition it had not used before for TOEIC.

precedents.parallel: A detector with modest accuracy, applied to a population where real cheats are rare, produces far more false accusations than true catches.
precedents.outcome: The National Research Council calculated that screening 10,000 employees with 10 spies at a setting that catches 8 of them would also fail about 1,598 loyal employees, and judged polygraph accuracy insufficient to justify reliance on it for screening.

ref.title: The Polygraph and Lie Detection (National Research Council, 2003)
ref.finding: Polygraph accuracy is insufficient to justify reliance on it for security screening because of the false positive versus missed threat tradeoff.

nodes.label: AI gives teachers time back
nodes.summary: In one Gallup poll of 2,232 US public school teachers, weekly AI users estimated they save 5.9 hours a week, about six weeks per school year[1], and 57% to 74% said work quality improved, depending on task[1]. The savings are self-reported, and only three in ten teachers use AI weekly[1].

refs.title: Gallup / Walton Family Foundation, Three in 10 Teachers Use AI Weekly, Saving Six Weeks a Year, 2025
refs.finding: Of 2,232 US public school teachers, weekly AI users estimated they save 5.9 hours a week, about six weeks per school year.

limiters.evidence: Over 80% of US students said teachers had not taught them how to use AI for schoolwork, and teacher training lags use.

ref.title: AI Use in Schools Is Quickly Increasing but Guidance Lags Behind (RAND, 2025)
ref.finding: Professional development for teachers and training for students on AI lag behind use.

limiters.evidence: Only 45% of principals reported school or district AI guidance, and 34% of teachers had academic-integrity policies on AI.

ref.title: AI Use in Schools Is Quickly Increasing but Guidance Lags Behind (RAND, 2025)
ref.finding: 45 percent of principals reported having school or district policies or guidance on AI.

limiters.limit: Only a minority use AI weekly
limiters.evidence: About 32% of US teachers use AI weekly, and the 5.9 hours saved is self-reported by those users.

ref.title: Three in 10 Teachers Use AI Weekly, Saving Six Weeks a Year (Gallup)
ref.finding: Teachers who use AI at least weekly estimate they save an average of 5.9 hours per week.

enablers.action: Train teachers on effective AI use
enablers.evidence: RAND recommends districts train teachers and students, distinguishing AI that complements learning from AI that supplants it.

ref.title: AI Use in Schools Is Quickly Increasing but Guidance Lags Behind (RAND, 2025)
ref.finding: School district leaders should create a coherent policy on AI use and train teachers and students.

enablers.action: Publish state guidance on AI policy
enablers.evidence: RAND recommends states act as trusted sources of regularly updated AI guidance.

ref.title: AI Use in Schools Is Quickly Increasing but Guidance Lags Behind (RAND, 2025)
ref.finding: Trusted sources, such as states, should provide guidance on what effective AI policies and training look like.

enablers.action: Measure time savings beyond self-report
enablers.counters: Only a minority use AI weekly
enablers.evidence: The Gallup estimate rests on teacher self-report, so independent time-use measurement would test it.

ref.title: Three in 10 Teachers Use AI Weekly, Saving Six Weeks a Year (Gallup)
ref.finding: Weekly AI users estimate 5.9 hours saved per week, about six weeks a year.

precedents.parallel: Technologies sold as time-savers for routine work often fail to shrink the hours spent on that work once rising standards absorb the gain.
precedents.outcome: Using the 1997 Australian Time Use Survey with appliance inventories, the authors found appliances seldom reduced women's unpaid work time and in some cases slightly increased it; housework differs from paid teaching, which has fixed contract hours.

ref.title: Appliances and their impact: the ownership of domestic technology and time spent on household work (British Journal of Sociology, 2004)
ref.finding: Domestic technology rarely reduced women's unpaid working time and sometimes increased domestic labour.

precedents.parallel: Time savings that teachers report about themselves are estimates, and time estimates drift from what diaries record.
precedents.outcome: Employed respondents overestimated their work hours by 5 to 10% compared with time diaries, mostly among those claiming long hours; a later BLS article disputed parts of this analysis, so the size of the bias is contested.

ref.title: The overestimated workweek revisited (Monthly Labor Review, US Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2011)
ref.finding: Respondents overestimated work hours by 5 to 10 percent relative to their time diaries, mostly those estimating longer hours.

nodes.label: Vision AI cuts herbicide use
nodes.summary: Camera sprayers recognise individual weeds and spray only those. John Deere says farmers using See & Spray on more than five million acres in 2025 cut non-residual herbicide use by almost 50%, saving nearly 31 million gallons of herbicide mix[1].

refs.title: Farms.com, John Deere See and Spray saves millions, 2025
refs.finding: In 2025, farmers using See & Spray cut non-residual herbicide use by almost 50%, saving nearly 31 million gallons of herbicide mix.

limiters.evidence: A $25,000 upgrade pays back after about 819 acres and a $75,000 upgrade after about 2,460 acres, which favors large farms.

ref.title: Precision agriculture research measures effectiveness of See & Spray technology (University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture, 2025)
ref.finding: For a $75,000 upgrade, the payback point was about 2,460 acres.

limiters.limit: Wrong settings grow weed seed banks
limiters.evidence: At low sensitivity, missed Palmer amaranth rose 280% a year, risking herbicide resistance and over $60 million a year in Arkansas.

ref.title: Precision agriculture research measures effectiveness of See & Spray technology (University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture, 2025)
ref.finding: Low sensitivity setting increased the weed seed bank by 280 percent per year.

limiters.evidence: Arkansas researchers note the technology takes time to master and that residual herbicides may need a separate broadcast pass.

ref.title: Precision agriculture research measures effectiveness of See & Spray technology (University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture, 2025)
ref.finding: Using the technology correctly takes time to master.

enablers.action: Default to high sensitivity settings
enablers.counters: Wrong settings grow weed seed banks
enablers.evidence: High sensitivity saved about $30.49 per acre over a season with no added risk versus broadcasting.

ref.title: Precision agriculture research measures effectiveness of See & Spray technology (University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture, 2025)
ref.finding: High sensitivity setting saved about $30.49 per acre with no added risk.

enablers.action: Publish independent university field trials
enablers.evidence: A three-year Arkansas soybean trial found 43% to 59% less herbicide than broadcast spraying.

ref.title: Precision agriculture research measures effectiveness of See & Spray technology (University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture, 2025)
ref.finding: Targeted spraying reduced herbicide use by 43 to 59 percent.

enablers.action: Offer cheaper entry-level models
enablers.evidence: The cheaper Premium model is more widely adopted in Arkansas than the Ultimate model.

ref.title: Precision agriculture research measures effectiveness of See & Spray technology (University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture, 2025)
ref.finding: The Premium model is less expensive and more widely adopted in Arkansas.

precedents.parallel: Herbicide-tolerant and Bt crops were sold partly on the promise that targeted technology would cut chemical use, as vision sprayers are now.
precedents.outcome: Bt crops cut insecticide use by about 56 million kg, but herbicide-tolerant crops added about 239 million kg of herbicide as glyphosate-resistant weeds spread, a net rise of about 7 percent; this is one modelled estimate by an author critical of GE crops, and spot spraying does not select for resistance in the same way.

ref.title: Impacts of genetically engineered crops on pesticide use in the U.S. -- the first sixteen years (Benbrook, Environmental Sciences Europe 2012)
ref.finding: Herbicide-resistant crops raised US herbicide use by 239 million kg in 1996-2011 while Bt crops cut insecticide use by 56 million kg; overall pesticide use rose about 183 million kg, roughly 7 percent.

nodes.label: AI's freshwater footprint
nodes.summary: Data centres consume freshwater for cooling and, indirectly, for power generation, which may strain water-stressed regions. One modelled study projects global AI demand at 4.2 to 6.6 billion cubic metres of water withdrawal in 2027, more than half the UK's annual total[1].

refs.title: Li et al., Making AI Less Thirsty: Uncovering and Addressing the Secret Water Footprint of AI Models, arXiv 2023
refs.finding: Global AI demand is projected to account for 4.2 to 6.6 billion cubic metres of water withdrawal in 2027, more than half of the UK's annual total.

nodes.control_note: Any growth in compute uses water for cooling and power. Siting, timing and cooling choices can reduce the strain, but cannot remove it.

actions.action: Require data centres to meter and report water
actions.evidence: EU data centres of 500 kW or more must report total and potable water input and WUE every year. This produces data but sets no limits, and the data is published only in aggregate.

ref.title: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364 on a rating scheme for data centres
ref.finding: Operators of data centres of 500 kW or more must report total water input, from which WUE is calculated, to an EU database.

actions.action: Schedule workloads where and when water efficiency is high
actions.evidence: Modelled only. Water efficiency varies by site and hour, and demand is projected at 4.2 to 6.6 billion cubic metres of withdrawal in 2027. No measured gains from scheduling have been reported.

ref.title: Li et al., Making AI Less Thirsty (arXiv 2304.03271)
ref.finding: AI's water efficiency varies across place and time, and the authors argue that water should be managed together with carbon.

precedents.parallel: Power plants, like data centres, draw large volumes of water for cooling, and the gap between water withdrawn and water actually consumed drives very different headline numbers.
precedents.outcome: In 2020 US thermoelectric plants withdrew about 59,889 million gallons of freshwater a day, yet only about 3.9 percent of withdrawals were consumed; power cooling is a far larger and older load than data centres, and USGS figures are partly estimated too.

ref.title: Thermoelectric Power Water Use (U.S. Geological Survey)
ref.finding: Thermoelectric power is one of the two largest US water use categories; in 2020 about 3.9 percent of its withdrawals (2,359 million gallons per day) was consumptive use.

nodes.label: Generative AI e-waste
nodes.summary: By one estimate, generative AI could add 1.2 to 5.0 million tonnes of cumulative e-waste between 2020 and 2030 as GPUs are replaced quickly[1]. Circular-economy measures could cut that by up to 86%[1].

refs.title: Wang et al., E-waste challenges of generative artificial intelligence, Nature Computational Science 2024
refs.finding: Generative AI could add 1.2 to 5.0 million tonnes of cumulative e-waste between 2020 and 2030, and circular-economy measures could cut that by up to 86%.

nodes.control_note: More AI compute means more servers that wear out. Longer use, reuse and recycling reduce the volume but do not remove it.

actions.action: Extend server lifetimes and reuse components
actions.evidence: Modelled only. Accumulated e-waste could reach 1.2 to 5.0 million tonnes over 2020 to 2030, and circular strategies cut it by 16 to 86% depending on the scenario.

ref.title: Wang et al., E-waste challenges of generative artificial intelligence, Nature Computational Science 2024
ref.finding: Circular economy strategies along the value chain could reduce generative-AI e-waste by 16 to 86%.

precedents.parallel: Bitcoin miners, like AI labs, replace specialised chips quickly as faster ones arrive, and the old chips cannot be repurposed.
precedents.outcome: Researchers estimated bitcoin mining produced about 30.7 thousand tonnes of e-waste a year as of May 2021, possibly above 64.4 thousand tonnes at peak prices; AI accelerators are more reusable than mining ASICs, so this is an upper-bound analogue.

ref.title: Bitcoin's growing e-waste problem (Stoll and de Vries, summarised by TU Munich)
ref.finding: Bitcoin mining generates about 30.7 metric kilotons of e-waste annually as of May 2021, and could exceed 64.4 kilotons in the midterm.

precedents.parallel: Fast replacement of phones, laptops and screens created a waste stream that grew much faster than recycling, which is the path GPU refresh cycles could follow.
precedents.outcome: Global e-waste reached 62 million tonnes in 2022, up 82 percent since 2010, and only 22.3 percent was documented as properly collected and recycled.

ref.title: The Global E-waste Monitor 2024 (ITU and UNITAR)
ref.finding: 62 million tonnes of e-waste were generated in 2022, an 82 percent increase from 2010, with 22.3 percent documented as collected and recycled.

nodes.label: Decoding animal communication
nodes.summary: Machine learning on bioacoustic datasets is revealing structure in animal calls: one analysis of about 8,700 sperm whale codas found combinable features forming a far larger repertoire than the roughly 21 known coda types[1]. This could change conservation and views of animal minds, but structure is not meaning.

refs.title: Sharma et al., Contextual and combinatorial structure in sperm whale vocalisations, Nature Communications 2024
refs.finding: Analysis of about 8,700 sperm whale codas found combinable features (rhythm, tempo, rubato, ornamentation) that make up a far larger repertoire than the roughly 21 previously known coda types.

limiters.evidence: The sperm whale study describes structure only, with no semantics and no playback experiments.

ref.title: Contextual and combinatorial structure in sperm whale vocalisations (Nature Communications, 2024)
ref.finding: Our study investigates the basic structural elements, and not the semantics.

limiters.evidence: The analysis rests on 8,719 codas from one clan, collected from 2005 to 2018 with 42 tags on 25 whales.

ref.title: Contextual and combinatorial structure in sperm whale vocalisations (Nature Communications, 2024)
ref.finding: The EC-1 dataset comprises 8719 codas making up 21 coda types.

limiters.evidence: Authors warn whale-in-the-loop tests could affect an extremely vulnerable population.

ref.title: Contextual and combinatorial structure in sperm whale vocalisations (Nature Communications, 2024)
ref.finding: Experiments with potentially long-term effects on the population, which is extremely vulnerable.

enablers.action: Release annotated data and code openly
enablers.evidence: The coda dataset and analysis code are public on GitHub.

ref.title: Contextual and combinatorial structure in sperm whale vocalisations (Nature Communications, 2024)
ref.finding: All data generated in this study has been deposited on GitHub.

enablers.action: Run careful, permitted playback studies
enablers.evidence: The authors say interactive playback is needed to ground semantic hypotheses, once structure is well understood.

ref.title: Contextual and combinatorial structure in sperm whale vocalisations (Nature Communications, 2024)
ref.finding: Future research requires interactive playback experiments with whales in the wild.

enablers.action: Fund long-term field recording programs
enablers.evidence: Project CETI and the Dominica Sperm Whale Project fund the multi-year tagging behind the dataset.

ref.title: Contextual and combinatorial structure in sperm whale vocalisations (Nature Communications, 2024)
ref.finding: Funded by Project CETI via grants from Dalio Philanthropies, Ocean X and others.

precedents.event: Von Frisch decodes the bee dance
precedents.parallel: Patient analysis of a structured animal signal led to a claim about what it means, the step machine learning on whale and bird calls has not yet reached.
precedents.outcome: Von Frisch showed the waggle dance encodes the direction and distance of food and shared the 1973 Nobel Prize; his first 1923 interpretation was wrong and had to be revised, and it took decades of experiments, not pattern-finding alone.

ref.title: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1973, press release (NobelPrize.org)
ref.finding: Von Frisch elucidated how bees communicate: a round dance for nearby food and a waggle dance for food beyond about 50 m whose direction encodes the location of the source.

precedents.parallel: Ape sign-language projects found apparent structure in animal output and read meaning and grammar into it, a warning for claims that detected patterns are language.
precedents.outcome: Analysis of more than 19,000 multisign utterances first suggested syntax, but videotape showed most were prompted by the teacher's prior signs, and the authors withdrew the grammar claim.

ref.title: Can an ape create a sentence? (Terrace et al., Science 1979)
ref.finding: Apparent structural regularities in Nim's signing were invalidated by videotape analyses showing most utterances were prompted by the teacher's prior utterance.

nodes.label: Facial recognition wrongful arrests
nodes.summary: Police have arrested people on erroneous face-recognition matches; the ACLU of Georgia lists at least 13 US cases, most of them Black people[1]. These are only the publicly known cases, so the true count is likely higher.

refs.title: ACLU of Georgia, More than a dozen wrongful arrests due to police reliance on facial recognition technology
refs.finding: ACLU of Georgia lists at least 13 people in the US who were wrongfully arrested after erroneous facial recognition matches.

nodes.control_note: An arrest on a face match alone is a policy choice, so rules that demand independent evidence can largely stop it. The matching itself will still err, and some police still rely on it.

actions.action: Bar arrests based only on face matches
actions.evidence: Detroit adopted this rule in a 2024 court settlement with four years of court enforcement; no published outcome data yet.

ref.title: ACLU, Civil Rights Advocates Achieve the Nation's Strongest Police Department Policy on Facial Recognition Technology, 2024
ref.finding: The Detroit settlement bars arrests based solely on facial recognition results and requires independent evidence, training and a case audit back to 2017.

actions.action: Test and pick algorithms with low demographic error
actions.evidence: NIST found false positive rates differ by factors of 10 to over 100 across demographic groups, but vary a lot by algorithm, so choice of algorithm matters.

ref.title: NIST, NISTIR 8280 Face Recognition Vendor Test Part 3: Demographic Effects, 2019
ref.finding: Across demographics, false positive rates often vary by factors of 10 to beyond 100 times, and differ across algorithms.

actions.action: Disclose face recognition use to the defense
actions.evidence: Advocates argue disclosure lets defendants challenge a bad match early; no evaluation of effect exists.

ref.title: Innocence Project, When Artificial Intelligence Gets It Wrong, 2023
ref.finding: Calls for immediate disclosure to the defense of any AI use in a case, and notes all six known falsely accused people were Black.

precedents.parallel: An automated database search returned a close but wrong candidate, and examiners' trust in the match led to the detention of an innocent man, as with face-recognition hits.
precedents.outcome: The FBI wrongly tied Mayfield, a Muslim lawyer, to the Madrid bombing print and held him for about two weeks until Spanish police identified the real source; the Inspector General blamed the unusual similarity of the prints, circular reasoning from his known prints and excessive faith in the IAFIS system.

ref.title: A Review of the FBI's Handling of the Brandon Mayfield Case, executive summary (US DOJ Office of the Inspector General, 2006)
ref.finding: Causes of the misidentification included the unusual similarity of the prints, bias from Mayfield's known prints, and excessive faith in IAFIS technology; he was released on May 20, 2004 after the SNP identified another man.

precedents.parallel: Human identification of strangers, especially across races, was trusted as evidence long before face recognition and produced wrongful convictions that came to light only later.
precedents.outcome: Eyewitness misidentification contributed to the overwhelming majority of wrongful convictions overturned by DNA testing, and cross-racial identification is a known risk factor; unlike face recognition, the error source is human memory.

ref.title: Eyewitness Misidentification (Innocence Project)
ref.finding: Eyewitness misidentification contributed to an overwhelming majority of wrongful convictions overturned by DNA evidence; cross-racial identification is listed as a reliability risk.

nodes.label: Liar's dividend: real evidence dismissed as fake
nodes.summary: Across five US survey experiments with over 15,000 adults, politicians who falsely called real scandal reports fake news or deepfakes gained support[1]. The effect worked against text reports but was largely ineffective against video evidence[1].

refs.title: Schiff, Schiff and Bueno, The Liar's Dividend: Can Politicians Claim Misinformation to Evade Accountability? (APSR), 2024
refs.finding: Across 5 survey experiments with over 15,000 US adults, false claims of misinformation raised support for politicians caught in text-reported scandals, across partisan groups.

nodes.control_note: Once realistic fakes exist, anyone can claim real evidence is fake, so the claim can only be blunted. Provenance labels help, but every label scheme also makes unlabelled real media easier to doubt.

actions.action: Attach signed provenance credentials to authentic media
actions.evidence: One experiment with 6,114 people found C2PA labels raised perceived credibility and trust; it did not test the liar's dividend directly.

ref.title: Trattner et al., C2PA Provenance Labels Increase Trust in Digital News Platforms Across Western Countries, ICWSM 2026
ref.finding: Provenance labels on news images improved perceived transparency and credibility and trust in the source.

actions.action: Fact-check false 'it is fake' claims quickly
actions.evidence: In survey experiments a fact-check removed the support gain from a fake-news claim, but rebuttals came almost at once, a best case.

ref.title: Schiff, Schiff and Bueno, The Liar's Dividend: Can Politicians Claim Misinformation to Evade Accountability?, APSR 2024
ref.finding: A fact-check rejecting the misinformation claim eliminated the support gain, and claims were largely ineffective against video.

actions.action: Require labelling of deepfakes by law
actions.evidence: The EU duty applies from August 2026; no evidence yet on whether it changes public trust.

ref.title: EU AI Act, Article 50: Transparency obligations
ref.finding: Providers must mark synthetic output machine-readably and deployers must disclose deepfakes.

precedents.parallel: Eisenhower expected that real evidence of atrocities would later be waved away as fabrication, the same move the liar's dividend describes.
precedents.outcome: He visited Ohrdruf deliberately to be a first-hand witness, ordered photographs and brought editors and members of Congress to see the camps; Holocaust denial still emerged later, and the source does not measure how far the witnesses blunted it.

ref.title: Documenting History: Eisenhower and the Holocaust (U.S. National Park Service)
ref.finding: Eisenhower wrote on April 15, 1945 that he made the visit to be able to give firsthand evidence if the allegations were ever charged to be propaganda, and pushed for press and Congressional visits.

nodes.label: AI mediators for citizen deliberation
nodes.summary: In experiments with over 5,000 UK participants, statements written by an LLM mediator were preferred over human mediators' about 56% of the time and left groups less divided on issues such as Brexit and immigration[1]. The results come from these UK experiments only.

refs.title: Complexity Digest, AI can help humans find common ground in democratic deliberation (on Tessler et al., Science), 2024
refs.finding: In experiments with over 5,000 UK participants, statements from the Habermas Machine were preferred over human mediators' about 56% of the time and reduced group division on issues such as Brexit and immigration.

limiters.evidence: All experiments used about 5,734 UK participants, including one virtual citizens' assembly.

ref.title: AI can help humans find common ground in democratic deliberation (Science, 2024)
ref.finding: Participants (N = 5734) preferred AI-generated statements to those written by human mediators.

limiters.evidence: The authors say fair debate requires representative users who contribute in good faith.

ref.title: AI can help humans find common ground in democratic deliberation (Science, 2024)
ref.finding: Steps must be taken to ensure users are representative and contribute in good faith.

limiters.evidence: The model was trained and tested on English statements from UK residents only.

ref.title: AI can help humans find common ground in democratic deliberation (Science, 2024)
ref.finding: Experiments with over 5000 participants from the United Kingdom.

enablers.action: Pair AI mediation with citizens' assemblies
enablers.evidence: Results replicated in a virtual citizens' assembly drawn from a representative UK sample.

ref.title: AI can help humans find common ground in democratic deliberation (Science, 2024)
ref.finding: Findings were replicated in a virtual citizens' assembly with a representative UK sample.

enablers.action: Open-source mediator data for audit
enablers.evidence: DeepMind published the question set and human feedback data for the Habermas Machine on GitHub.

ref.title: AI can help humans find common ground in democratic deliberation (Science, 2024)
ref.finding: Human feedback data are publicly available on GitHub.

enablers.action: Replicate in other countries and languages
enablers.evidence: No trial outside the UK has been reported in the paper.

ref.title: AI can help humans find common ground in democratic deliberation (Science, 2024)
ref.finding: AI-mediated deliberation tested with UK participants on Brexit, immigration and other issues.

precedents.parallel: A randomly selected citizen body produced a consensus recommendation on a divisive issue that elected politicians had avoided, the role AI mediators aim to support.
precedents.outcome: 99 randomly chosen citizens met over five weekends, a parliamentary committee then recommended a referendum, and repeal passed 66.4 to 33.6 percent in May 2018; this used human facilitation, expert testimony and months of time, and nobody can isolate the assembly's causal effect on the vote.

ref.title: Ireland: public debate concerning abortion and the repeal of the eighth amendment (Council of Europe)
ref.finding: 99 random citizens met five weekends between October 2016 and April 2017; their report led to a committee recommendation and a referendum that passed 66.4 percent to 33.6 percent.

nodes.label: Grief bots and digital resurrection
nodes.summary: Chatbots built from a dead person's digital traces are already sold commercially[2]. Cambridge researchers warn of prolonged grief, ads delivered in a loved one's voice, and harm to children, drawing on three design scenarios, so evidence of harm is so far scenario-based[1][2].

refs.title: Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence (Hollanek and Nowaczyk-Basinska), Deathbots, griefbots and the digital afterlife, 2024
refs.finding: Cambridge researchers lay out 3 design scenarios showing psychological and commercial harms from deadbots, and call for opt-outs and age restrictions.

refs.title: University of Cambridge, Call for safeguards to prevent unwanted 'hauntings' by AI chatbots of dead loved ones, 2024
refs.finding: Some companies already offer deadbot services; researchers warn of psychological harm and overwhelming emotional weight, advertising in the manner of a departed loved one, and distress to children.

nodes.control_note: The same companion chatbots that ease loneliness can imitate a dead person from their messages, and a ban is not seen as feasible. Design rules on consent and endings can reduce the harm.

actions.action: Require consent from the person before death
actions.evidence: Recommended by ethicists from scenario analysis; untested, and the authors think a ban on non-consensual bots is not feasible.

ref.title: University of Cambridge, Call for safeguards to prevent unwanted hauntings by AI chatbots of dead loved ones, 2024
ref.finding: Hollanek and Nowaczyk-Basinska (Philosophy and Technology) urge consent, age limits, no advertising use and clear AI disclosure.

actions.action: Offer opt-out and a dignified retirement of the bot
actions.evidence: Proposed to give users emotional closure; no outcome data.

ref.title: University of Cambridge, Call for safeguards to prevent unwanted hauntings by AI chatbots of dead loved ones, 2024
ref.finding: Recommends ways to end the relationship, such as a digital funeral, and protecting the people who interact with the bot.

precedents.event: Seance boom after the First World War
precedents.parallel: Mass bereavement created a market for contact with the dead through mediums, the same need grief bots now sell to.
precedents.outcome: Demand for mediums surged after nearly 9 million soldiers died, Oliver Lodge's book about contacting his dead son spawned dozens of copycats, and fraud was common; the historian argues it also comforted families, so harm and solace coexisted.

ref.title: Article by historian Alice Vernon on the post-WWI seance boom (Aberystwyth University news, from The Conversation, 2025)
ref.finding: After the war spiritualism was reinvigorated as bereaved families sought contact with dead sons and husbands; critics saw mediums exploiting grief and fraud was common.

precedents.parallel: Even a trivially simple chatbot drew people into private emotional conversations, the attachment that grief bots build on.
precedents.outcome: Weizenbaum's secretary asked him to leave the room so she could talk to ELIZA alone, and he spent the rest of his career warning about it; ELIZA impersonated a therapist, not a dead relative.

ref.title: Why Joseph Weizenbaum Invented the Eliza Chatbot (Smithsonian Magazine)
ref.finding: When Weizenbaum's secretary first tested ELIZA she asked him to leave the room so she could continue privately; projecting human qualities onto a machine became known as the Eliza effect.

nodes.label: AI-generated kill lists compress targeting decisions
nodes.summary: AI decision support can produce strike targets faster than people can meaningfully review them. Six anonymous Israeli intelligence sources said one system flagged up to 37,000 Palestinians as suspected militants, with officers spending about 20 seconds per target[1]; the IDF denies much of this[1].

refs.title: +972 Magazine (Yuval Abraham), 'Lavender': The AI machine directing Israel's bombing spree in Gaza, 2024
refs.finding: Intelligence sources said the system flagged up to 37,000 Palestinians as suspected militants, and officers spent about 20 seconds reviewing each target.

nodes.control_note: States are adopting AI for intelligence and targeting and no binding ban exists, so only limits and real human review can reduce errors. Agreement is slow and the main users abstain or stay outside.

actions.action: Negotiate binding limits on autonomous weapons
actions.evidence: A 2024 UN First Committee resolution passed 161 to 3, but it only calls for consultations, not a treaty.

ref.title: Stop Killer Robots, 161 states vote against the machine at the UN General Assembly, 2024
ref.finding: Resolution L.77 was adopted 161 in favour, 3 against and 13 abstentions.

actions.action: Mandate human control and limits on target types
actions.evidence: The ICRC position sets out concrete limits; there is no evidence on how well human review works under time pressure.

ref.title: ICRC, ICRC position on autonomous weapon systems
ref.finding: Calls to ban unpredictable and anti-personnel systems and to require human oversight with timely intervention for the rest.

precedents.parallel: Patriot batteries ran a largely automatic engagement protocol with operators trained to trust the software, compressing human review as AI targeting is said to.
precedents.outcome: Patriot was involved in three fratricide incidents, two of them shootdowns of coalition aircraft that killed three aircrew, amid a 4,000-to-1 ratio of friendly sorties to enemy missiles; the review called for more operator involvement and control.

ref.title: Report of the Defense Science Board Task Force on Patriot System Performance, report summary (2005)
ref.finding: The operating protocol was largely automatic and operators were trained to trust the system's software; the solution is more operator involvement and control.

precedents.parallel: Crew on an Aegis cruiser acted on a fast, system-mediated threat picture and misread a civilian airliner as an attacking fighter.
precedents.outcome: All 290 people aboard were killed; the official investigation found the plane was squawking a civilian code yet judged the crew's actions appropriate, and the US paid Iran $131.8 million in 1996 without accepting liability.

ref.title: USS Vincennes Shoots Down Iran Air Flight 655 (Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training)
ref.finding: Operators believed the airliner was an F-14 preparing to attack; 290 died; the Fogarty report found it was squawking the civilian channel; a 1996 settlement paid $131.8 million.

nodes.label: AI revitalises endangered languages
nodes.summary: Communities are building speech models for Indigenous languages while keeping data sovereignty; in New Zealand, Te Hiku Media reports 92% accuracy for its te reo Maori speech recognition, and 82% on mixed English and Maori speech[1]. These figures are self-reported, not independently evaluated.

refs.title: NVIDIA Blog, Maori speech AI model helps preserve and promote New Zealand Indigenous language, 2023
refs.finding: Te Hiku Media's te reo Maori speech recognition reaches 92% accuracy, and 82% on mixed English and Maori speech.

limiters.evidence: Large speech models trained on 680,000 hours of mostly high-resource audio say little about tiny Indigenous corpora.

ref.title: Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision
ref.finding: Whisper trained on 680,000 hours of multilingual supervision.

limiters.evidence: Te Hiku built its own licence because communities fear outside firms taking their recordings.

ref.title: Data Sovereignty and the Kaitiakitanga License
ref.finding: All tehiku.nz content is under a stewardship licence tied to Maori data sovereignty principles.

limiters.evidence: About 2.6 billion people, 32% of the world, were offline in 2024, many in remote language communities.

ref.title: Global Internet use continues to rise but disparities remain, especially in low-income regions
ref.finding: 2.6 billion people offline in 2024.

enablers.action: License community data under Indigenous stewardship terms
enablers.evidence: Te Hiku applies the Kaitiakitanga licence to its content and prioritises Indigenous requesters.

ref.title: Data Sovereignty and the Kaitiakitanga License
ref.finding: Licensing prioritised for Indigenous groups revitalising their language.

enablers.action: Crowdsource open speech data in minority languages
enablers.evidence: Common Voice collects volunteer recordings per language for open reuse; no independent accuracy evaluation for small languages is cited here.

ref.title: Common Voice
ref.finding: Open platform for contributing voice data by language.

precedents.parallel: Archive recordings made with new technology were later restored and returned to the community for language revival, the same pipeline speech models now extend.
precedents.outcome: Fewkes's 31 surviving cylinders, the oldest known ethnographic field recordings, have been digitised since 2015 and worked through with the Passamaquoddy, with the tribe deciding what is released; the source gives no measure of speakers gained.

ref.title: Language is Life and Native American Historical Voices (Library of Congress blog)
ref.finding: The Library worked with the Passamaquoddy to recover language from the 1890 cylinders; communities decide what is released; projections suggest only 20 Native North American languages may be spoken by 2050, versus more than 300 in 1492.

nodes.label: AI classifiers find unseen child abuse material
nodes.summary: Thorn reports its Safer tools detected 4.16 million suspected abuse files in 2024, 2.24 million of them flagged by classifiers rather than matched to known hashes[1]. This could help investigators find victims sooner; the counts are vendor-reported with no published precision.

refs.title: Thorn, 2024 Impact Report, 2025
refs.finding: Thorn's Safer tools detected 4.16 million suspected CSAM files in 2024, 2.24 million of them flagged by classifiers rather than matched to known hashes.

limiters.evidence: Vendors describe novel CSAM classifiers but publish no figures on files classified or error rates.

ref.title: CSAM Detection from Experts in Child Safety Technology | Safer by Thorn
ref.finding: Offers predictive classifiers for novel CSAM; page gives no accuracy figures.

limiters.evidence: NCMEC received 21.3 million CyberTipline reports in 2025, more than police can triage.

ref.title: CyberTipline Data
ref.finding: 21.3 million reports in 2025.

limiters.evidence: EU data protection authorities issued a formal joint opinion challenging the proposed detection regulation.

ref.title: EDPB-EDPS Joint Opinion 04/2022 on the Proposal for a Regulation to prevent and combat child sexual abuse
ref.finding: Joint opinion of 28 July 2022 on the CSA proposal.

enablers.action: Fund hotlines that confirm and triage reports
enablers.evidence: IWF assessed 424,047 reports in 2024 and confirmed 291,273 contained abuse imagery.

ref.title: IWF Annual Data & Insights Report 2024
ref.finding: 291,273 confirmed reports in 2024.

enablers.action: Offer self-hosted detection that shares minimal data
enablers.evidence: Safer offers self-hosted deployment that limits data shared with the vendor.

ref.title: CSAM Detection from Experts in Child Safety Technology | Safer by Thorn
ref.finding: Self-hosted option shares limited data.

precedents.parallel: Microsoft and NCMEC deployed automated matching to find abuse images at platform scale, the step before classifiers that flag unseen images.
precedents.outcome: PhotoDNA matched resized or altered copies of already-known images and was shared with platforms; NCMEC had reviewed almost 30 million images and videos since 2003, but the vendor release gives no accuracy figures and the method cannot find new material.

ref.title: Microsoft and National Center for Missing & Exploited Children Push for Action to Fight Child Pornography (Microsoft press release)
ref.finding: PhotoDNA creates a signature for an image that still matches when resized; NCMEC had reviewed almost 30 million images and videos since 2003 and was reviewing about 250,000 a week.

nodes.label: AI flood warnings for data-poor regions
nodes.summary: In one Nature study, an AI model extended reliable river flood forecasts to 5 days ahead in ungauged basins, matching or beating the leading global physics-based system[1]. Google says the forecasts cover 80 countries where 460 million people live[2]; whether warnings change behaviour is less proven.

refs.title: Nearing et al., Global prediction of extreme floods in ungauged watersheds (Nature), 2024
refs.finding: An AI model extended reliable riverine flood forecasts to 5 days lead time in ungauged basins, matching or beating the leading global physics-based system.

refs.title: Google, How Google uses AI to improve global flood forecasting, 2024
refs.finding: Google says the forecasts cover 80 countries where 460 million people live.

limiters.evidence: 2.6 billion people were offline in 2024, so online flood maps miss many people at risk.

ref.title: Global Internet use continues to rise but disparities remain, especially in low-income regions
ref.finding: 32% of the world offline in 2024.

limiters.evidence: Only half of countries report adequate multi-hazard early warning systems to act on forecasts.

ref.title: Early Warnings for All
ref.finding: Only half of countries report adequate multi-hazard early warning systems.

limiters.limit: Forecast skill drops past five days
limiters.evidence: The AI model matched benchmark nowcast reliability up to five days lead time in ungauged basins, not beyond.

ref.title: Global prediction of extreme floods in ungauged watersheds
ref.finding: Reliability similar to or better than same-day benchmark up to 5-day lead time.

enablers.action: Link forecasts to national warning and response systems
enablers.evidence: The UN Early Warnings for All push targets full early warning coverage, starting from half of countries.

ref.title: Early Warnings for All
ref.finding: UN initiative to close early warning gaps.

enablers.action: Publish free forecasts for ungauged basins
enablers.evidence: Flood Hub publishes free public river flood forecasts, labelled approximate and informational.

ref.title: Flood Hub
ref.finding: Public flood forecast map with informational disclaimer.

precedents.parallel: An early-warning system built for a poor, exposed coastline paired forecasts with volunteers and shelters so that warnings actually reached people.
precedents.outcome: After the 1970 Bhola cyclone, which may have killed up to a million people, deaths fell to 138,000 in 1991, 10,000 or more in Sidr in 2007, and under 30 each in Bulbul (2019) and Amphan (2020), with 76,000 volunteers and 5,500 shelters; better forecasts were only one part of this.

ref.title: Congratulatory message on 50 years of the Cyclone Preparedness Programme (UNDRR)
ref.finding: Bhola may have killed up to one million; 138,000 died in 1991 and 10,000 or more in Sidr 2007; Bulbul and Amphan each caused fewer than 30 deaths; the programme has over 76,000 volunteers.

precedents.parallel: Famine early-warning systems flagged the crisis in time, but warnings did not turn into action, the gap the AI flood summary flags.
precedents.outcome: Warnings clearly identified famine risk in South Central Somalia, yet timely action was not taken and about 258,000 people died; war and access restrictions, not forecast quality, were the main barriers.

ref.title: The 2011 Famine in Somalia: lessons learnt from a failed response? (Conflict and Health 2013)
ref.finding: Famine early warning systems clearly identified the risk of famine in 2010-2011 but timely action was not taken; the famine is thought to have cost 258,000 lives.

nodes.label: Faces scraped into police search engines
nodes.summary: Firms scrape public photos into face-search databases offered to police. The Dutch regulator fined Clearview AI 30.5 million euros for an illegal database of over 30 billion scraped facial images, after earlier fines by other European regulators[1].

refs.title: Hunton Andrews Kurth, Dutch regulator fines Clearview AI 30.5 million euros, 2024
refs.finding: The Dutch DPA fined Clearview 30.5 million euros for building an illegal biometric database of over 30 billion scraped facial images.

nodes.control_note: Scraping faces into a search engine is not needed for any listed benefit, and law can ban it. Enforcement against firms based abroad is the weak point.

actions.action: Ban untargeted scraping of facial images
actions.evidence: The EU ban is in force; its effect on firms outside the EU is untested.

ref.title: EU AI Act, Article 5: Prohibited AI practices
ref.finding: Prohibits AI systems that build facial recognition databases through untargeted scraping from the internet or CCTV.

actions.action: Enforce biometric privacy law through lawsuits
actions.evidence: Under Illinois BIPA, a 2022 consent order barred Clearview from selling to most private firms nationwide; police sales outside Illinois continue.

ref.title: ACLU, ACLU v. Clearview AI
ref.finding: Clearview is permanently barred from selling its faceprint database to most private entities and banned from Illinois sales for five years.

actions.action: Restrict police real-time biometric identification
actions.evidence: EU law allows it only for listed serious cases with prior authorisation; no data on use since.

ref.title: EU AI Act, Article 5: Prohibited AI practices
ref.finding: Real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces is banned for police except narrow cases with judicial or independent authorisation.

precedents.event: FTC fines Facebook over user data
precedents.parallel: Facebook let third-party apps harvest users' and friends' data without real consent, a mass collection of personal data that regulators then punished.
precedents.outcome: The FTC imposed a $5 billion penalty, nearly 20 times the previous largest privacy penalty worldwide; unlike non-EU face-search firms, Facebook had assets inside the regulator's reach, which is what made the fine collectable.

ref.title: FTC Imposes $5 Billion Penalty and Sweeping New Privacy Restrictions on Facebook (Federal Trade Commission)
ref.finding: The $5 billion penalty, for violating a 2012 order including sharing friends' data with third-party apps, is the largest ever imposed for violating consumers' privacy.

nodes.label: AI-drafted police reports
nodes.summary: Police are trialling tools that turn body-camera audio into draft reports. In one randomized trial, Axon Draft One did not significantly cut report-writing time[1]; Anchorage police dropped such a tool after 90 days because review time cancelled out the drafting savings[2].

refs.title: Adams et al., No man's hand: artificial intelligence does not improve police report writing speed (Journal of Experimental Criminology), 2024
refs.finding: In a randomized trial, Axon Draft One produced no significant reduction in officers' report-writing time.

refs.title: Alaska Public Media, Anchorage police not moving forward with using AI to write reports, for now, 2024
refs.finding: After a 90-day trial, Anchorage police dropped the tool because review time cancelled out the drafting savings.

nodes.control_note: Agencies can choose not to use AI drafting, or require disclosure, review and kept drafts, while keeping the time savings. The harm is tied to the same drafting tools that save clerical time.

actions.action: Label AI-drafted reports and require officer certification
actions.evidence: Utah enacted this in 2025; no published data yet on whether it reduces errors in reports.

ref.title: Utah S.B. 180 (2025), Law Enforcement Usage of Artificial Intelligence, enrolled text
ref.finding: Reports made wholly or partly with generative AI must carry a disclaimer and the author's certification that they reviewed it for accuracy.

actions.action: Keep the first AI draft and an audit trail
actions.evidence: California's law took effect in 2026, so defence lawyers can compare drafts with final reports; its effect is not yet measured.

ref.title: California SB 524 (2025), Law enforcement agencies: artificial intelligence, Chapter 587
ref.finding: Agencies must disclose AI use in official reports and retain the AI-created draft.

precedents.event: Electronic health records and documentation time
precedents.parallel: EHRs were adopted partly to make documentation more efficient, as AI report-writing tools are now, yet paperwork did not shrink.
precedents.outcome: Observed physicians spent 27 percent of the office day with patients and 49.2 percent on EHR and desk work, nearly two hours of screen work per hour of face time plus 1 to 2 hours each night; the study sampled 57 doctors in self-selected practices.

ref.title: Allocation of Physician Time in Ambulatory Practice: A Time and Motion Study in 4 Specialties (Sinsky et al., Annals of Internal Medicine 2016)
ref.finding: For every hour of direct clinical face time, physicians spent nearly 2 additional hours on EHR and desk work in the clinic day, plus 1 to 2 hours after hours.

precedents.parallel: Police relied on a machine whose output carried an air of objectivity in investigations, the worry defence lawyers raise about AI wording in reports.
precedents.outcome: The National Academies found polygraph accuracy too low to justify federal screening: in 10,000 employees with 10 spies, a setting that catches 8 would wrongly fail about 1,600 people; the polygraph measures physiology, whereas AI drafts shape narrative wording.

ref.title: The Polygraph and Lie Detection (National Academies, statement by committee chair Stephen Fienberg)
ref.finding: Polygraph accuracy is insufficient to justify reliance on it for employee screening, and overconfidence in its accuracy can create a false sense of security.

nodes.label: Algorithms screen child-neglect reports
nodes.summary: In Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, a risk score helps decide which neglect calls get investigated. From 2016 to 2018 it flagged 32.5% of Black children reported for neglect for mandatory investigation, against 20.8% of white children; one study found caseworkers reduced the gap[1].

refs.title: AP via KTVZ, An algorithm that screens for child neglect raises concerns, 2022
refs.finding: From 2016 to 2018, the Allegheny tool flagged 32% of Black children reported for neglect for mandatory investigation, against 20.8% of white children.

nodes.control_note: Agencies will keep screening large volumes of reports with some decision aid, so errors and bias will occur to some degree. Evaluation and legal duties can reduce how often and how badly families are wrongly targeted.

actions.action: Commission independent impact evaluations before scaling
actions.evidence: A Stanford quasi-experimental evaluation of about 31,000 pre and 34,000 post children found more children in need were screened in without a rise in investigations; it was not a randomised trial and the agency paid for it.

ref.title: Allegheny County DHS, Impact Evaluation Summary of the Allegheny Family Screening Tool, April 2019
ref.finding: The tool did not increase the screen-in rate and increased identification of children needing intervention.

actions.action: Require bias audits for public-benefit decision tools
actions.evidence: The EU AI Act lists systems that assess eligibility for public assistance as high-risk, with risk management and data rules phasing in from 2026; whether child-welfare screening falls under it depends on use, and no effect data exist yet.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), Annex III
ref.finding: Annex III classes AI used by public authorities to evaluate eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services as high-risk.

precedents.parallel: A statistical risk score used to guide decisions about people produced unequal error rates by race, as child-neglect screening tools have.
precedents.outcome: In Broward County, Florida, 44.9 percent of Black defendants who did not reoffend had been labelled higher risk, against 23.5 percent of white defendants; this is journalistic analysis of over 7,000 people in criminal justice, not child welfare.

ref.title: Machine Bias (ProPublica)
ref.finding: Among defendants who did not reoffend, 44.9 percent of Black and 23.5 percent of white defendants were labelled higher risk; only 20 percent predicted to commit violent crimes did so.

nodes.label: Algorithmic price collusion
nodes.summary: In one simulation study, simple pricing algorithms learned to keep prices high and punish price cuts without communicating[1]. The US Justice Department has sued RealPage, alleging landlords used its software to coordinate rents across millions of units[2]. How widespread this is in real markets is still disputed.

refs.title: Calvano et al., Artificial Intelligence, Algorithmic Pricing, and Collusion, AER 2020
refs.finding: In simulated markets, simple Q-learning pricing agents consistently learned to charge supracompetitive prices and punished price cuts, all without communicating.

refs.title: US DOJ, Justice Department sues RealPage for algorithmic pricing scheme that harms millions of American renters, 2024
refs.finding: DOJ alleged that landlords pooled nonpublic rent data in RealPage software to coordinate rents across millions of US units.

nodes.control_note: Pricing software can work from a firm's own data without pooling rivals' private data, so antitrust law can block the harmful version while keeping the tool.

actions.action: Bar pricing software from pooling rivals' private data
actions.evidence: The proposed RealPage settlement bans live nonpublic competitor data and requires a monitor; it awaits court approval and its effect on rents is unmeasured.

ref.title: US Department of Justice, Justice Department Requires RealPage to End the Sharing of Competitively Sensitive Information
ref.finding: RealPage must stop using competitors' nonpublic data in live pricing, train only on data at least 12 months old, and accept a monitor.

actions.action: Make shared pricing algorithms an antitrust violation
actions.evidence: California's law took effect in 2026; it still needs a conspiracy or coercion, so its added reach may be limited.

ref.title: California AB 325 (2025), Cartwright Act: violations, Chapter 338
ref.finding: Makes it unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of an anticompetitive contract, combination or conspiracy.

precedents.parallel: Airlines used a shared computerised fare system to signal and coordinate price rises without meeting, the template for shared rent-setting software.
precedents.outcome: The Justice Department found over 50 price-fixing agreements across hundreds of routes, estimated consumer harm at up to $1.9 billion, and in 1994 a consent decree stripped out the signalling features; the signalling was done by people, not learning algorithms.

ref.title: Justice Department press release on the 1994 airline fare settlement (DOJ Antitrust Division)
ref.finding: Six airlines used ATP's system to float trial fare increases and agree on fares; a government economist estimated harm of $238 million to $1.9 billion from 1988 to 1992.

precedents.event: Algorithmic pricing in German petrol stations
precedents.parallel: Petrol stations adopted pricing software in a concentrated local market, a real-world test of whether algorithms soften competition.
precedents.outcome: Adoption raised margins only in non-monopoly markets, by about 9 percent, and in duopolies by 28 percent when both stations adopted; the study infers adoption from price patterns rather than observing it.

ref.title: Algorithmic Pricing and Competition: Empirical Evidence from the German Retail Gasoline Market (Assad, Clark, Ershov and Xu, CESifo working paper)
ref.finding: Algorithmic pricing adoption raised margins in non-monopoly markets; in duopolies margins rose 28 percent where both stations adopted.

nodes.label: AI hiring discrimination
nodes.summary: Audit studies show language models ranking otherwise identical CVs differently by name or disability: embedding models favoured white-associated names in 85% of tests[1], GPT-3.5 ranked Black-associated names last more often for several jobs[2], and GPT-4 ranked disability-enhanced CVs first in 15 of 60 trials[3].

refs.title: Wilson & Caliskan, Gender, Race, and Intersectional Bias in Resume Screening via Language Model Retrieval, 2024
refs.finding: Across about 3 million resume/job comparisons, embedding models favoured white-associated names in 85% of tests and Black-associated names in only 9%.

refs.title: Bloomberg, OpenAI GPT Sorts Resume Names With Racial Bias, Test Shows, 2024
refs.finding: Given equally qualified resumes, GPT-3.5 ranked names associated with Black Americans last more often than other groups for several job types.

refs.title: UW News, ChatGPT is biased against resumes with credentials that imply a disability, 2024
refs.finding: GPT-4 ranked the disability-enhanced CVs first in only 15 of 60 trials against an otherwise identical control CV.

nodes.control_note: Screening tools learn from past hiring data, so some bias will persist even with audits. Audits and explanation rights can lower its frequency and give rejected candidates a way to challenge it.

actions.action: Require annual public bias audits of hiring tools
actions.evidence: Evidence of effect is weak: of 391 NYC employers checked, only 18 posted audit reports and 13 posted notices.

ref.title: Wright et al., Null Compliance: NYC Local Law 144 and the Challenges of Algorithm Accountability, arXiv 2024
ref.finding: Only 18 of 391 employers posted bias audits under Local Law 144.

actions.action: Classify hiring AI as high-risk with oversight duties
actions.evidence: High-risk obligations in the EU apply from 2026 and later; no outcome data yet.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), Annex III point 4(a)
ref.finding: AI systems intended for recruitment or selection of natural persons are high-risk.

actions.action: Give rejected people a right to an explanation
actions.evidence: Lets affected people contest decisions; how often it is used and whether it changes outcomes is unknown.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), Article 86
ref.finding: Article 86 grants a right to explanation of individual decisions made with high-risk AI systems.

precedents.event: Emily and Greg CV audit study
precedents.parallel: Researchers sent identical CVs with names signalling race to real employers, the same audit design now used on language-model screeners.
precedents.outcome: White-sounding names got 50 percent more callbacks than African American-sounding names, and better CVs helped white names far more; unlike the LLM audits, this measured real employer responses.

ref.title: Are Emily and Greg More Employable than Lakisha and Jamal? A Field Experiment on Labor Market Discrimination (Bertrand and Mullainathan, NBER w9873)
ref.finding: White names receive 50 percent more callbacks for interviews; discrimination was uniform across occupations and industries, including federal contractors.

nodes.label: AI credit scoring widens financial inclusion
nodes.summary: Models built on alternative data such as digital footprints can score people who have no credit file; in one study, ten simple digital-footprint variables predicted default about as well as a credit bureau score[1]. This may help the unbanked but could raise privacy and fairness concerns.

refs.title: Berg, Burg, Gombovic & Puri, On the Rise of FinTechs: Credit Scoring using Digital Footprints, NBER 2018 (RFS 2020)
refs.finding: Ten simple digital-footprint variables predicted default about as well as a credit bureau score, and they also work for people without a credit history.

limiters.evidence: About 21% of adults still have no account, so many lack the digital footprint these models need.

ref.title: The Global Findex Database 2025
ref.finding: 79% of adults globally have an account.

limiters.evidence: US regulator says lenders using black-box models still must give specific denial reasons.

ref.title: CFPB Issues Guidance on Credit Denials by Lenders Using Artificial Intelligence
ref.finding: There is no special exemption for artificial intelligence.

limiters.evidence: The EU AI Act lists credit scoring of natural persons as high-risk, adding obligations.

ref.title: Annex III: High-Risk AI Systems Referred to in Article 6(2)
ref.finding: Point 5(b) covers creditworthiness evaluation and credit scores.

enablers.action: Combine digital footprints with bureau data
enablers.evidence: Digital footprint data predicted default about as well as bureau scores and complemented them in a German retailer study.

ref.title: On the Rise of FinTechs: Credit Scoring Using Digital Footprints
ref.finding: Footprints match bureau scores and widen access while lowering defaults.

enablers.action: Require specific reasons for AI credit denials
enablers.evidence: Guidance bars lenders from relying on vague checkbox reasons when AI drives decisions.

ref.title: CFPB Issues Guidance on Credit Denials by Lenders Using Artificial Intelligence
ref.finding: Lenders must give accurate, specific adverse action reasons.

precedents.parallel: Fast, cheap statistical scoring of borrowers was expected to widen access to credit, as alternative-data AI scoring is now.
precedents.outcome: The Federal Reserve concluded scoring likely contributed to greater availability and affordability of credit and predicted default across demographic groups, though average scores were lower for Black and Hispanic borrowers; it could not isolate scoring's effect precisely.

ref.title: Report to the Congress on Credit Scoring and Its Effects on the Availability and Affordability of Credit, executive summary (Federal Reserve Board, 2007)
ref.finding: Credit scoring likely contributed to increased availability and affordability of credit; scores predict default risk for all major demographic groups.

precedents.parallel: A loan product delivered fully on mobile phones reached Kenyan households outside formal lending, an earlier version of the fintech inclusion story.
precedents.outcome: 34 percent of eligible people took the loans, which did not crowd out other credit, and borrowing households were 6.3 percentage points less likely to forgo expenses after shocks; the authors call digital loans not a panacea.

ref.title: Fintech and Household Resilience to Shocks: Evidence from Digital Loans in Kenya (Bharadwaj, Jack and Suri, NBER w25604)
ref.finding: Take-up was 34 percent; households were 6.3 percentage points less likely to forgo expenses due to negative shocks.

nodes.label: Opaque credit models entrench exclusion
nodes.summary: Alternative-data credit scoring could use proxies for race or poverty and deny credit with no explanation applicants can contest. The concern comes from an analogous US tax-audit model that selected Black taxpayers at 2.9 to 4.7 times the rate of non-Black taxpayers[1]; direct measurement in credit is scarce.

refs.title: Elzayn et al., Measuring and Mitigating Racial Disparities in Tax Audits, SIEPR 2023
refs.finding: An analogous government risk model selected Black taxpayers for audit at 2.9 to 4.7 times the rate of non-Black taxpayers.

nodes.control_note: Lenders will keep using complex models, so some unfair exclusion will occur. Explanation duties and high-risk rules reduce how often it happens and let applicants correct errors.

actions.action: Require specific reasons for algorithmic credit denials
actions.evidence: Applies existing US adverse action rules to black-box models; no study measures its effect on exclusion.

ref.title: CFPB Circular 2022-03, Adverse action notification requirements in connection with credit decisions based on complex algorithms
ref.finding: Creditors must give specific principal reasons for denials even when using complex algorithms.

actions.action: Treat credit scoring AI as high-risk
actions.evidence: EU high-risk duties on data quality and oversight phase in from 2026; untested so far.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), Annex III point 5(b)
ref.finding: AI used to evaluate creditworthiness or establish credit scores of natural persons is high-risk.

precedents.parallel: Government risk maps graded neighbourhoods partly by race, so a lending tool used geography as a proxy that cut off credit, the risk with opaque alternative-data models.
precedents.outcome: The maps led to lower home ownership, house values and rents and more segregation in graded areas for decades, through reduced credit access and disinvestment; the maps were explicit about race, while AI proxies are usually hidden.

ref.title: The Effects of the 1930s HOLC Redlining Maps (Aaronson, Hartley and Mazumder, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago WP 2017-12)
ref.finding: The maps led to reduced home ownership rates, house values and rents and increased racial segregation in later decades through reduced credit access and disinvestment.

precedents.event: Fed review of credit score proxies
precedents.parallel: Regulators tested whether conventional credit scores acted as proxies for race, the same question asked of alternative-data models.
precedents.outcome: Black and Hispanic borrowers had lower average scores, but rebuilding the model race-neutrally barely changed scores, while length of credit history partly proxied for age and hurt young people and recent immigrants; this cuts against assuming proxies are always present.

ref.title: Report to the Congress on Credit Scoring and Its Effects on the Availability and Affordability of Credit, executive summary (Federal Reserve Board, 2007)
ref.finding: Credit characteristics did not substantially proxy for race, ethnicity or sex, but length of credit history partly proxied for age.

nodes.label: Low-paid data labelling in the Global South
nodes.summary: Frontier models depend on outsourced annotators in poorer countries; one TIME investigation found Kenyan contractors labelling violent and sexual content for OpenAI took home roughly $1.32 to $2 per hour[1]. The work is low-paid and sometimes traumatic, but it is also a source of jobs.

refs.title: TIME (Perrigo), OpenAI Used Kenyan Workers on Less Than $2 Per Hour to Make ChatGPT Less Toxic, 2023
refs.finding: Kenyan Sama contractors labelling violent and sexual content for OpenAI took home roughly $1.32 to $2 per hour.

nodes.control_note: Labelling and feedback work is part of how current models are trained, so the work will exist. Pay, safety and status rules can reduce the harm but not remove the work.

actions.action: Require human review of algorithmic worker management
actions.evidence: The EU Platform Work Directive sets a presumption of employment and human oversight of automated decisions, but it only covers platform work in the EU and its effect is not yet measured.

ref.title: Directive (EU) 2024/2831 on improving working conditions in platform work
ref.finding: Article 5 creates a legal presumption of employment and Article 10 requires human oversight of automated monitoring and decision systems.

actions.action: Ratify ILO platform work convention
actions.evidence: Convention No. 193 was adopted in June 2026 and covers online platform work, including pay and review of automated decisions, but it binds no state until ratified.

ref.title: ILO, How will the new Convention No.193 promote decent work in the platform economy?
ref.finding: The convention covers location-based and online platform work and sets principles for transparent use of automated decision systems.

precedents.parallel: Crowdworkers on Mechanical Turk did the microtasks, including data labelling, that earlier machine learning depended on.
precedents.outcome: Logs from 2,676 workers across 3.8 million tasks showed median earnings of about $2 an hour, with only 4 percent above $7.25; the sample was mostly US-based workers using a browser plugin.

ref.title: A Data-Driven Analysis of Workers' Earnings on Amazon Mechanical Turk (Hara et al., CHI 2018)
ref.finding: Median hourly wage was about $2; only 4 percent earned more than $7.25 per hour.

precedents.parallel: Outsourced content moderators reviewed graphic material for a platform at scale, the same traumatic work some AI data labellers do.
precedents.outcome: Facebook agreed to pay $52 million to more than 11,000 current and former moderators, at least $1,000 each and up to $50,000, without admitting wrongdoing; these were US contractor workers, so it says little about pay and redress in poorer countries.

ref.title: TechCrunch report on Facebook's $52 million content moderator settlement (May 2020)
ref.finding: $52 million settlement covering more than 11,000 moderators in four US states; each gets at least $1,000 and up to $50,000.

nodes.label: Developing countries left behind by AI
nodes.summary: About 60% of jobs in advanced economies are exposed to AI, against 40% in emerging markets and 26% in low-income countries, so poorer countries face less disruption now[1]. Many lack the infrastructure and skills to capture the gains, which could widen the gap between countries[1].

refs.title: IMF (Georgieva), AI Will Transform the Global Economy. Let's Make Sure It Benefits Humanity, 2024
refs.finding: About 60% of jobs in advanced economies are exposed to AI, against 40% in emerging markets and 26% in low-income countries.

nodes.control_note: Compute, talent and capital are concentrated in a few countries, and that will not change quickly. Shared infrastructure and capacity building can narrow the gap.

actions.action: Fund shared AI compute for developing countries
actions.evidence: UNCTAD reports that 100 firms account for 40% of global corporate R&D and that 118 countries are absent from major AI governance talks; the shared facility is a proposal with no track record.

ref.title: UNCTAD, AI's $4.8 trillion future: UN Trade and Development alerts on divides, urges action (Technology and Innovation Report 2025)
