ref.finding: UNCTAD proposes a global shared facility for equitable access to AI infrastructure, plus open data and open source models.

actions.action: Run AI capacity-building programmes
actions.evidence: The UN General Assembly adopted a resolution on AI capacity building in July 2024 without a vote; it is non-binding and its effect has not been measured.

ref.title: UN General Assembly resolution A/RES/78/311, Enhancing international cooperation on capacity-building of artificial intelligence
ref.finding: Calls for international cooperation to build AI capacity in developing countries.

precedents.parallel: Poor countries adopted each new technology sooner over time but used it far less intensively, the pattern feared for AI.
precedents.outcome: Adoption lags converged between rich and poor countries while long-run penetration diverged, and the authors' model attributes 80 percent of the income divergence since 1820 to these diffusion patterns; mobile phones show leapfrogging is possible.

ref.title: If Technology Has Arrived Everywhere, Why has Income Diverged? (Comin and Mestieri, NBER w19010)
ref.finding: Adoption lags have converged while penetration rates have diverged; diffusion patterns account for 80 percent of the Great Income Divergence since 1820.

nodes.label: AI investment bubble and crash risk
nodes.summary: The Bank of England said equity valuations appear stretched, particularly for AI-focused technology companies, raising the risk of a sharp correction[1]; the IMF also warned of sharp corrections[2]. A correction could spill into the wider economy; this is a risk assessment, not a forecast.

refs.title: Bank of England, Financial Policy Committee Record, October 2025
refs.finding: The FPC said equity valuations appear stretched, particularly for AI-focused technology companies, raising the risk of a sharp market correction.

refs.title: IMF, Global Financial Stability Report, October 2025
refs.finding: The IMF found risk-asset prices well above fundamentals and warned of sharp corrections.

nodes.control_note: Heavy investment comes with expectations that may not be met, so some repricing is likely. Regulators can limit how far a crash spreads, not whether valuations fall.

actions.action: Monitor and warn on stretched AI valuations
actions.evidence: The Bank of England flagged stretched AI valuations in October 2025; AI equities then fell sharply in July 2026 with no spillover to core markets, so warnings did not prevent the fall.

ref.title: Bank of England, Financial Policy Committee Record, September 2026
ref.finding: Equity valuations for AI companies fell sharply in July, there were no spillovers to core markets, and the risk of a sharper correction persists.

actions.action: Stress test banks against an AI equity correction
actions.evidence: Bank staff modelled an AI-driven equity correction scenario; stress tests show resilience to past shock types, but no test can show resilience to an untested scenario.

ref.title: Bank of England, Financial Stability Report, July 2026
ref.finding: A reassessment of AI prospects could trigger a fall in equity prices, made worse by concentrated, leveraged positions.

precedents.parallel: Investors poured money into a transformative technology on revenue expectations that the numbers already contradicted, as some fear with AI capex.
precedents.outcome: Railway revenues were about 6 million pounds in 1845, investors implicitly expected about 60 million by 1850-52, and they reached only 15 million in 1852, one of the greatest crashes; yet almost all lines kept running and Britain probably gained overall.

ref.title: Collective hallucinations and inefficient markets: The British Railway Mania of the 1840s (Odlyzko, University of Minnesota)
ref.finding: Investors ignored trustworthy measures showing demand could not support expected revenues; shareholders lost heavily but almost all lines continued in service.

nodes.label: AI catches fraud against the public purse
nodes.summary: The US Treasury reported more than $4 billion in fraud prevented and recovered in fiscal year 2024, including about $1 billion in check fraud recovered with machine-learning AI[1]. The figures are self-reported.

refs.title: US Treasury, Enhanced Fraud Detection Processes, Including Machine Learning AI, Prevented and Recovered Over $4 Billion in Fiscal Year 2024
refs.finding: Treasury reported more than $4 billion in fraud prevented and recovered in FY2024, including about $1 billion in check fraud recovered with machine-learning AI.

limiters.evidence: GAO estimates federal fraud losses of $233 to $521 billion a year, against $1 billion recovered with machine learning at Treasury.

ref.title: Fraud Risk Management: 2018-2022 Data Show Federal Government Loses an Estimated $233 Billion to $521 Billion
ref.finding: $233-521 billion lost per year, FY2018-2022.

limiters.evidence: Treasury's $1 billion recovery figure is from its own press release, not an audit.

ref.title: Treasury Announces Enhanced Fraud Detection Processes, Including Machine Learning AI
ref.finding: Machine learning on check fraud resulted in $1 billion in recovery.

limiters.evidence: GAO's estimate covers all programs, implying uneven fraud controls across agencies.

ref.title: Fraud Risk Management: 2018-2022 Data Show Federal Government Loses an Estimated $233 Billion to $521 Billion
ref.finding: Losses equal 3 to 7 percent of average obligations.

enablers.action: Apply machine learning to payment screening
enablers.evidence: Treasury reported $1 billion recovered from check fraud using machine learning.

ref.title: Treasury Announces Enhanced Fraud Detection Processes, Including Machine Learning AI
ref.finding: $1 billion recovery attributed to machine learning.

enablers.action: Audit fraud estimates independently
enablers.evidence: GAO built a government-wide fraud estimate that gives a baseline for judging agency claims.

ref.title: Fraud Risk Management: 2018-2022 Data Show Federal Government Loses an Estimated $233 Billion to $521 Billion
ref.finding: Independent estimate of federal fraud losses.

precedents.parallel: The US Medicare programme ran predictive models over claims to stop improper payments, a pre-generative case of machine learning against fraud on the public purse.
precedents.outcome: The inspector general certified $133.2 million in savings in the third year, a return of $2.84 per dollar, against $454 million the agency itself identified, and found contractor guidance too weak to produce accurate savings estimates.

ref.title: The Fraud Prevention System Increased Recovery and Prevention of Improper Medicare Payments, but Updated Procedures Would Improve Reported Savings (HHS OIG, 2015)
ref.finding: OIG certified $133.2 million in actual and projected savings (ROI $2.84) and $454 million unadjusted; directives were not sufficient to ensure accurate savings estimates.

nodes.label: Automated welfare and tax enforcement harms citizens
nodes.summary: Australia's automated debt-raising unlawfully asserted debts against about 433,000 people[1], and the Dutch Tax Administration was fined for using nationality to flag childcare benefit claims as risky[2]. These scandals predate generative AI; agents could repeat them at greater scale.

refs.title: Prygodicz v Commonwealth of Australia (No 2) [2021] FCA 634, Federal Court of Australia
refs.finding: The Commonwealth unlawfully asserted debts of at least $1.763 billion against about 433,000 people, recovered about $751 million from about 381,000 of them, and settled for a further $112 million.

refs.title: Dutch Data Protection Authority, Tax Administration fined for discriminatory and unlawful data processing, 2021
refs.finding: The Tax Administration was fined 2.75 million euros for using applicants' nationality (Dutch or not) as an indicator in a system that flagged childcare benefit applications as risky.

nodes.control_note: Both scandals came from unlawful design choices: income averaging in Australia and nationality as a risk factor in the Netherlands. Legal limits, audits and human review can stop them while keeping automated processing.

actions.action: Classify public-benefit AI as high-risk
actions.evidence: The EU AI Act lists AI used to assess eligibility for public assistance benefits as high-risk, with risk management and human oversight duties; effects are not yet measured.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), Annex III
ref.finding: Annex III lists AI systems used by public authorities to evaluate eligibility for public assistance benefits as high-risk.

actions.action: Fine unlawful profiling by public agencies
actions.evidence: The Dutch DPA fined the Tax Administration 2.75 million euros; the agency had already stopped using nationality for risk in 2018, so the fine came after the harm.

ref.title: Dutch Data Protection Authority, Tax Administration fined for discriminatory and unlawful data processing, 2021
ref.finding: Using nationality data to assess applications, combat fraud and determine risk was found unlawful and discriminatory.

actions.action: Legislate a framework for automated government decisions
actions.evidence: The Royal Commission made 57 recommendations, including a chapter on automated decision making; adoption is partial and unmeasured.

ref.title: Report of the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme, 2023
ref.finding: The report sets out 57 recommendations, including on data matching and automated decision making.

precedents.parallel: An automated system issued unemployment fraud findings with no human review, the kind of enforcement agents could repeat at scale.
precedents.outcome: Computer-only fraud findings had a 93 percent error rate and more than 20,000 people were wrongly accused and hit with steep penalties; by late 2016 the state had refunded $5.4 million to 2,571 claimants.

ref.title: Michigan Public report on false MiDAS unemployment fraud penalties (January 2017)
ref.finding: The automated system's fraud findings had an error rate of 93 percent; more than 20,000 people were wrongly accused.

precedents.parallel: Faulty accounting software was treated as reliable evidence and used to pursue hundreds of subpostmasters, showing how institutions defend a system over the people it flags.
precedents.outcome: By September 2026, 620 people in England and Wales had at least one conviction quashed by the 2024 Act, covering 2,250 convictions; Horizon was bookkeeping software, not a risk model.

ref.title: Post Office (Horizon System) Offences Act 2024: quashed convictions management information, 24 September 2026 (GOV.UK)
ref.finding: 620 individuals identified as having at least one conviction quashed by the Act, and 2,250 convictions quashed, out of 1,011 assessed.

nodes.label: Algorithms improve bail decisions
nodes.summary: In one simulation on New York City data, an algorithmic release rule could cut crime by up to 24.7% with no change in jailing, or cut jail populations by up to 41.9% with no rise in crime[1]. No deployed system has shown this.

refs.title: Kleinberg et al., Human Decisions and Machine Predictions, NBER 2017 (QJE 2018)
refs.finding: Using NYC data, an algorithmic release rule could cut crime by up to 24.7% with no change in jailing, or cut jail populations by up to 41.9% with no rise in crime.

limiters.evidence: In Broward County, 44.9% of Black non-reoffenders were labelled higher risk versus 23.5% of white ones.

ref.title: Machine Bias
ref.finding: False positive rates differed sharply by race for COMPAS.

limiters.evidence: The 24.7% crime cut or 41.9% jail cut are simulated on historical New York data, not measured in deployment.

ref.title: Human Decisions and Machine Predictions
ref.finding: Simulated crime reductions up to 24.7% or jailing reductions up to 41.9%.

limiters.evidence: The EU AI Act lists reoffending risk assessment as high-risk, raising the bar for use.

ref.title: Annex III: High-Risk AI Systems Referred to in Article 6(2)
ref.finding: Point 6(d) covers assessing risk of offending or re-offending.

enablers.action: Impose conformity and oversight duties on risk tools
enablers.evidence: High-risk classification brings documentation and human oversight requirements.

ref.title: Annex III: High-Risk AI Systems Referred to in Article 6(2)
ref.finding: Reoffending risk assessment listed as high-risk.

enablers.action: Publish tools and validate them on local outcomes
enablers.evidence: COMPAS is proprietary and a 2013 review rated such tools moderate at best in predictive validity.

ref.title: Machine Bias
ref.finding: Only 20% of those predicted to commit violent crime did so.

precedents.parallel: New Jersey replaced money bail with decisions guided by the Public Safety Assessment, a statistical risk score, which is the closest real deployment of algorithm-guided release.
precedents.outcome: The pretrial jail population fell 43.9% from January 2015 to January 2018 with no reported rise in pretrial crime, but the reform also abolished most money bail, so the score's own share of the effect cannot be separated out.

ref.title: Study Finds New Jersey's Pretrial Reform Shows Early Signs of Wide-Reaching, Positive Impacts on Criminal Justice System (MDRC)
ref.finding: Pretrial jail population fell 43.9% from January 2015 to January 2018; courts report no uptick in pretrial crime; detention rates were lower than pre-reform trends predicted.

precedents.parallel: Kentucky's HB 463 required judges to use a risk score and presumed release for low and moderate risk defendants, the same promise of fewer jailed people at no cost to safety.
precedents.outcome: Release rose only trivially, failures to appear and pretrial crime rose with it, judges ignored the release default in more than two thirds of cases, and within a couple of years release rates fell below pre-law levels.

ref.title: Assessing Risk Assessment in Action (Megan Stevenson, Minnesota Law Review 103, 2018)
ref.finding: HB 463 led to only a trivial increase in pretrial release, matched by more FTA and pretrial crime; the change eroded as judges returned to earlier practice.

precedents.parallel: Decades of studies compared expert judgment with simple statistical formulas, the same comparison that bail simulations make between judges and models.
precedents.outcome: A meta-analysis found formulas about 10% more accurate on average, substantially better in 33% to 47% of studies and substantially worse in only 6% to 16%, though most studies were outside criminal justice.

ref.title: Clinical versus mechanical prediction: a meta-analysis (Grove, Zald, Lebow, Snitz and Nelson, Psychological Assessment 12(1), 2000)
ref.finding: Mechanical prediction was about 10% more accurate than clinical prediction on average, regardless of judgment task.

nodes.label: Biased risk scores in criminal justice
nodes.summary: One ProPublica analysis found the COMPAS risk tool falsely flagged Black defendants as future criminals at almost twice the rate of white defendants (45% vs 23%)[1]. Whether that counts as bias depends on the fairness metric, since common ones cannot all hold at once[2].

refs.title: ProPublica (Angwin et al.), Machine Bias, 2016
refs.finding: COMPAS falsely flagged Black defendants as future criminals at almost twice the rate of white defendants (45% vs 23%).

refs.title: Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan, Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores (2016)
refs.finding: Except in highly constrained special cases, no method can satisfy three common fairness conditions for risk scores at the same time.

nodes.control_note: Courts can sentence without risk scores, so the harm is not a by-product of a benefit. Bans on profiling-only prediction and audit duties limit it.

actions.action: Ban crime prediction based only on profiling
actions.evidence: The EU AI Act prohibits assessing a person's risk of offending based solely on profiling and makes judicial and re-offending risk tools high-risk; enforcement data is not yet available.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), Article 5 and Annex III
ref.finding: Annex III covers law enforcement AI that assesses the risk of offending or re-offending as high-risk.

actions.action: Benchmark risk tools against simple baselines
actions.evidence: Untrained people predicted recidivism about as well as COMPAS (67.0% vs 65.2% accuracy) and a two-feature model matched it, which weakens the case for opaque scores.

ref.title: Dressel and Farid, The accuracy, fairness, and limits of predicting recidivism, Science Advances 2018
ref.finding: COMPAS was no more accurate or fair than predictions by people with little or no criminal justice expertise.

precedents.parallel: A commercial recidivism score used in Florida courts is the direct pre-generative-AI case of unequal error rates by race.
precedents.outcome: ProPublica found 44.85% of Black defendants who did not reoffend were labelled higher risk versus 23.45% of white defendants, across 7,214 defendants.

ref.title: How We Analyzed the COMPAS Recidivism Algorithm (ProPublica, 2016)
ref.finding: False positive rate 44.85% for Black versus 23.45% for white non-reoffending defendants scored in 2013 and 2014.

precedents.parallel: A race-neutral sentencing formula produced racially concentrated harsher sentences, the way a facially neutral risk score can.
precedents.outcome: The US Sentencing Commission found the ratio was not appropriate and that about 85% of offenders under the heavier crack penalties in 2000 were Black; unlike a model, this was a fixed statutory rule, not learned from data.

ref.title: US Sentencing Commission press release on the 2002 Report to Congress on Federal Cocaine Sentencing Policy
ref.finding: The 100-to-1 drug quantity ratio is not appropriate; about 85 percent of offenders subject to heightened crack penalties in 2000 were black.

nodes.label: AI abundance funds income for everyone
nodes.summary: AI-driven wealth could grow large enough to pay every adult a living income, as Altman's proposed American Equity Fund would[1]. Growth models show sharp growth but a shrinking labor share[2]; the political will to redistribute is unproven.

refs.title: Moore's Law for Everything (Sam Altman, 2021)
refs.finding: Proposes an American Equity Fund paid by a yearly 2.5% tax on large company value and private land, distributed to every adult; the author calls it a conversation starter.

refs.title: Economic Growth under Transformative AI (Trammell and Korinek, NBER w31815)
refs.finding: Full automation would likely raise growth sharply and shrink labor's share of income; the effect on wages is ambiguous.

refs.title: Machines of Loving Grace (Dario Amodei, 2024)
refs.finding: Argues powerful AI could compress 50 to 100 years of progress into 5 to 10 years.

refs.title: AI 2027: slowdown ending
refs.finding: Growth accelerates by about 1.5 orders of magnitude; basic income promised in 2028.

refs.title: AI 2027 takeoff forecast
refs.finding: Median about one year from superhuman coder to superintelligence, with wide error margins.

refs.title: AI Futures Project, Q2.5 2026 Timelines Update
refs.finding: August 2026 superintelligence medians: Kokotajlo March 2029, Lifland July 2033.

refs.title: Vivalt et al., Employment Effects of a Guaranteed Income, NBER w32719
refs.finding: $1,000 a month for three years cut recipients' work by about 1.3 hours a week, with no clear gains in job quality.

refs.title: OpenResearch Unconditional Cash Study
refs.finding: Recipients spent more on basic needs and support for others; health effects were small.

refs.title: AI 2027: race ending
refs.finding: Displaced humans live on an incredibly luxurious universal basic income by 2029.

refs.title: Economics of Plan A (AI 2040)
refs.finding: Permit revenue paid as a citizen's dividend of about $1M per person a year in 2035.

limiters.limit: Gains accrue to capital owners while labor's share falls
limiters.evidence: Trammell and Korinek find labor share shrinks under full automation

ref.title: Economic Growth under Transformative AI
ref.finding: Labor share falls; wage effects ambiguous.

limiters.limit: Redistribution plans exist only as proposals
limiters.evidence: Altman's fund needs a constitutional amendment and is framed as a conversation starter

ref.title: Moore's Law for Everything
ref.finding: Proposal, not policy; phase-in only after GDP grows 50%.

enablers.action: Tax company equity and land and pay dividends to every adult
enablers.evidence: Altman's American Equity Fund design

ref.title: Moore's Law for Everything
ref.finding: 2.5% yearly tax on large company value and land, paid out to adults.

precedents.parallel: Alaska pays every resident an annual dividend from a resource-wealth fund, the closest real case of a windfall shared universally and permanently.
precedents.outcome: Studies find no effect on overall employment and a 1.8 point (17%) rise in part-time work, but the dividend is a partial supplement, not a living income, and the fund is far smaller than an AI-wealth fund would need to be.

ref.title: The Labor Market Impacts of Universal and Permanent Cash Transfers: Evidence from the Alaska Permanent Fund (Jones and Marinescu, NBER WP 24312)
ref.finding: A universal, permanent cash transfer did not significantly decrease aggregate employment; part-time work rose 1.8 percentage points.

precedents.parallel: Mechanisation raised output per worker sharply while gains went to capital, the scenario where labour's share collapses instead of wealth being shared.
precedents.outcome: Real wages stagnated for roughly half a century while output per worker expanded and the profit rate doubled; wages only tracked productivity after about 1850.

ref.title: Engel's Pause: A Pessimist's Guide to the British Industrial Revolution (Robert C. Allen, Oxford Economics WP 315)
ref.finding: In the first half of the 19th century the real wage stagnated while output per worker expanded and the profit share grew.

nodes.label: AI decisively speeds climate solutions
nodes.summary: AI in grids, buildings, industry, materials and fusion control could cut emissions far more than data centres add[1][2][3]; the IEA sees no momentum behind that cut, so marginal help is the likelier outcome[1].

refs.title: Energy and AI: AI and climate change (IEA, 2025)
refs.finding: Existing AI applications could cut about 1,400 Mt CO2 in 2035 under widespread adoption, about 3 to 4 times data centre emissions, but there is no momentum ensuring that adoption.

refs.title: Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning (Rolnick et al.)
refs.finding: Maps high-impact areas from power grids to disaster response where ML can help cut emissions and adapt.

refs.title: Accelerating fusion science through learned plasma control (Google DeepMind, 2022)
refs.finding: A single deep RL network controlled all 19 magnetic coils of the TCV tokamak and shaped the plasma.

refs.title: AI 2027 takeoff forecast
refs.finding: Median about one year from superhuman coder to superintelligence, with wide error margins.

refs.title: AI Futures Project, Q2.5 2026 Timelines Update
refs.finding: August 2026 superintelligence medians: Kokotajlo March 2029, Lifland July 2033.

limiters.evidence: IEA says aggregate impact could be marginal even by 2035 without enabling conditions

ref.title: Energy and AI: AI and climate change
ref.finding: Barriers: data access, infrastructure, skills, regulation.

limiters.evidence: IEA cites shifts from public transport to autonomous cars

ref.title: Energy and AI: AI and climate change
ref.finding: Rebound effects could offset savings.

enablers.action: Open energy data and digital infrastructure for AI optimisation
enablers.evidence: IEA names data access and infrastructure as the binding barriers

ref.title: Energy and AI: AI and climate change
ref.finding: Net impact depends on rollout, incentives and regulation.

enablers.action: AI control systems for fusion plasmas
enablers.evidence: RL controller ran on the TCV tokamak

ref.title: Accelerating fusion science through learned plasma control
ref.finding: One network controlled all 19 coils.

precedents.parallel: An earlier machine learning controller optimised a real energy system, the kind of grid and building gain AI climate claims rest on.
precedents.outcome: Google reported a 40% cut in cooling energy and a 15% cut in PUE overhead at its data centres, a real but narrow gain at the site level.

ref.title: DeepMind AI Reduces Google Data Centre Cooling Bill by 40% (Google DeepMind blog, 2016)
ref.finding: Cooling energy use cut by 40%; overall PUE overhead reduced by 15%.

precedents.parallel: The same company that cut cooling energy with machine learning then grew its compute, the rebound that makes AI's net climate effect uncertain.
precedents.outcome: Google's emissions rose 48% from 2019 to 14.3 million tonnes CO2e in 2023, mainly from data centre energy and supply chain, so efficiency gains were swamped by growth.

ref.title: Google datacenter emissions (The Register, 2 July 2024, reporting Google's 2024 Environmental Report)
ref.finding: Google's greenhouse gas emissions rose 48% since 2019, to 14.3 million tons CO2e in 2023, mainly from datacenter energy use.

precedents.parallel: A national digital programme promised energy savings through data and feedback, a precedent for software-led demand reduction.
precedents.outcome: The National Audit Office found costs escalating, installs costing 50% more than assumed in 2017, the programme late, and benefit forecasts more uncertain than costs, and the case kept shrinking (net benefit forecast cut from 6.7 to 5.7 billion pounds).

ref.title: Rolling out smart meters (National Audit Office, November 2018)
ref.finding: Installation in 2017 cost 50% more than assumed; forecast net benefits fell from 6.7bn pounds (2013) to 5.7bn pounds (2016).

nodes.label: Robot care lifts birth rates
nodes.summary: If robots took over much elder and child care, families might have more of the children they want; in one Norwegian simulation, more childcare raised children born by age 35 from 1.51 to 2.18[1]. Whether robots can deliver this is unproven; UN projections show fertility still low[2][3].

refs.title: Rindfuss, Guilkey, Morgan & Kravdal, Child-Care Availability and Fertility in Norway, Population and Development Review 2010
refs.finding: In simulations on Norwegian register data, moving from 0 to 60% childcare availability raised children born by age 35 from 1.51 to 2.18.

refs.title: World population projected to peak at 10.3 billion in mid-2080s (UN News, 2024)
refs.finding: More than half of countries are below 2.1 births per woman; nearly a fifth, including China, Italy, South Korea and Spain, are below 1.4.

refs.title: World Population Prospects (UN DESA)
refs.finding: The official UN population estimates and projections used as the baseline.

refs.title: AI 2027 takeoff forecast
refs.finding: Median about one year from superhuman coder to superintelligence, with wide error margins.

refs.title: AI Futures Project, Q2.5 2026 Timelines Update
refs.finding: August 2026 superintelligence medians: Kokotajlo March 2029, Lifland July 2033.

limiters.limit: Fertility keeps falling as incomes rise
limiters.evidence: Women have about one child fewer than around 1990

ref.title: UN News on WPP 2024
ref.finding: Global fertility down about one child per woman since 1990.

limiters.limit: No causal evidence linking AI or automation to higher births
limiters.evidence: No study found; the claim rests on argument only

ref.title: World Population Prospects
ref.finding: Baseline projections assume continued decline.

enablers.action: Use automation gains to fund childcare and care work
enablers.evidence: Speculative; no tested link

ref.title: UN News on WPP 2024
ref.finding: Ultra-low fertility is widespread.

precedents.parallel: Norway expanded subsidised childcare unevenly across municipalities, the cleanest test of whether cheaper, available care raises births.
precedents.outcome: Going from zero to 60% coverage raised completed fertility by about 0.5 to 0.7 children per woman, but this was human, state-funded care, not robots.

ref.title: Child-Care Availability and Fertility in Norway (Rindfuss, Guilkey, Morgan and Kravdal, Population and Development Review 36(4), 2010)
ref.finding: Increased availability of child care increases completed fertility, at every parity transition.

precedents.event: Household appliances and the baby boom
precedents.parallel: Labour-saving home technology was proposed as the cause of the US baby boom, the same mechanism as robots taking over care work.
precedents.outcome: Bailey and Collins found appliance ownership and electrification negatively correlated with fertility across counties and women, and the technology-shunning Amish had a baby boom too, so labour-saving machines did not clearly raise births.

ref.title: Did Improvements in Household Technology Cause the Baby Boom? (Bailey and Collins, NBER WP 14641; AEJ Macroeconomics 2011)
ref.finding: Appliance ownership and electrification were negatively correlated with fertility; the Amish experienced a large baby boom.

nodes.label: AI drives longevity escape velocity
nodes.summary: AI-accelerated biology could slow or repair aging faster than people age; one essay suggests lifespan could double to about 150[1]. One study found life expectancy rose only about 6.5 years since 1990 in the longest-lived populations[2].

refs.title: Machines of Loving Grace (Dario Amodei, 2024)
refs.finding: Suggests a compressed 21st century could double lifespan to about 150, presented as a possibility.

refs.title: Despite medical advances, life expectancy gains are slowing (UIC, 2024)
refs.finding: Olshansky et al. report life expectancy at birth rose only about 6.5 years since 1990 in the longest-lived populations and argue humans near a biological limit.

refs.title: The debate on the limits of human life extension continues (MPIDR, 2024)
refs.finding: Jdanov and Jasilionis argue optimistic scenarios should not be ignored.

refs.title: AI 2027 takeoff forecast
refs.finding: Median about one year from superhuman coder to superintelligence, with wide error margins.

refs.title: AI Futures Project, Q2.5 2026 Timelines Update
refs.finding: August 2026 superintelligence medians: Kokotajlo March 2029, Lifland July 2033.

limiters.limit: Aging, not disease, is the barrier
limiters.evidence: Olshansky: life expectancy gains slowing

ref.title: UIC release
ref.finding: About 6.5 years gained since 1990.

limiters.limit: AI drugs still need slow human trials
limiters.evidence: Insilico's AI-designed drug showed lung gains in 71 patients; investigators say larger trials are needed

ref.title: Insilico rentosertib Phase IIa press release
ref.finding: +98.4 mL FVC at 60 mg vs -20.3 mL placebo at 12 weeks; small sample.

enablers.action: AI target discovery and molecule design
enablers.evidence: First AI-discovered target and drug with Phase IIa efficacy signal

ref.title: Insilico rentosertib Phase IIa press release
ref.finding: Published in Nature Medicine June 2025.

precedents.parallel: Life expectancy in the leading country has risen steadily for 160 years, the baseline any longevity acceleration must beat.
precedents.outcome: Record female life expectancy rose about three months per year, and asserted ceilings were broken on average within 5 years of publication; this is steady linear gain, not open-ended escape velocity.

ref.title: The rise of maximum life expectancy (Our World in Data, updating Oeppen and Vaupel, Science 2002)
ref.finding: In the twentieth century, life expectancy in the leading country increased by three months every year; predicted maxima were broken within 5 years on average.

precedents.parallel: The 1971 National Cancer Act promised a decisive medical breakthrough through concentrated research, like AI-accelerated biology promises for aging.
precedents.outcome: Cancer mortality fell 27% from 1971 to 2019, mostly from less smoking, screening and better treatment, real progress that took nearly 50 years and fell far short of a cure.

ref.title: War on Cancer press release (American Cancer Society, November 2021, on a JAMA Oncology study)
ref.finding: Overall cancer mortality fell 27% since 1971 and 32% since the 1991 peak; declines driven by reduced smoking, screening and treatment.

nodes.label: Life extension only for the rich
nodes.summary: If life extension arrives, the rich may get it first and hold power far longer. The richest 1% of US men already outlive the poorest 1% by about 14.6 years[1], though living to 100 stays an outlier this century[2].

refs.title: The Association Between Income and Life Expectancy in the United States, 2001-2014 (Chetty et al., JAMA)
refs.finding: The richest 1% outlive the poorest 1% by about 14.6 years for men and 10.1 years for women.

refs.title: Despite medical advances, life expectancy gains are slowing (UIC, 2024)
refs.finding: Living to 100 remains an outlier outcome this century, which caps how large the divide can get.

refs.title: AI 2027 takeoff forecast
refs.finding: Median about one year from superhuman coder to superintelligence, with wide error margins.

refs.title: AI Futures Project, Q2.5 2026 Timelines Update
refs.finding: August 2026 superintelligence medians: Kokotajlo March 2029, Lifland July 2033.

nodes.control_note: Access is a pricing and coverage choice; the measured lifespan gap shows it is not handled today.

actions.action: Public coverage of proven longevity therapies
actions.evidence: Income gap in lifespan already 10 to 15 years in the US

ref.title: Chetty et al., JAMA 2016
ref.finding: 14.6 year gap for men.

actions.action: Term limits and age-independent tenure rules
actions.evidence: Speculative response to gerontocracy

ref.title: UIC release
ref.finding: Radical extension unlikely this century.

precedents.event: US income gap in life expectancy
precedents.parallel: Existing health gains already flow unequally by income, the mechanism that would let the rich get life extension first.
precedents.outcome: The richest 1% of men lived 14.6 years longer than the poorest 1% (10.1 years for women), and from 2001 to 2014 the top 5% gained 2.34 years versus 0.32 for the bottom 5%.

ref.title: The Association Between Income and Life Expectancy in the United States, 2001-2014 (Chetty et al., JAMA 2016)
ref.finding: Gap between richest and poorest 1%: 14.6 years for men, 10.1 for women; gains much larger at the top.

precedents.parallel: Life-saving combination therapy was widely used in rich countries while most patients in poor ones went without, a real case of a longevity technology rationed by wealth.
precedents.outcome: The WHO and UNAIDS 3 by 5 push reached 1.3 million people in low and middle income countries by end 2005, short of its 3 million target, as first-line prices fell 37% to 53%, so access in poor countries still lagged far behind rich ones.

ref.title: Global HIV therapy access tripled in past two years but challenges remain (UN News, March 2006)
ref.finding: Treatment access in low and middle income countries reached 1.3 million, short of the 3 million target; first-line drug prices fell 37 to 53 percent.

nodes.label: AI causes extinction or permanent disempowerment
nodes.summary: Advanced AI could kill or permanently sideline humanity through misalignment, a race or misuse[4]. In one forecasting tournament, superforecasters put AI extinction by 2100 at about 0.4% and domain experts at 3%[2]; critics call such numbers unreliable[3].

refs.title: Thousands of AI Authors on the Future of AI (Grace et al., 2024)
refs.finding: 38% to 51% of respondents gave at least a 10% chance of outcomes as bad as human extinction.

refs.title: The Extinction Tournament (Astral Codex Ten, on FRI's XPT)
refs.finding: Superforecasters gave about 0.4% chance of AI-caused extinction by 2100; domain experts about 3%.

refs.title: AI existential risk probabilities are too unreliable to inform policy (Narayanan and Kapoor)
refs.finding: No reference class, no validated models, and expert estimates vary by over 100 times.

refs.title: AI 2027: race ending
refs.finding: In mid 2030 Consensus-1 releases biological weapons and drones hunt survivors.

refs.title: AI 2027 takeoff forecast
refs.finding: Median about one year from superhuman coder to superintelligence, with wide error margins.

refs.title: AI Futures Project, Q2.5 2026 Timelines Update
refs.finding: August 2026 superintelligence medians: Kokotajlo March 2029, Lifland July 2033.

refs.title: AI 2040 (PDF)
refs.finding: PDF p.2 footnote 4: team estimates of literal AI-driven extinction vary between 10% and 30%.

nodes.control_note: No physical law forces it; it depends on development pace, alignment progress and governance, all human choices.

actions.action: Treat AI extinction risk as a global priority
actions.evidence: Signed statement by AI scientists and leaders

ref.title: Statement on AI Risk (CAIS)
ref.finding: Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside pandemics and nuclear war.

ref.finding: Four risk categories, each with mitigations.

ref.finding: Favor policies that help across a range of estimates.

precedents.parallel: Manhattan Project physicists seriously asked whether a new technology could end all life, the first formal extinction-risk analysis of a technology.
precedents.outcome: Calculations concluded ignition could not occur for bombs then considered, and later fusion data and the 1961 Tsar Bomba test confirmed it; the risk was assessed before use, but the estimate rested on theory without data at the time.

ref.title: Manhattan Project astrophysics (Physics Today, AIP)
ref.finding: The 1946 Konopinski, Marvin and Teller report found radiation losses always exceed fusion gains, so ignition could not occur.

precedents.event: Submarine B-59 in the Cuban Missile Crisis
precedents.parallel: A near-use of a nuclear torpedo under stress shows how a catastrophic technology can come close to use through one commander's misreading.
precedents.outcome: The captain ordered a nuclear torpedo prepared after mistaking US signalling for attack; Arkhipov calmed him and no order reached the torpedo officer; the account is only partly confirmed and was suppressed for about 40 years.

ref.title: The Underwater Cuban Missile Crisis at 60 (National Security Archive Briefing Book 808, 2022)
ref.finding: On 27 October 1962 Savitsky called for nuclear torpedo preparation; Arkhipov intervened; the launch order was never passed.

nodes.label: Automated AI research speeds itself up
nodes.summary: Once AI does AI research, progress could compound: AI 2027 has a 10x research multiplier by June 2027[1] and superintelligence about a year after the superhuman coder, with wide error margins[2]. Measured progress has run at roughly 65% to 75% of the predicted pace[3].

refs.title: AI 2027 (main scenario)

refs.title: AI 2027 takeoff forecast
refs.finding: Median about one year from superhuman coder to superintelligence, with wide error margins.

refs.finding: Quantitative progress ran at roughly 65% of the pace AI 2027 predicted, later revised toward 75%; most qualitative predictions on pace.

refs.title: 80,000 Hours #253, Daniel Kokotajlo
refs.finding: Kokotajlo's median for full automation of AI R&D is end of 2028.

limiters.evidence: Takeoff stages have 80% ranges spanning orders of magnitude.

ref.title: AI 2027 takeoff forecast
ref.finding: Median about one year from superhuman coder to superintelligence, with wide error margins.

ref.title: Grading AI 2027's 2025 Predictions
ref.finding: Quantitative progress ran at roughly 65% of the pace AI 2027 predicted, later revised toward 75%; most qualitative predictions on pace.

enablers.action: Devote about half of compute to automating AI research
enablers.evidence: Kokotajlo says roughly half of compute goes to this and wants it cut to about 10%.

ref.title: Senate Testimony Sept 2026
ref.finding: Kokotajlo urges far more transparency into the AI industry, redirecting compute away from automating AI research, and US government intervention to pace the frontier.

precedents.parallel: Computers helped design better computers for decades, a real feedback loop of technology improving its own research.
precedents.outcome: Keeping chip density doubling required more than 18 times as many researchers as in the early 1970s, so research productivity fell sharply instead of compounding; AI could differ if it replaces researchers rather than assisting them.

ref.title: Are Ideas Getting Harder to Find? (Bloom, Jones, Van Reenen and Webb, American Economic Review 2020)
ref.finding: Researchers needed to double chip density are more than 18 times the early 1970s number; research productivity is declining sharply.

precedents.event: Lighthill report and first AI winter
precedents.parallel: Early AI researchers forecast rapid progress toward general reasoning, as takeoff models do now.
precedents.outcome: The UK Science Research Council's report was extremely negative and led to sharp AI funding cuts in the UK and beyond; it shows forecasts of fast AI progress have stalled before, though today's systems are far more capable.

ref.title: Alan Bundy: The Lighthill Report on Artificial Intelligence (Institute for Advanced Studies in the Humanities, University of Edinburgh)
ref.finding: The 1973 report was extremely negative and led to a sharp cut in AI funding in the UK and worldwide, the AI Winter.

nodes.label: A rival state steals frontier model weights
nodes.summary: A state hacking team could copy a leading lab's model weights, erasing its lead and fuelling the race. The AI 2027 scenario sets this in February 2027[1], and 78% of 27 workshop respondents expected a state actor to steal frontier US weights before 2030[2].

refs.title: AI 2027 (main scenario)
refs.finding: China steals Agent-2's weights in February 2027; the active operation takes under two hours.

refs.title: AI 2027 security forecast
refs.finding: Models China exfiltrating Agent-2 weights in early 2027; 78% of 27 workshop respondents agreed a state actor will most likely steal frontier US weights before 2030.

nodes.control_note: Weight security levels up to WSL5 can stop exfiltration, but the forecast says no company will get there voluntarily.

actions.action: Reach SL5 weight security with government help
actions.evidence: 63% of workshop respondents agreed no company reaches SL5 without legal incentives and government help.

ref.title: AI 2027 security forecast
ref.finding: Models China exfiltrating Agent-2 weights in early 2027; 78% of 27 workshop respondents agreed a state actor will most likely steal frontier US weights before 2030.

actions.evidence: Kokotajlo's testimony calls for dramatically improved transparency.

ref.title: Senate Testimony Sept 2026
ref.finding: Kokotajlo urges far more transparency into the AI industry, redirecting compute away from automating AI research, and US government intervention to pace the frontier.
